$$ x^T\operatorname{sym}K(\xi)x\ge0\quad(x\in\mathbb R^3),\qquad \operatorname{sym}K=(K+K^T)/2. $$

$$ \tau=2\mu(\xi)D_0+\zeta(\xi)\theta I_3,\qquad \sigma=-pI_3+\tau,\qquad q=-K(\xi)\nabla T. $$

Under a rigid observer rotation $Q\in\operatorname{SO}(3)$, the tensor fields transform by $S^*=QSQ^T$; $\mu,\zeta$ are scalar state functions and $K^*=QKQ^T$. The closure is therefore form-invariant under those rotations. after.exact_statement:
Use a Cartesian inertial frame in Newtonian spacetime. At an event let $u$ be the fluid velocity, $T>0$ its temperature, $\rho>0$ its mass density, and $\xi=(\rho,T)$ its local state in a specified open set $\mathcal S\subset(0,\infty)^2$. The velocity gradient has components $L_{ij}=\partial_{x_j}u_i$; define the symmetric rate matrix $D=(L+L^T)/2$, its trace $\theta=\operatorname{tr}D$, and its trace-free part $D_0=D-\theta I_3/3$, where $I_3$ is the $3\times3$ identity matrix. For $A,B\in\mathbb R^{3\times3}$, use the Frobenius contraction $A:B=\sum_{i,j=1}^3A_{ij}B_{ij}$.

Adopt specified scalar state laws $\mu,\zeta:\mathcal S\to[0,\infty)$ and a specified conductivity matrix law $K:\mathcal S\to\mathbb R^{3\times3}$, with
$$ x^T\operatorname{sym}K(\xi)x\ge0\quad(x\in\mathbb R^3),\qquad \operatorname{sym}K:=(K+K^T)/2. $$
The conductivity law is tensor-valued and may be anisotropic; no restriction $K=kI_3$ is imposed. Define $\operatorname{Sym}(3):=\{D\in\mathbb R^{3\times3}:D^T=D\}$ and $\operatorname{SO}(3):=\{Q\in\mathbb R^{3\times3}:Q^TQ=I_3,\ \det Q=1\}$. At a fixed state, let $\mathcal A_\xi:\operatorname{Sym}(3)\to\operatorname{Sym}(3)$ assign the viscous stress to the symmetric rate matrix. Assume it is real-linear, meaning $\mathcal A_\xi(aD+bE)=a\mathcal A_\xi(D)+b\mathcal A_\xi(E)$ for all $a,b\in\mathbb R$ and $D,E\in\operatorname{Sym}(3)$, and equivariant in the sense $\mathcal A_\xi(QDQ^T)=Q\mathcal A_\xi(D)Q^T$ for every $Q\in\operatorname{SO}(3)$. Adopt
$$ \tau=\mathcal A_\xi(D)=2\mu(\xi)D_0+\zeta(\xi)\theta I_3,\qquad \sigma=-pI_3+\tau,\qquad q=-K(\xi)\nabla T. $$
Here $p$ is the scalar pressure field in the tension-positive convention: the traction on an outward unit normal $n$ is $\sigma n$. Under a rigid observer rotation $Q\in\operatorname{SO}(3)$, tensor fields transform by $S^*=QSQ^T$; $\mu,\zeta$ are scalar state functions and $K^*=QKQ^T$. The viscous response is isotropic in this proper-rotation sense, while the conductivity tensor transforms covariantly and may be anisotropic. The mathematical linear-isotropic classification identifies this stress form from the stated domain, codomain, linearity and equivariance hypotheses; it does not establish that any material adopts them.

In SI units, $D,\theta,D_0$ are in $\mathrm{s^{-1}}$, $\mu,\zeta$ in $\mathrm{Pa\,s}$, $K$ in $\mathrm{W\,m^{-1}\,K^{-1}}$, $q$ in $\mathrm{W\,m^{-2}}$, and $\sigma,\tau,p$ in $\mathrm{Pa}$. If the same stress is written $2\mu D+\lambda\theta I_3$, then $\lambda=\zeta-2\mu/3$; no nonnegativity of $\lambda$ is assumed. These specified constitutive functions are adopted model inputs, not measured coefficient values or consequences of balance laws.

before.quote:
Adopt a smooth single-component material continuum on a stated macroscopic regime in a Cartesian inertial chart. Let $\rho_0\in C^1(\overline B)$ be positive. On each swept material region, require $\rho,u,e,T,s,q,\sigma\in C^1$ and $b,r\in C^0$, with $\rho>0$ and $T>0$; the motion has the regularity and positive Jacobian in the preceding definition. A material subregion is $\chi_t(V)$ for a nonempty bounded open set $V\Subset B$ whose boundary is locally, after a rigid coordinate change, a $C^1$ graph with $V$ on one side; its boundary moves with the material velocity. The Jordan integral convention for such regions and their smooth images is the one in the mathematical interface identified below. The continuum approximation, its empirical regime, and the following balance laws are physical assumptions of this model, not deductions from the mathematical definition of a motion or from molecular mechanics.

Assume there are no mass sources and no diffusion relative to $u$. Adopt a positive reference mass density $\rho_0$, a positive current density $\rho$, a body-acceleration field $b$, a contact traction $t(t,x,n)=\sigma(t,x)n$ depending only on the local outward unit normal $n$, a $C^1$ Cauchy stress field $\sigma$, specific internal energy $e$, positive temperature $T$, specific entropy $s$, heat-flux vector $q$, and specific heat supply $r$, with the types and SI units fixed in the preceding definition. Contact traction and volume-force densities are continuous and locally bounded on the smooth material regions under consideration. There are no surface couples or intrinsic spin angular momentum; a micropolar or couple-stress model is outside this postulate.

For every such material subregion, adopt conservation of mass,

$$\int_{\chi_t(V)}\rho(t,x)\,dx=\int_V\rho_0(a)\,da.$$

In the same inertial chart, adopt the balances of linear and angular momentum,

$$\frac{d}{dt}\int_{\chi_t(V)}\rho u\,dx=\int_{\chi_t(V)}\rho b\,dx+\int_{\partial\chi_t(V)}t(t,x,n)\,dS,$$

$$\frac{d}{dt}\int_{\chi_t(V)}x\times(\rho u)\,dx=\int_{\chi_t(V)}x\times(\rho b)\,dx+\int_{\partial\chi_t(V)}x\times t(t,x,n)\,dS.$$

Adopt the total-energy balance and entropy inequality

$$\frac{d}{dt}\int_{\chi_t(V)}\rho\left(e+\frac{|u|^2}{2}\right)\,dx=\int_{\chi_t(V)}\rho b\cdot u\,dx+\int_{\partial\chi_t(V)}t(t,x,n)\cdot u\,dS-\int_{\partial\chi_t(V)}q\cdot n\,dS+\int_{\chi_t(V)}\rho r\,dx,$$

$$\frac{d}{dt}\int_{\chi_t(V)}\rho s\,dx\ge-\int_{\partial\chi_t(V)}\frac{q}{T}\cdot n\,dS+\int_{\chi_t(V)}\frac{\rho r}{T}\,dx.$$

The entropy flux uses the local material temperature at the heat-transfer point. A reservoir at a different temperature, a singular surface force, a shock, vacuum, or a weak solution requires a separately stated model and is not covered here. The postulate reports no experiment and asserts no measurement or universal claim that nature obeys these assumptions.

Use a smooth single-component, nonpolar fluid branch in a Cartesian inertial frame. Let $\mathcal U\subset(0,\infty)\times\mathbb R$ be an open state domain with coordinates $v$ and $s$, where $v$ is specific volume and $s$ is specific entropy. Adopt a specific internal-energy function $e:\mathcal U\to\mathbb R$ of class $C^2$, meaning that its coordinate partial derivatives through total order two exist and are continuous. At a state $(v,s)$, define the temperature and thermodynamic pressure by
$$ T(v,s)=\frac{\partial e}{\partial s}(v,s),\qquad p(v,s)=-\frac{\partial e}{\partial v}(v,s),\qquad \rho=\frac1v, $$
where each partial derivative holds the other state coordinate fixed. Assume the local material states lie in $\mathcal U$ and $T>0$. Local equilibrium here means that the fields $e,T,p$ at each event are assigned by these state functions of the local $v,s$.

In the physical SI interpretation, $v$ is in $\mathrm{m^3\,kg^{-1}}$, $s$ in $\mathrm{J\,kg^{-1}\,K^{-1}}$, $e$ in $\mathrm{J\,kg^{-1}}$, $T$ in $\mathrm K$, $p$ in $\mathrm{Pa}$, and $\rho$ in $\mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}$. Positivity of $e_{ss}$, global invertibility of $s\mapsto T$, convexity, and the dynamical entropy inequality are separate assumptions or postulates; none follows from this local equilibrium adoption. This closure is an additional physical model choice, not a consequence of global equilibrium thermodynamics.

Use a Cartesian inertial frame in Newtonian spacetime. At an event let $u$ be the fluid velocity, $T>0$ its temperature, $\rho>0$ its mass density, and $\xi=(\rho,T)$ its local state in a specified open set $\mathcal S\subset(0,\infty)^2$. The velocity gradient has components $L_{ij}=\partial_{x_j}u_i$; define the symmetric rate matrix $D=(L+L^T)/2$, its trace $\theta=\operatorname{tr}D$, and its trace-free part $D_0=D-\theta I_3/3$, where $I_3$ is the $3\times3$ identity matrix. For $A,B\in\mathbb R^{3\times3}$, use the Frobenius contraction $A:B=\sum_{i,j=1}^3A_{ij}B_{ij}$.

Adopt specified scalar state laws $\mu,\zeta:\mathcal S\to[0,\infty)$ and a specified conductivity matrix law $K:\mathcal S\to\mathbb R^{3\times3}$, with
$$ x^T\operatorname{sym}K(\xi)x\ge0\quad(x\in\mathbb R^3),\qquad \operatorname{sym}K=(K+K^T)/2. $$
Assume the viscous response at a fixed state is linear in $D$ and equivariant under proper rotations, and adopt
$$ \tau=2\mu(\xi)D_0+\zeta(\xi)\theta I_3,\qquad \sigma=-pI_3+\tau,\qquad q=-K(\xi)\nabla T. $$
Here $p$ is the scalar pressure field in the tension-positive convention: the traction on an outward unit normal $n$ is $\sigma n$. Under a rigid observer rotation $Q\in\operatorname{SO}(3)$, the tensor fields transform by $S^*=QSQ^T$; $\mu,\zeta$ are scalar state functions and $K^*=QKQ^T$. The closure is therefore form-invariant under those rotations. The mathematical linear-isotropic classification identifies this stress form from the stated linearity and equivariance hypotheses; it does not establish that any material adopts them.

In SI units, $D,\theta,D_0$ are in $\mathrm{s^{-1}}$, $\mu,\zeta$ in $\mathrm{Pa\,s}$, $K$ in $\mathrm{W\,m^{-1}\,K^{-1}}$, $q$ in $\mathrm{W\,m^{-2}}$, and $\sigma,\tau,p$ in $\mathrm{Pa}$. If the same stress is written $2\mu D+\lambda\theta I_3$, then $\lambda=\zeta-2\mu/3$; no nonnegativity of $\lambda$ is assumed. These specified constitutive functions are adopted model inputs, not measured coefficient values or consequences of balance laws.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$: every sequence $(X_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ of nonempty sets has a function $f$ with $f(n)\in X_n$ for every $n$. Let $U\subset(0,\infty)\times\mathbb R$ be open and let $e:U\to\mathbb R$ have continuous total derivatives through order two. For $(v,s)\in U$, $v$ is the specific-volume coordinate, $s$ the specific-entropy coordinate, and $e(v,s)$ the specific-energy value; set $T=e_s(v,s)$ and $p=-e_v(v,s)$, with each state partial derivative holding the other coordinate fixed.

Let $I\subset\mathbb R$ be a nonempty open interval. Let $B\subset\mathbb R^3$ be a nonempty bounded open set with $C^1$ boundary, meaning that near every boundary point it is the graph of a continuously differentiable function after a rigid coordinate change. Let $N\subset\mathbb R^3$ be open with $\overline B\subset N$, and let $\chi\in C^2(I\times N,\mathbb R^3)$, where $C^r$ means that all coordinate partial derivatives through total order $r$ exist and are continuous. For each $t\in I$, assume $\chi_t(a):=\chi(t,a)$ is a bijection from $N$ onto an open set with a $C^2$ inverse and $\det D_a\chi(t,a)>0$. Define $\Omega_t:=\chi_t(B)$, $\Omega:=\{(t,x):t\in I,\ x\in\Omega_t\}$, and $u(t,x):=\partial_t\chi(t,\chi_t^{-1}(x))$; this swept set $\Omega$ is open. For a scalar or vector field $f$ on $\Omega$, set $D_tf:=\partial_tf+\sum_{j=1}^3u_j\partial_{x_j}f$ componentwise. For each nonempty bounded open $C^1$ subdomain $V$ with $\overline V\subset B$, set $P_t:=\chi_t(V)$; here a $C^1$ domain is locally on one side of a $C^1$ boundary graph.

Let $\rho,v,s,T,p,q,r,b$ be fields on $\Omega$ with continuous first partial derivatives, with $\rho>0$, $(v,s)\in U$, $v=1/\rho$, $T=e_s(v,s)>0$, and $p=-e_v(v,s)$. Let $e$ on $\Omega$ denote the composition $e(v,s)$. Let $\sigma$ be a continuously differentiable $3\times3$ stress matrix field, let $\tau$ be a continuously differentiable $3\times3$ matrix field, and suppose $\sigma=-pI+\tau$, where $I$ is the $3\times3$ identity. For a scalar field $h$, define $(\nabla h)_i:=\partial_{x_i}h$; define $L:=\nabla u$ by $L_{ij}:=\partial_{x_j}u_i$, $D:=(L+L^T)/2$, and $\theta:=\operatorname{tr}D=\sum_{i=1}^3\partial_{x_i}u_i$. Define $A:B:=\sum_{i,j=1}^3A_{ij}B_{ij}$ for matrices, $\operatorname{div}q:=\sum_i\partial_{x_i}q_i$, and $\operatorname{div}(q/T)$ componentwise. Put $a_m:=\partial_tu+(u\cdot\nabla)u$, $k:=|u|^2/2$, and $E:=e+k$. The fields $u,q,b$ are vector-valued and $r$ is scalar-valued.

Assume there is a contact traction $t_c(t,y,n)\in\mathbb R^3$ depending on a surface only through its point $y$ and outward unit normal $n\in S^2$, continuous in $(y,n)$ and uniformly bounded near each point. Assume its local force balance $\int_{\partial P}t_c(t,y,\nu_P(y))\,dS_y+\int_P\rho(t,y)(b(t,y)-a_m(t,y))\,dy=0$ for every nonempty bounded open $C^1$ subdomain $P$ whose closure is compactly contained in $\Omega_t$. Surface integrals use Euclidean surface measure with chart area density $\sqrt{\det(DX^TDX)}$. Suppose the unique Cauchy stress supplied by this contact balance satisfies $t_c(t,y,n)=\sigma(t,y)n$ and has the stated $C^1$ regularity; the contact result alone does not imply that regularity.

Assume the pointwise continuity equation $\partial_t\rho+\operatorname{div}(\rho u)=0$ and, for every such material subdomain $V$ and every $t\in I$, the integral balances
$$\frac{d}{dt}\int_{P_t}\rho u\,dx=\int_{P_t}\rho b\,dx+\int_{\partial P_t}\sigma\nu\,dS,$$
$$\frac{d}{dt}\int_{P_t}x\times(\rho u)\,dx=\int_{P_t}x\times(\rho b)\,dx+\int_{\partial P_t}x\times(\sigma\nu)\,dS,$$
$$\frac{d}{dt}\int_{P_t}\rho E\,dx=\int_{P_t}\rho b\cdot u\,dx+\int_{\partial P_t}(\sigma\nu)\cdot u\,dS-\int_{\partial P_t}q\cdot\nu\,dS+\int_{P_t}\rho r\,dx,$$
where $\nu$ is the outward unit normal, $\times$ is the ordinary vector cross product, and all fields are continuous up to the swept closures. The angular-momentum balance gives $\sigma=\sigma^T$, and the local internal-energy equation supplied by these hypotheses is $\rho D_te=\sigma:D-\operatorname{div}q+\rho r$. Define the entropy residual $\mathcal G:=\rho D_ts+\operatorname{div}(q/T)-\rho r/T$. Then
$$\mathcal G=\frac{\tau:D}{T}-\frac{q\cdot\nabla T}{T^2}.$$
At any state with $e_{ss}>0$, a unique local $C^1$ branch $s(v,T)$ satisfies $e_s(v,s(v,T))=T$; the local Helmholtz function $a(v,T):=e(v,s(v,T))-Ts(v,T)$ then satisfies $a_T=-s$ and $a_v=-p$. The entropy identity does not assert $\mathcal G\ge0$ and makes no empirical claim. In the physical SI interpretation, $\rho$ is in $\mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}$, $u$ in $\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, $b$ in $\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$, $v$ in $\mathrm{m^3\,kg^{-1}}$, $e,k,E$ in $\mathrm{J\,kg^{-1}}$, $s$ in $\mathrm{J\,kg^{-1}\,K^{-1}}$, $T$ in $\mathrm K$, $p,\sigma,\tau,t_c$ in $\mathrm{Pa}$, $q$ in $\mathrm{W\,m^{-2}}$, and $r$ in $\mathrm{W\,kg^{-1}}$.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$: every sequence of nonempty sets admits a choice function. At a fixed state, let $\mu,\lambda\in\mathbb R$, $K\in\mathbb R^{3\times3}$, $T>0$, $g\in\mathbb R^3$, and let $D\in\mathbb R^{3\times3}$ be symmetric. Put
$$\theta:=\operatorname{tr}D=\sum_{i=1}^3D_{ii},\qquad D_0:=D-\frac{\theta}{3}I,\qquad \zeta:=\lambda+\frac{2\mu}{3},\qquad \operatorname{sym}K:=\frac{K+K^T}{2},$$

$$\mathcal Q(D,g,T):=\frac{\tau:D}{T}-\frac{q\cdot g}{T^2}, \qquad \tau:D:=\sum_{i,j=1}^3\tau_{ij}D_{ij}.$$

Let $I\subset\mathbb R$ be an open time interval and $\Omega\subset I\times\mathbb R^3$ open. A smooth constant-density incompressible Newtonian branch has a constant $\rho_0>0$ in $\mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}$, a constant dynamic shear viscosity $\mu\ge0$ in $\mathrm{Pa\,s}$, a velocity field $u\in C^2(\Omega,\mathbb R^3)$, and a pressure multiplier $p\in C^1(\Omega,\mathbb R)$. Define $L_{ij}=\partial_{x_j}u_i$, $D=(L+L^T)/2$, and $D_tu=\partial_tu+(u\cdot\nabla)u$. The branch is specified by
$$ \rho=\rho_0,\qquad \operatorname{div}u=0,\qquad \sigma=-pI_3+2\mu D,\qquad \rho_0D_tu=\operatorname{div}\sigma, $$
where $(\operatorname{div}\sigma)_i=\sum_{j=1}^3\partial_{x_j}\sigma_{ij}$. Equivalently, for constant $\mu$, its momentum equation is
$$ \rho_0D_tu+\nabla p=\mu\Delta u,\qquad \Delta u_i=\sum_{j=1}^3\partial_{x_jx_j}u_i. $$
Indeed, $\operatorname{div}(2\mu D)=\mu\Delta u+\mu\nabla(\operatorname{div}u)=\mu\Delta u$. This is the incompressible specialization of the adopted Newtonian closure: $\theta=\operatorname{div}u=0$ implies $D_0=D$, so the bulk-viscosity and Fourier-flux terms do not enter this mechanical equation. The pressure is a constraint multiplier and is not identified with a compressible equation-of-state pressure. Define the kinematic viscosity $\nu=\mu/\rho_0$, in $\mathrm{m^2\,s^{-1}}$. Boundary and initial data are not part of this definition, and the item asserts no solution existence.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, meaning that every countable sequence of nonempty sets has a choice function. Let $I\subset\mathbb R$ be a nonempty open interval containing $0$, let $B\subset\mathbb R^3$ be a nonempty bounded open set with $C^1$ boundary, and let $U\subset\mathbb R^3$ be open with $\overline B\subset U$. Let $\chi\in C^2(I\times U;\mathbb R^3)$ have slices $\chi_t:U\to\chi_t(U)$ that are orientation-preserving bijections with $C^2$ inverses and $\det D_a\chi(t,a)>0$. Put $\Omega_t=\chi_t(B)$, $\mathcal W=\{(t,x):t\in I,\ x\in\chi_t(U)\}$, $u(t,x)=\partial_t\chi(t,\chi_t^{-1}(x))$ on $\mathcal W$, $D_t=\partial_t+u\cdot\nabla_x$, $k=|u|^2/2$, and $E=e+k$. For each nonempty bounded $C^1$ domain $V\Subset B$ with compact closure in $B$, set $P_t=\chi_t(V)$. A bounded $C^1$ domain means a nonempty bounded open set locally on one side of a $C^1$ boundary graph; its unit normal $\nu$ points outward. All fields below are continuously differentiable on open neighborhoods of the swept closures $\{(t,x):t\in I,\ x\in\chi_t(\overline V)\}$ for each such $V$, and $\rho>0$: let $\rho$ be scalar, $u,b,q$ vector-valued, $e,r$ scalar, and $\sigma$ a $3\times3$ matrix field. Define $L=\nabla_xu$ by $L_{ij}=\partial_{x_j}u_i$, $A:B=\sum_{i,j}A_{ij}B_{ij}$, $\operatorname{div}v=\sum_j\partial_{x_j}v_j$ for vector fields $v$, and $(\operatorname{div}M)_i=\sum_j\partial_{x_j}M_{ij}$ for $3\times3$ fields $M$; define $(u\otimes u)_{ij}=u_i u_j$. Interpret $\rho,u,b,\sigma,q,e,r$ as mass density, velocity, body acceleration, Cauchy stress, heat flux, specific internal energy, and specific energy supply rate. All cross products are the standard right-handed product in $\mathbb R^3$. In SI, $x,a$ are in metres, $t$ in seconds, $\rho$ in $\mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}$, $u$ in $\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, $b$ in $\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$, $\sigma$ in pascals, $q$ in $\mathrm{W\,m^{-2}}$, $e$ in $\mathrm{J\,kg^{-1}}$, and $r$ in $\mathrm{W\,kg^{-1}}$. The traction is $\sigma\nu$ on the outward boundary normal, and $q\cdot\nu$ is outward heat flux; thus $-\int_{\partial P_t}q\cdot\nu\,dS$ is heat entering $P_t$. Surface integrals use the chart measure with area density $\sqrt{\det(DX^TDX)}$.

Assume the continuity equation $\partial_t\rho+\operatorname{div}(\rho u)=0$, and suppose the following integral balances hold for every such $V$ and every $t\in I$:
$$\frac{d}{dt}\int_{P_t}\rho u\,dx=\int_{P_t}\rho b\,dx+\int_{\partial P_t}\sigma\nu\,dS,$$
$$\frac{d}{dt}\int_{P_t}x\times(\rho u)\,dx=\int_{P_t}x\times(\rho b)\,dx+\int_{\partial P_t}x\times(\sigma\nu)\,dS,$$
$$\frac{d}{dt}\int_{P_t}\rho E\,dx=\int_{P_t}\rho b\cdot u\,dx+\int_{\partial P_t}(\sigma\nu)\cdot u\,dS-\int_{\partial P_t}q\cdot\nu\,dS+\int_{P_t}\rho r\,dx.$$
Assume the Cauchy contact result supplies the pointwise traction $\tau=\sigma\nu$, and that its unique matrix field $\sigma$ has the stated $C^1$ regularity; the pointwise contact result alone does not imply this regularity. Then the linear momentum balance is equivalent to
$$\partial_t(\rho u)+\operatorname{div}(\rho u\otimes u-\sigma)=\rho b.$$
Together with the angular-momentum balance, it is equivalent to this momentum equation and $\sigma=\sigma^T$. The kinetic-energy identity is
$$\partial_t(\rho k)+\operatorname{div}(\rho k u-\sigma^T u)=\rho b\cdot u-\sigma:L.$$
The total-energy balance is equivalent to
$$\partial_t(\rho E)+\operatorname{div}(\rho E u-\sigma^T u+q)=\rho b\cdot u+\rho r,$$
and, after subtracting the kinetic identity, to the internal-energy equation
$$\partial_t(\rho e)+\operatorname{div}(\rho e u+q)=\sigma:L+\rho r,\qquad \rho D_t e=\sigma:L-\operatorname{div}q+\rho r.$$
Conversely, adding the kinetic and internal-energy equations recovers the total-energy equation. These are conditional identities for smooth fields; no balance postulate is derived.

Let $I\subset\mathbb R$ be a nonempty open interval containing $0$, let $B\subset\mathbb R^3$ be a nonempty bounded open set with $C^1$ boundary, and let $U\subset\mathbb R^3$ be open with $\overline B\subset U$. Let $\chi\in C^2(I\times U;\mathbb R^3)$ have slices $\chi_t:U\to\chi_t(U)$ that are orientation-preserving bijections with $C^2$ inverses and $\det D_a\chi(t,a)>0$. Put $\Omega_t=\chi_t(B)$, $\mathcal W=\{(t,x):t\in I,\ x\in\chi_t(U)\}$, $u(t,x)=\partial_t\chi(t,\chi_t^{-1}(x))$ on $\mathcal W$, $D_t=\partial_t+u\cdot\nabla_x$, $k=|u|^2/2$, and $E=e+k$. For each nonempty bounded $C^1$ domain $V\Subset B$ with compact closure in $B$, set $P_t=\chi_t(V)$. A bounded $C^1$ domain means a nonempty bounded open set locally on one side of a $C^1$ boundary graph; its unit normal $\nu$ points outward. All fields below are continuously differentiable on open neighborhoods of the swept closures $\{(t,x):t\in I,\ x\in\chi_t(\overline V)\}$ for each such $V$, and $\rho>0$: let $\rho$ be scalar, $u,b,q$ vector-valued, $e,r$ scalar, and $\sigma$ a $3\times3$ matrix field. Define $L=\nabla_xu$ by $L_{ij}=\partial_{x_j}u_i$, $A:B=\sum_{i,j}A_{ij}B_{ij}$, $\operatorname{div}v=\sum_j\partial_{x_j}v_j$ for vector fields $v$, and $(\operatorname{div}M)_i=\sum_j\partial_{x_j}M_{ij}$ for $3\times3$ fields $M$; define $(u\otimes u)_{ij}=u_i u_j$. Interpret $\rho,u,b,\sigma,q,e,r$ as mass density, velocity, body acceleration, Cauchy stress, heat flux, specific internal energy, and specific energy supply rate. All cross products are the standard right-handed product in $\mathbb R^3$. In SI, $x,a$ are in metres, $t$ in seconds, $\rho$ in $\mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}$, $u$ in $\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, $b$ in $\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$, $\sigma$ in pascals, $q$ in $\mathrm{W\,m^{-2}}$, $e$ in $\mathrm{J\,kg^{-1}}$, and $r$ in $\mathrm{W\,kg^{-1}}$. The traction is $\sigma\nu$ on the outward boundary normal, and $q\cdot\nu$ is outward heat flux; thus $-\int_{\partial P_t}q\cdot\nu\,dS$ is heat entering $P_t$. Surface integrals use the chart measure with area density $\sqrt{\det(DX^TDX)}$.

Assume the continuity equation $\partial_t\rho+\operatorname{div}(\rho u)=0$, and suppose the following integral balances hold for every such $V$ and every $t\in I$:
$$\frac{d}{dt}\int_{P_t}\rho u\,dx=\int_{P_t}\rho b\,dx+\int_{\partial P_t}\sigma\nu\,dS,$$
$$\frac{d}{dt}\int_{P_t}x\times(\rho u)\,dx=\int_{P_t}x\times(\rho b)\,dx+\int_{\partial P_t}x\times(\sigma\nu)\,dS,$$
$$\frac{d}{dt}\int_{P_t}\rho E\,dx=\int_{P_t}\rho b\cdot u\,dx+\int_{\partial P_t}(\sigma\nu)\cdot u\,dS-\int_{\partial P_t}q\cdot\nu\,dS+\int_{P_t}\rho r\,dx.$$
Assume the Cauchy contact result supplies the pointwise traction $\tau=\sigma\nu$, and that its unique matrix field $\sigma$ has the stated $C^1$ regularity; the pointwise contact result alone does not imply this regularity. Then the linear momentum balance is equivalent to
$$\partial_t(\rho u)+\operatorname{div}(\rho u\otimes u-\sigma)=\rho b.$$
Together with the angular-momentum balance, it is equivalent to this momentum equation and $\sigma=\sigma^T$. The kinetic-energy identity is
$$\partial_t(\rho k)+\operatorname{div}(\rho k u-\sigma^T u)=\rho b\cdot u-\sigma:L.$$
The total-energy balance is equivalent to
$$\partial_t(\rho E)+\operatorname{div}(\rho E u-\sigma^T u+q)=\rho b\cdot u+\rho r,$$
and, after subtracting the kinetic identity, to the internal-energy equation
$$\partial_t(\rho e)+\operatorname{div}(\rho e u+q)=\sigma:L+\rho r,\qquad \rho D_t e=\sigma:L-\operatorname{div}q+\rho r.$$
Conversely, adding the kinetic and internal-energy equations recovers the total-energy equation. These are conditional identities for smooth fields; no balance postulate is derived.

Let $I\subset\mathbb R$ be a nonempty open time interval and $\Omega\subset I\times\mathbb R^3$ a nonempty open domain for the model fields. Let $e\in C^2(\mathcal U)$ be the local specific-energy relation on an open $\mathcal U\subset(0,\infty)\times\mathbb R$, with state coordinates $(v,s)$, $T=e_s$, and $p=-e_v$; each state partial derivative holds the other coordinate fixed. Fix $(v_b,s_b)\in\mathcal U$ with $T_b>0$ and $e_{ss}(v_b,s_b)>0$, set $\rho_b=1/v_b$, and take the barotropic pressure law to be $P(\rho)=p(1/\rho,s_b)$ near $\rho_b$. This is the fixed-entropy restriction of the adopted local state relation. The smooth barotropic Euler model is linearized about the uniform rest state $(\rho,u)=(\rho_b,0)$. For $C^2$ perturbation fields $\delta\rho:I\times\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R$ and $w:I\times\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R^3$, the first variation at $\varepsilon=0$ after $\rho=\rho_b+\varepsilon\delta\rho$, $u=\varepsilon w$ is
$$ \partial_t\delta\rho+\rho_b\operatorname{div}w=0,\qquad \rho_b\partial_tw+P'(\rho_b)\nabla\delta\rho=0,\qquad \partial_{tt}\delta\rho=c_s^2\Delta\delta\rho, \quad c_s^2=P'(\rho_b)=v_b^2e_{vv}(v_b,s_b). $$
The sign of $c_s^2$ is not assumed in the base model. If $c_s^2>0$, define $c_s=\sqrt{c_s^2}$. For every nonzero $k\in\mathbb R^3$, with $\omega=c_s|k|$, the fields
$$ \delta\rho=A\cos(k\cdot x-\omega t),\qquad w=\frac{\omega A}{\rho_b|k|^2}k\cos(k\cdot x-\omega t) $$
solve the first-variation system for every real amplitude $A$. They are exact solutions of the linearized equations, not finite-amplitude approximations with an automatic error or lifespan bound. No empirical value of $c_s$ is asserted.

Assume the viscous response at a fixed state is linear in $D$ and equivariant under proper rotations, and adopt
$$ \tau=2\mu(\xi)D_0+\zeta(\xi)\theta I_3,\qquad \sigma=-pI_3+\tau,\qquad q=-K(\xi)\nabla T. $$

Let a pressure field have continuous first spatial partial derivatives. Write $(D_xu)_{ij}=\partial_{x_j}u_i$, $D=(D_xu+(D_xu)^{\mathsf T})/2$, $\operatorname{div}u=\sum_{j=1}^3\partial_{x_j}u_j$, and let $\Delta u$ act componentwise. Fix constants $\rho_0>0$, $\mu>0$, $U>0$, $L>0$, and $c>0$, and define $\nu=\mu/\rho_0$, $\operatorname{Re}=UL/\nu$, and $\operatorname{Ma}=U/c$.

$$\partial_\Theta u^*+(u^*\cdot\nabla_X)u^*=-\nabla_Xp_{\mathrm{inc}}^*+\operatorname{Re}^{-1}\Delta_Xu^*,\qquad \operatorname{div}_Xu^*=0.$$

Write $I_3$ for the $3\times3$ identity matrix and set $\operatorname{SO}(3):=\{Q\in\mathbb R^{3\times3}:Q^{\mathsf T}Q=I_3,\ \det Q=1\}$. Inertial-chart changes have the form $t'=t+t_0$, $x'=Qx+vt+a$, where $t_0$ is a constant time translation in seconds, $a\in\mathbb R^3$ is a constant spatial translation in metres, $v\in\mathbb R^3$ is a constant relative velocity in metres per second, and $Q\in\operatorname{SO}(3)$ is constant. All derivatives below are Cartesian derivatives in this fixed chart; the positive coordinate rescaling defined below is not a change of observer.

For a scalar field $f$, $\nabla_x f=(\partial_{x_1}f,\partial_{x_2}f,\partial_{x_3}f)$.

For a vector field $u=(u_i)$, define $D_xu,D:I\times\Omega\to\mathbb R^{3\times3}$, $\operatorname{div}_xu:I\times\Omega\to\mathbb R$, and $\Delta_xu,D_tu:I\times\Omega\to\mathbb R^3$ by $(D_xu)_{ij}=\partial_{x_j}u_i$, $D=(D_xu+(D_xu)^{\mathsf T})/2$, $\operatorname{div}_xu=\sum_{j=1}^3\partial_{x_j}u_j$, $(\Delta_xu)_i=\sum_{j=1}^3\partial_{x_jx_j}u_i$, and $D_tu=\partial_tu+(u\cdot\nabla_x)u$. In SI units, $[u]=[U]=[c]=\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, $[x]=[L]=\mathrm m$, $[\rho]=[\rho_0]=\mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}$, $[p]=[P(\rho)]=[p_{\mathrm{ref}}]=[\sigma]=\mathrm{Pa}$, $[\mu]=\mathrm{Pa\,s}$, $[\nu]=\mathrm{m^2\,s^{-1}}$, and $[\Theta]=[X]=[\operatorname{Re}]=[\operatorname{Ma}]=1$; thus the two ratios are dimensionless.

Define the dimensionless coordinates and their domains by
$$\Theta=\frac{Ut}{L},\qquad X=\frac{x}{L},\qquad I^*=\left\{\frac{Ut}{L}:t\in I\right\},\qquad \Omega^*=\left\{\frac{x}{L}:x\in\Omega\right\}.$$
The map $\Phi:I\times\Omega\to I^*\times\Omega^*$, $\Phi(t,x)=(Ut/L,x/L)$, is bijective with inverse $\Phi^{-1}(\Theta,X)=(L\Theta/U,LX)$. The corresponding $X$-derivatives are defined by the same component formulas.

In the first, force-free branch, let $u:I\times\Omega\to\mathbb R^3$ have continuous first time partial derivatives and continuous first and second spatial partial derivatives, and let the pressure field $p:I\times\Omega\to\mathbb R$ be continuous with continuous first spatial partial derivatives. Let the density field $\rho:I\times\Omega\to(0,\infty)$ be the constant $\rho_0$. Assume $\operatorname{div}_xu=0$ and the selected incompressible Newtonian equations
$$\sigma=-pI_3+2\mu D,\qquad \rho_0D_tu=\operatorname{div}_x\sigma,\qquad (\operatorname{div}_x\sigma)_i=\sum_{j=1}^3\partial_{x_j}\sigma_{ij},$$
where $\sigma:I\times\Omega\to\mathbb R^{3\times3}$ is stress, $p$ is the constraint multiplier, not an equation-of-state pressure, and the tension-positive stress convention identifies $\sigma n$ as traction on an outward unit normal $n$. Define $u^*:I^*\times\Omega^*\to\mathbb R^3$ and $p_{\mathrm{inc}}^*:I^*\times\Omega^*\to\mathbb R$ by
$$u^*(\Theta,X)=\frac{1}{U}u\bigl(\Phi^{-1}(\Theta,X)\bigr),\qquad p_{\mathrm{inc}}^*(\Theta,X)=\frac{p\bigl(\Phi^{-1}(\Theta,X)\bigr)-p_{\mathrm{ref}}}{\rho_0U^2},$$
for a constant reference pressure $p_{\mathrm{ref}}\in\mathbb R$. The scaled fields are dimensionless, $[u^*]=[p_{\mathrm{inc}}^*]=1$, and have respectively the same stated velocity and spatial-pressure regularity. Equivalently, $u(t,x)=Uu^*(\Theta,X)$ and $p(t,x)=p_{\mathrm{ref}}+\rho_0U^2p_{\mathrm{inc}}^*(\Theta,X)$. The governing equations become exactly
$$\partial_\Theta u^*+(u^*\cdot\nabla_X)u^*=-\nabla_Xp_{\mathrm{inc}}^*+\operatorname{Re}^{-1}\Delta_Xu^*,\qquad \operatorname{div}_Xu^*=0.$$

In the separate, unforced barotropic Euler branch, let $\rho:I\times\Omega\to(0,\infty)$ and $u:I\times\Omega\to\mathbb R^3$ have continuous partial derivatives through total order two, and let $P:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ have continuous derivatives through order two, with pressure measured in pascals. Set the potential $V:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ to the zero function. Assume
$$\partial_t\rho+\operatorname{div}_x(\rho u)=0,\qquad \rho D_tu+\nabla_xP(\rho)=0,$$
and assume at the chosen reference density that $P'(\rho_0)=c^2>0$, where $[P'(\rho_0)]=\mathrm{m^2\,s^{-2}}$. Define $\rho^*:I^*\times\Omega^*\to(0,\infty)$, $u^*:I^*\times\Omega^*\to\mathbb R^3$, and $p_{\mathrm{bar}}^*:I^*\times\Omega^*\to\mathbb R$ by
$$\rho^*(\Theta,X)=\frac{\rho\bigl(\Phi^{-1}(\Theta,X)\bigr)}{\rho_0},\qquad u^*(\Theta,X)=\frac{u\bigl(\Phi^{-1}(\Theta,X)\bigr)}{U},\qquad p_{\mathrm{bar}}^*(\Theta,X)=\frac{P\bigl(\rho_0\rho^*(\Theta,X)\bigr)-P(\rho_0)}{\rho_0c^2}.$$
These scaled fields are dimensionless, $[\rho^*]=[u^*]=[p_{\mathrm{bar}}^*]=1$, and have continuous partial derivatives through order two. The exact transformed mass and momentum equations are
$$\partial_\Theta\rho^*+\operatorname{div}_X(\rho^*u^*)=0,\qquad \partial_\Theta u^*+(u^*\cdot\nabla_X)u^*=-\operatorname{Ma}^{-2}(\rho^*)^{-1}\nabla_Xp_{\mathrm{bar}}^*.$$

Initial values are data on a slice $t=t_0\in I$; boundary values are data on a chosen subset $\Gamma\subseteq I\times\partial\Omega$ wherever the relevant traces exist. Extend $\Phi$ to $I\times\mathbb R^3$ by the same coordinate formula and put $S^*=\Phi(S)$ for any such initial or boundary data set $S$. If $g_u:S\to\mathbb R^3$, $g_p:S\to\mathbb R$, $g_\rho:S\to(0,\infty)$, and $g_P:S\to\mathbb R$ are prescribed velocity, incompressible pressure-multiplier, density, and barotropic-pressure data, respectively, define $g_u^*:S^*\to\mathbb R^3$, $g_{p,\mathrm{inc}}^*:S^*\to\mathbb R$, $g_\rho^*:S^*\to(0,\infty)$, and $g_{P,\mathrm{bar}}^*:S^*\to\mathbb R$ by
$$g_u^*(\Phi(t,x))=\frac{g_u(t,x)}{U},\qquad g_{p,\mathrm{inc}}^*(\Phi(t,x))=\frac{g_p(t,x)-p_{\mathrm{ref}}}{\rho_0U^2},\qquad g_\rho^*(\Phi(t,x))=\frac{g_\rho(t,x)}{\rho_0},\qquad g_{P,\mathrm{bar}}^*(\Phi(t,x))=\frac{g_P(t,x)-P(\rho_0)}{\rho_0c^2}.$$
Here $g_p$ and $g_{p,\mathrm{inc}}^*$ apply to the incompressible branch, while $g_\rho$ and $g_P$ apply to the barotropic branch; a prescribed wall-velocity field uses the same velocity map. The spatial dilation takes each boundary trace portion to its image and preserves its outward Euclidean unit normal wherever that normal exists. For momentum density $m:I\times\Omega\to\mathbb R^3$, with units $\mathrm{kg\,m^{-2}\,s^{-1}}$, define $m^*:I^*\times\Omega^*\to\mathbb R^3$ by
$$m^*(\Phi(t,x))=\frac{m(t,x)}{\rho_0U}=\rho^*(\Phi(t,x))u^*(\Phi(t,x)),$$
where $\rho^*(\Phi(t,x))=1$ in the constant-density branch. Thus $m^*$ is dimensionless. Whenever the integrals exist, total momentum on corresponding spatial regions $A\subseteq\Omega$ and $A^*=A/L$ satisfies
$$\int_A \rho u\,dx=\rho_0UL^3\int_{A^*}\rho^*u^*\,dX.$$
The total momentum has units $\mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-1}}$, as does its scale factor $\rho_0UL^3$.
Because $\Phi$ and each field-value scaling are invertible, these formulas carry any already-compatible initial or boundary data to the corresponding scaled data; they assert no compatibility or solvability beyond the selected model and its separate data assumptions. Thermal evolution and heat-flux scaling are not part of this calculation. The coefficient identities do not assert an incompressible or inviscid limit, an error bound, uniqueness, identical solutions for different geometries or rescaled data, or a turbulence threshold. They are conditional predictions of the adopted model formulations and are not experimental observations or proof that either model describes a material.

The channel flux per unit width is in square metres per second and the pipe volume flux is in cubic metres per second.

The velocity gradient has components $L_{ij}=\partial_{x_j}u_i$; define the symmetric rate matrix $D=(L+L^T)/2$, its trace $\theta=\operatorname{tr}D$, and its trace-free part $D_0=D-\theta I_3/3$, where $I_3$ is the $3\times3$ identity matrix. For $A,B\in\mathbb R^{3\times3}$, use the Frobenius contraction $A:B=\sum_{i,j=1}^3A_{ij}B_{ij}$.

Adopt specified scalar state laws $\mu,\zeta:\mathcal S\to[0,\infty)$ and a specified conductivity matrix law $K:\mathcal S\to\mathbb R^{3\times3}$, with
$$ x^T\operatorname{sym}K(\xi)x\ge0\quad(x\in\mathbb R^3),\qquad \operatorname{sym}K=(K+K^T)/2. $$
Assume the viscous response at a fixed state is linear in $D$ and equivariant under proper rotations, and adopt
$$ \tau=2\mu(\xi)D_0+\zeta(\xi)\theta I_3,\qquad \sigma=-pI_3+\tau,\qquad q=-K(\xi)\nabla T. $$
Here $p$ is the scalar pressure field in the tension-positive convention: the traction on an outward unit normal $n$ is $\sigma n$. Under a rigid observer rotation $Q\in\operatorname{SO}(3)$, the tensor fields transform by $S^*=QSQ^T$; $\mu,\zeta$ are scalar state functions and $K^*=QKQ^T$. The closure is therefore form-invariant under those rotations. The mathematical linear-isotropic classification identifies this stress form from the stated linearity and equivariance hypotheses; it does not establish that any material adopts them.

In SI units, $D,\theta,D_0$ are in $\mathrm{s^{-1}}$, $\mu,\zeta$ in $\mathrm{Pa\,s}$, $K$ in $\mathrm{W\,m^{-1}\,K^{-1}}$, $q$ in $\mathrm{W\,m^{-2}}$, and $\sigma,\tau,p$ in $\mathrm{Pa}$. Let $I\subset\mathbb R$ be an open time interval and $\Omega\subset I\times\mathbb R^3$ open. A smooth constant-density incompressible Newtonian branch has a constant $\rho_0>0$ in $\mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}$, a constant dynamic shear viscosity $\mu\ge0$ in $\mathrm{Pa\,s}$, a velocity field $u\in C^2(\Omega,\mathbb R^3)$, and a pressure multiplier $p\in C^1(\Omega,\mathbb R)$. Define $L_{ij}=\partial_{x_j}u_i$, $D=(L+L^T)/2$, and $D_tu=\partial_tu+(u\cdot\nabla)u$. The branch is specified by
$$ \rho=\rho_0,\qquad \operatorname{div}u=0,\qquad \sigma=-pI_3+2\mu D,\qquad \rho_0D_tu=\operatorname{div}\sigma, $$
where $(\operatorname{div}\sigma)_i=\sum_{j=1}^3\partial_{x_j}\sigma_{ij}$. Equivalently, for constant $\mu$, its momentum equation is
$$ \rho_0D_tu+\nabla p=\mu\Delta u,\qquad \Delta u_i=\sum_{j=1}^3\partial_{x_jx_j}u_i. $$
Indeed, $\operatorname{div}(2\mu D)=\mu\Delta u+\mu\nabla(\operatorname{div}u)=\mu\Delta u$. This is the incompressible specialization of the adopted Newtonian closure: $\theta=\operatorname{div}u=0$ implies $D_0=D$, so the bulk-viscosity and Fourier-flux terms do not enter this mechanical equation. The pressure is a constraint multiplier and is not identified with a compressible equation-of-state pressure. Define the kinematic viscosity $\nu=\mu/\rho_0$, in $\mathrm{m^2\,s^{-1}}$. Boundary and initial data are not part of this definition, and the item asserts no solution existence.

before.exact_statement:
Let $h,a,\rho_0,\mu>0$, let $p_0,G,V_0,V_1\in\mathbb R$, and set $\nu=\mu/\rho_0$. In the constant-density model

$$\partial_tu+(u\cdot\nabla)u+\rho_0^{-1}\nabla p-\nu\Delta u=0,\qquad \operatorname{div}u=0,$$

take the infinite plane channel $\Omega_{\rm ch}=\{(x,y,z):x\in\mathbb R,\ 0<y<h,\ z\in\mathbb R\}$, with $u=(v(y),0,0)$, $p=p_0-Gx$, $v\in C^2([0,h])$, and wall values $v(0)=V_0$, $v(h)=V_1$. Then the unique profile within this ansatz is

$$v(y)=V_0+(V_1-V_0)\frac yh+\frac{G}{2\mu}y(h-y).$$

Its volume flux per unit width in the $z$ direction and its fixed-coordinate shear component are

$$Q_{\rm ch}=\int_0^h v(y)\,dy=\frac h2(V_0+V_1)+\frac{Gh^3}{12\mu},\qquad \sigma_{xy}(0)=\mu\frac{V_1-V_0}{h}+\frac{Gh}{2},\qquad \sigma_{xy}(h)=\mu\frac{V_1-V_0}{h}-\frac{Gh}{2}.$$

For the infinite circular pipe $\Omega_a=\{(x,y,z):x\in\mathbb R,\ y^2+z^2<a^2\}$, take $x$ as the axial coordinate, $r=(y^2+z^2)^{1/2}$, $u=(w(r),0,0)$, $p=p_0-Gx$, and require the radial field $(y,z)\mapsto w((y^2+z^2)^{1/2})$ to be $C^2$ on the closed cross-sectional disk with no slip $w(a)=0$. Then the unique profile within this ansatz is

$$w(r)=\frac{G}{4\mu}(a^2-r^2),\qquad Q_{\rm pipe}=\int_0^a2\pi r\,w(r)\,dr=\frac{\pi G a^4}{8\mu}.$$

Both fields satisfy the exact stationary Navier–Stokes equations for every choice of the positive constants and also satisfy the corresponding steady Stokes equations, because their time derivative and convective acceleration vanish. The pipe uniqueness claim uses regularity on the full disk, including the axis. Both uniqueness claims are restricted to the stated one-dimensional ansatz; neither asserts uniqueness among all flows. The domains are infinite or fully developed and give no finite entrance or exit error estimate. Under SI interpretation, $h,a,x,y,z,r$ are in metres, $u,V_0,V_1,v,w$ in metres per second, $\rho_0$ in kilograms per cubic metre, $\mu$ in pascal-seconds, $\nu$ in square metres per second, $p,p_0$ in pascals, and $G$ in pascals per metre. The channel flux per unit width is in square metres per second and the pipe volume flux is in cubic metres per second.

$$\rho=\rho_0,\qquad \operatorname{div}u=0,\qquad \rho_0D_tu+\nabla p=0.$$

$$u_v(x,y,z)=\left(-\frac{\kappa y}{r^2},\frac{\kappa x}{r^2},0\right),\qquad p_v(x,y,z)=p_0-\frac{\rho_0\kappa^2}{2r^2}.$$

For every $R>0$ and fixed $z_0$, the positively oriented circle $\gamma_R(\theta)=(R\cos\theta,R\sin\theta,z_0)$, $0\le\theta\le2\pi$, has circulation $\oint_{\gamma_R}u_v\cdot d\mathbf r=2\pi\kappa$. Consequently no single-valued $C^1$ function $\phi:D\to\mathbb R$ satisfies $u_v=\nabla\phi$ on all of $D$, even though $\operatorname{curl}u_v=0$ there. $$\partial_tu_v+(u_v\cdot\nabla)u_v+\rho_0^{-1}\nabla p_v-\nu\Delta u_v=0$$

holds for every $\nu>0$, with $\partial_tu_v=0$.

Its Bernoulli quantity $B=|u_s|^2/2+p_s/\rho_0=p_0/\rho_0+\Omega_0^2r^2$ is constant on each circular streamline but varies with $r$. Thus a common Bernoulli constant is not implied for all steady constant-density flows. before.exact_statement:
Let $D=\{(x,y,z)\in\mathbb R^3:r=(x^2+y^2)^{1/2}>0\}$, let $\rho_0>0$, $p_0\in\mathbb R$, and let $\kappa\ne0$. On $D$ define

$$u_v(x,y,z)=\left(-\frac{\kappa y}{r^2},\frac{\kappa x}{r^2},0\right),\qquad p_v(x,y,z)=p_0-\frac{\rho_0\kappa^2}{2r^2}.$$

For every $R>0$ and fixed $z_0$, the positively oriented circle $\gamma_R(\theta)=(R\cos\theta,R\sin\theta,z_0)$, $0\le\theta\le2\pi$, has circulation $\oint_{\gamma_R}u_v\cdot d\mathbf r=2\pi\kappa$. Consequently no single-valued $C^1$ function $\phi:D\to\mathbb R$ satisfies $u_v=\nabla\phi$ on all of $D$, even though $\operatorname{curl}u_v=0$ there. Both $\operatorname{div}u_v=0$ and $\Delta u_v=0$ on $D$, and the pointwise identity

$$\partial_tu_v+(u_v\cdot\nabla)u_v+\rho_0^{-1}\nabla p_v-\nu\Delta u_v=0$$

holds for every $\nu>0$, with $\partial_tu_v=0$.

Separately, for $\Omega_0\ne0$ set $u_s=(-\Omega_0y,\Omega_0x,0)$ and $p_s=p_0+\rho_0\Omega_0^2r^2/2$ on $\mathbb R^3$. This smooth steady field is divergence-free and satisfies the same constant-density equation for every $\nu>0$. Its Bernoulli quantity $B=|u_s|^2/2+p_s/\rho_0=p_0/\rho_0+\Omega_0^2r^2$ is constant on each circular streamline but varies with $r$. Thus a common Bernoulli constant is not implied for all steady constant-density flows. This example does not contradict a Bernoulli theorem that assumes an irrotational field or a separate barotropic model. Under SI interpretation, $r$ is in metres, the velocities in metres per second, $\kappa$ in square metres per second, $\Omega_0$ in inverse seconds, $\rho_0$ in kilograms per cubic metre, and $p,p_0$ in pascals.

Adopt a smooth single-component material continuum on a stated macroscopic regime in a Cartesian inertial chart. Let $\rho_0\in C^1(\overline B)$ be positive. A material subregion is $\chi_t(V)$ for a nonempty bounded open set $V\Subset B$ whose boundary is locally, after a rigid coordinate change, a $C^1$ graph with $V$ on one side; its boundary moves with the material velocity. The Jordan integral convention for such regions and their smooth images is the one in the mathematical interface identified below. The continuum approximation, its empirical regime, and the following balance laws are physical assumptions of this model, not deductions from the mathematical definition of a motion or from molecular mechanics.

Assume there are no mass sources and no diffusion relative to $u$. Adopt a positive reference mass density $\rho_0$, a positive current density $\rho$, a body-acceleration field $b$, a contact traction $t(t,x,n)=\sigma(t,x)n$ depending only on the local outward unit normal $n$, a $C^1$ Cauchy stress field $\sigma$, specific internal energy $e$, positive temperature $T$, specific entropy $s$, heat-flux vector $q$, and specific heat supply $r$, with the types and SI units fixed in the preceding definition. Contact traction and volume-force densities are continuous and locally bounded on the smooth material regions under consideration. There are no surface couples or intrinsic spin angular momentum; a micropolar or couple-stress model is outside this postulate.

For every such material subregion, adopt conservation of mass,

$$\int_{\chi_t(V)}\rho(t,x)\,dx=\int_V\rho_0(a)\,da.$$

In the same inertial chart, adopt the balances of linear and angular momentum,

$$\frac{d}{dt}\int_{\chi_t(V)}\rho u\,dx=\int_{\chi_t(V)}\rho b\,dx+\int_{\partial\chi_t(V)}t(t,x,n)\,dS,$$

$$\frac{d}{dt}\int_{\chi_t(V)}x\times(\rho u)\,dx=\int_{\chi_t(V)}x\times(\rho b)\,dx+\int_{\partial\chi_t(V)}x\times t(t,x,n)\,dS.$$

before.exact_statement:
Work in the nonrelativistic SI fluid model on an open time interval $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ measured in seconds and oriented Euclidean three-space measured in metres. Let $\Omega_t$ be the fluid region at time $t$ and $\mathcal O:=\{(t,x):t\in I,\ x\in\Omega_t\}$ its open spacetime region. Let $u:\mathcal O\to\mathbb R^3$ be fluid velocity in metres per second, $T:\mathcal O\to(0,\infty)$ absolute temperature in kelvins, and $q:\mathcal O\to\mathbb R^3$ conductive heat flux in watts per square metre. A moving solid boundary is locally parameterized by a $C^2$ embedding $X_b:I\times\Xi\to\mathbb R^3$, where $\Xi\subseteq\mathbb R^2$ is open and $D_\xi X_b$ has rank two; its material boundary velocity is $w_b(t,X_b(t,\xi)):=\partial_tX_b(t,\xi)$ in metres per second. The boundary patches have continuous outward Euclidean unit normal $n$. In the smooth branch, assume $u,T,q$ have continuous traces wherever boundary values are imposed. The no-penetration or impermeability condition is the adopted equality $(u-w_b)\cdot n=0$ on the wall. When separately selected, no-slip is the stronger adopted equality $u=w_b$ on the wall. Neither equality is deduced from an interior balance equation; no-slip is not part of the inviscid wall model unless explicitly adopted.

At each thermal boundary patch, select and state compatible data of one of these forms: insulation, $q\cdot n=0$; prescribed temperature, $T=T_b$ for a specified field $T_b>0$ in kelvins; or prescribed outward conductive heat flux, $q\cdot n=q_b$ for a specified field $q_b$ in watts per square metre. These are alternative boundary models. Their energy and entropy fluxes are accounted for through the chosen boundary data; no separate surface storage or reservoir entropy law is implicit.

A periodic cell with side lengths $L_1,L_2,L_3>0$ metres is the quotient torus $\mathbb T^3_L:=\mathbb R^3/(L_1\mathbb Z\times L_2\mathbb Z\times L_3\mathbb Z)$. Periodicity identifies opposite faces by the corresponding translations and requires equality of the fields and of each derivative trace required by the selected evolution problem. Paired fluxes then cancel in cell integrals. These identified faces are not physical walls.

At an initial time $t_0\in I$, prescribe only the fields present in the selected model. Require them to satisfy the exact function-space regularity, positivity, differential constraints, constitutive state-domain restrictions, and wall or periodic compatibility hypotheses of the particular evolution result being used. In the weak formulation, initial data enter through the test-function initial term; that fixes a distributional initial datum but does not by itself supply a strong trace. This postulate selects model data only. It asserts no existence, uniqueness, regularity improvement, approximation, or solvability for any initial-boundary value problem.

$$\operatorname{div}u=0,\qquad \sigma=-pI+2\mu D,\qquad \operatorname{div}\sigma+ho_0b=0,\qquad D=	frac12(
abla u+
abla u^{\mathsf T}).$$
Here $(
abla u)_{ij}=\partial_j u_i$ and $(\operatorname{div}\sigma)_i=\sum_j\partial_j\sigma_{ij}$. This is an alternative zero-inertia branch: the full material-acceleration momentum equation is not also imposed on the same field. For constant $\mu$, the adopted balance is equivalent to $-
abla p+\mu\Delta u+ho_0b=0$. The Postulate does not assert that small Reynolds number alone yields this branch, provide an approximation error or solution-existence result, or establish empirical validity. Boundary and far-field data remain separate.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Let $a,\mu,\rho_0>0$, $p_\infty\in\mathbb R$, $U\in\mathbb R^3$, and $\nu=\mu/\rho_0$. On the exterior domain $\Omega_a=\{x\in\mathbb R^3:r=|x|>a\}$ put $s=U\cdot x$ and define

$$u(x)=A(r)U+B(r)sx,\qquad A(r)=1-\frac{3a}{4r}-\frac{a^3}{4r^3},\qquad B(r)=-\frac{3a}{4r^3}+\frac{3a^3}{4r^5},\qquad p(x)=p_\infty-\frac{3\mu a}{2}\frac{s}{r^3}.$$

This field is $C^2$ up to the spherical boundary from the exterior, $p$ is $C^1$, $u=0$ at $r=a$, and $u\to U$ uniformly in direction as $r\to\infty$. It satisfies the steady Stokes system $\rho_0^{-1}\nabla p-\nu\Delta u=0$, $\operatorname{div}u=0$ on $\Omega_a$. $$\int_{S_a}\sigma n\,dS=6\pi\mu aU.$$

Moreover, among classical pairs $(\widetilde u,\widetilde p)$ satisfying the same Stokes system on $\Omega_a$, the same zero boundary velocity and far-field limits, and the uniform decay conditions $\widetilde u-U=O(r^{-1})$, $\nabla\widetilde u=O(r^{-2})$, $\widetilde p-p_\infty=O(r^{-2})$, this pair is unique. Let $\Omega_t$ be the fluid region at time $t$ and $\mathcal O:=\{(t,x):t\in I,\ x\in\Omega_t\}$ its open spacetime region. Let $u:\mathcal O\to\mathbb R^3$ be fluid velocity in metres per second, $T:\mathcal O\to(0,\infty)$ absolute temperature in kelvins, and $q:\mathcal O\to\mathbb R^3$ conductive heat flux in watts per square metre. The no-penetration or impermeability condition is the adopted equality $(u-w_b)\cdot n=0$ on the wall. When separately selected, no-slip is the stronger adopted equality $u=w_b$ on the wall. Neither equality is deduced from an interior balance equation; no-slip is not part of the inviscid wall model unless explicitly adopted.

For $A,B\in\mathbb R^{3\times3}$, use the Frobenius contraction $A:B=\sum_{i,j=1}^3A_{ij}B_{ij}$.

$$ x^T\operatorname{sym}K(\xi)x\ge0\quad(x\in\mathbb R^3),\qquad \operatorname{sym}K=(K+K^T)/2. $$

$$ \tau=2\mu(\xi)D_0+\zeta(\xi)\theta I_3,\qquad \sigma=-pI_3+\tau,\qquad q=-K(\xi)\nabla T. $$

Adopt a smooth single-component material continuum on a stated macroscopic regime in a Cartesian inertial chart. Let $\rho_0\in C^1(\overline B)$ be positive. On each swept material region, require $\rho,u,e,T,s,q,\sigma\in C^1$ and $b,r\in C^0$, with $\rho>0$ and $T>0$; the motion has the regularity and positive Jacobian in the preceding definition. A material subregion is $\chi_t(V)$ for a nonempty bounded open set $V\Subset B$ whose boundary is locally, after a rigid coordinate change, a $C^1$ graph with $V$ on one side; its boundary moves with the material velocity. The Jordan integral convention for such regions and their smooth images is the one in the mathematical interface identified below. The continuum approximation, its empirical regime, and the following balance laws are physical assumptions of this model, not deductions from the mathematical definition of a motion or from molecular mechanics.

Assume there are no mass sources and no diffusion relative to $u$. Adopt a positive reference mass density $\rho_0$, a positive current density $\rho$, a body-acceleration field $b$, a contact traction $t(t,x,n)=\sigma(t,x)n$ depending only on the local outward unit normal $n$, a $C^1$ Cauchy stress field $\sigma$, specific internal energy $e$, positive temperature $T$, specific entropy $s$, heat-flux vector $q$, and specific heat supply $r$, with the types and SI units fixed in the preceding definition. Contact traction and volume-force densities are continuous and locally bounded on the smooth material regions under consideration. There are no surface couples or intrinsic spin angular momentum; a micropolar or couple-stress model is outside this postulate.

For every such material subregion, adopt conservation of mass,

$$\int_{\chi_t(V)}\rho(t,x)\,dx=\int_V\rho_0(a)\,da.$$

In the same inertial chart, adopt the balances of linear and angular momentum,

$$\frac{d}{dt}\int_{\chi_t(V)}\rho u\,dx=\int_{\chi_t(V)}\rho b\,dx+\int_{\partial\chi_t(V)}t(t,x,n)\,dS,$$

$$\frac{d}{dt}\int_{\chi_t(V)}x\times(\rho u)\,dx=\int_{\chi_t(V)}x\times(\rho b)\,dx+\int_{\partial\chi_t(V)}x\times t(t,x,n)\,dS.$$

Adopt the total-energy balance and entropy inequality

$$\frac{d}{dt}\int_{\chi_t(V)}\rho\left(e+\frac{|u|^2}{2}\right)\,dx=\int_{\chi_t(V)}\rho b\cdot u\,dx+\int_{\partial\chi_t(V)}t(t,x,n)\cdot u\,dS-\int_{\partial\chi_t(V)}q\cdot n\,dS+\int_{\chi_t(V)}\rho r\,dx,$$

$$\frac{d}{dt}\int_{\chi_t(V)}\rho s\,dx\ge-\int_{\partial\chi_t(V)}\frac{q}{T}\cdot n\,dS+\int_{\chi_t(V)}\frac{\rho r}{T}\,dx.$$

The entropy flux uses the local material temperature at the heat-transfer point. A reservoir at a different temperature, a singular surface force, a shock, vacuum, or a weak solution requires a separately stated model and is not covered here. The postulate reports no experiment and asserts no measurement or universal claim that nature obeys these assumptions.

Work in the nonrelativistic SI fluid model on an open time interval $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ measured in seconds and oriented Euclidean three-space measured in metres. Let $\Omega_t$ be the fluid region at time $t$ and $\mathcal O:=\{(t,x):t\in I,\ x\in\Omega_t\}$ its open spacetime region. Let $u:\mathcal O\to\mathbb R^3$ be fluid velocity in metres per second, $T:\mathcal O\to(0,\infty)$ absolute temperature in kelvins, and $q:\mathcal O\to\mathbb R^3$ conductive heat flux in watts per square metre. A moving solid boundary is locally parameterized by a $C^2$ embedding $X_b:I\times\Xi\to\mathbb R^3$, where $\Xi\subseteq\mathbb R^2$ is open and $D_\xi X_b$ has rank two; its material boundary velocity is $w_b(t,X_b(t,\xi)):=\partial_tX_b(t,\xi)$ in metres per second. The boundary patches have continuous outward Euclidean unit normal $n$. In the smooth branch, assume $u,T,q$ have continuous traces wherever boundary values are imposed. The no-penetration or impermeability condition is the adopted equality $(u-w_b)\cdot n=0$ on the wall. When separately selected, no-slip is the stronger adopted equality $u=w_b$ on the wall. Neither equality is deduced from an interior balance equation; no-slip is not part of the inviscid wall model unless explicitly adopted.

At each thermal boundary patch, select and state compatible data of one of these forms: insulation, $q\cdot n=0$; prescribed temperature, $T=T_b$ for a specified field $T_b>0$ in kelvins; or prescribed outward conductive heat flux, $q\cdot n=q_b$ for a specified field $q_b$ in watts per square metre. These are alternative boundary models. Their energy and entropy fluxes are accounted for through the chosen boundary data; no separate surface storage or reservoir entropy law is implicit.

A periodic cell with side lengths $L_1,L_2,L_3>0$ metres is the quotient torus $\mathbb T^3_L:=\mathbb R^3/(L_1\mathbb Z\times L_2\mathbb Z\times L_3\mathbb Z)$. Periodicity identifies opposite faces by the corresponding translations and requires equality of the fields and of each derivative trace required by the selected evolution problem. Paired fluxes then cancel in cell integrals. These identified faces are not physical walls.

At an initial time $t_0\in I$, prescribe only the fields present in the selected model. Require them to satisfy the exact function-space regularity, positivity, differential constraints, constitutive state-domain restrictions, and wall or periodic compatibility hypotheses of the particular evolution result being used. In the weak formulation, initial data enter through the test-function initial term; that fixes a distributional initial datum but does not by itself supply a strong trace. This postulate selects model data only. It asserts no existence, uniqueness, regularity improvement, approximation, or solvability for any initial-boundary value problem.

Suppose $u:I\times\Omega\to\mathbb R^3$ has continuous first time, first spatial, and second spatial derivatives; $\rho:I\times\Omega\to(0,\infty)$ has continuous first time and first spatial derivatives; and $V:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ is time-independent and $C^2$. A material subregion is $\chi_t(V)$ for a nonempty bounded open set $V\Subset B$ whose boundary is locally, after a rigid coordinate change, a $C^1$ graph with $V$ on one side; its boundary moves with the material velocity. The continuum approximation, its empirical regime, and the following balance laws are physical assumptions of this model, not deductions from the mathematical definition of a motion or from molecular mechanics.

Contact traction and volume-force densities are continuous and locally bounded on the smooth material regions under consideration. There are no surface couples or intrinsic spin angular momentum; a micropolar or couple-stress model is outside this postulate.

$$\int_{\chi_t(V)}\rho(t,x)\,dx=\int_V\rho_0(a)\,da.$$

before.exact_statement:
Let $a,\rho_0>0$, $p_\infty\in\mathbb R$, $U\in\mathbb R^3$, and on $\Omega_a=\{x\in\mathbb R^3:r=|x|>a\}$ define $n=x/r$, $\phi(x)=(U\cdot x)(1+a^3/(2r^3))$, $u=\nabla\phi$, and $p=p_\infty+\rho_0(|U|^2-|u|^2)/2$. Then $u,p$ are smooth in the exterior and up to $r=a$, $u\to U$ and $p\to p_\infty$ uniformly in direction at infinity, and $u\cdot n=0$ on $r=a$. The pair solves $(u\cdot\nabla)u+\rho_0^{-1}\nabla p=0$, $\operatorname{div}u=0$, the steady formal constant-density incompressible Euler system. Its boundary condition is impermeable slip/no-through: $u$ is generally nonzero tangent to the sphere, so this is not a no-slip solution. For the formal Euler stress $\sigma_E=-pI_3$ and sphere normal $n=x/a$ pointing from the center into the exterior, the exact resultant is

$$\int_{|x|=a}\sigma_E n\,dS=-\int_{|x|=a}p n\,dS=0.$$

The theorem concerns only this explicit inviscid mathematical model; it asserts neither a viscous zero-drag result nor an observed force. Under SI interpretation, $a,r,x$ are in metres, $U,u$ in metres per second, $\rho_0$ in kilograms per cubic metre, and $p,p_\infty$ in pascals.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Let $a,\mu,ho_0>0$, $p_\infty\in\mathbb R$, $U\in\mathbb R^3$, $
u=\mu/ho_0$, and $\Omega_a=\{x\in\mathbb R^3:r=|x|>a\}$. Set $s=U\cdot x$ and
$$u=A(r)U+B(r)sx,\quad A(r)=1- rac{3a}{4r}- rac{a^3}{4r^3},\quad B(r)=- rac{3a}{4r^3}+ rac{3a^3}{4r^5},\quad p=p_\infty- rac{3\mu a}{2} rac{s}{r^3},$$
where the force-free, steady creeping model is selected. In Cartesian coordinates, $\operatorname{div}u=\sum_i\partial_i u_i$ and $(\Delta u)_i=\sum_j\partial_{jj}u_i$. The field is $C^2$ up to the sphere from outside, $p\in C^1$, $u=0$ at $r=a$, and $u	o U$ uniformly in direction at infinity. It solves $ho_0^{-1}
abla p-
u\Delta u=0$, $\operatorname{div}u=0$. For $n=x/a$ on $S_a$, with $\sigma=-pI+\mu(
abla u+(
abla u)^{\mathsf T})$, the oriented resultant is
$$\int_{S_a}\sigma n\,dS=6\pi\mu aU.$$
Among classical pairs solving the same Stokes system, boundary condition and far-field limits, this pair is unique in the uniform decay class $u-U=O(r^{-1})$, $
abla u=O(r^{-2})$, $p-p_\infty=O(r^{-2})$, with all bounds uniform in direction and pressure normalized by its limit. The classical regularity is $u\in C^2$, $p\in C^1$ locally up to $S_a$. Under SI units, $a,r,x$ are metres, $U$ is $\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, $ho_0$ is $\mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}$, $\mu$ is $\mathrm{Pa\,s}$, $
u$ is $\mathrm{m^2\,s^{-1}}$, pressure is pascals, and resultant is newtons. This is an exact zero-inertia model result, not a finite-Reynolds-number estimate or exterior Navier–Stokes existence claim.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

before.quote:
Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be a nonempty open time interval measured in seconds, $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ nonempty and open in metres, and $P:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ be $C^2$. Use SI units: $u$ in $\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, $\rho$ in $\mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}$, $P$ in pascals, and $V,h,B$ in $\mathrm{m^2\,s^{-2}}$. Let $\rho:I\times\Omega\to(0,\infty)$ have continuous first time and spatial derivatives, $u:I\times\Omega\to\mathbb R^3$ have continuous first time, first spatial and second spatial derivatives, and $V:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ be a time-independent $C^2$ potential per unit mass. Adopt the barotropic Euler equations with conservative body acceleration $-\nabla V$:
$$\partial_t\rho+\operatorname{div}(\rho u)=0,\qquad \partial_tu+(u\cdot\nabla)u=-\rho^{-1}\nabla(P(\rho))-\nabla V.$$
For a fixed $\rho_{\rm ref}>0$, define $h(q)=\int_{\rho_{\rm ref}}^qP'(r)/r\,dr$. A steady streamline is a $C^1$ curve $x:J\to\Omega$ satisfying $x'(s)=u(x(s))$. If $u,\rho$ are steady, then
$$B=\frac{|u|^2}{2}+h(\rho)+V$$
is constant along each streamline. If additionally $\operatorname{curl}u=0$ on a connected component, then $B$ is constant throughout that component; here $\operatorname{curl}$ is the Cartesian curl. For every closed $C^1$ material loop $X:J\times[0,1]\to\Omega$ with $X(t,0)=X(t,1)$, $X_t=u(t,X)$, and continuous $X_s,X_{ts}$, the circulation
$$\Gamma(t)=\int_0^1u(t,X(t,s))\cdot X_s(t,s)\,ds$$
is constant. The conservative body acceleration and local barotropic branch are model inputs; no statement concerns shocks, nonbarotropic pressure, nonconservative forcing, or viscous circulation.

In particular, take $P(\rho)=c^2\rho$ with $c>0$ in $\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, $V=0$, angular speed $\Omega_0\ne0$ in $\mathrm{s^{-1}}$, density $\rho_c,\rho_{\rm ref}>0$ in $\mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}$, angular and reference lengths $R,H$ in metres, and the open cylinder $D=\{(x,y,z):x^2+y^2<R^2,\ |z|<H\}$ for $R,H>0$ measured in metres. Set $r=(x^2+y^2)^{1/2}$, $e_\theta=(-y/r,x/r,0)$ for $r>0$, $u=\Omega_0(-y,x,0)$, and $\rho=\rho_c\exp(\Omega_0^2r^2/(2c^2))$ for $\rho_c>0$. These smooth fields satisfy both equations. For each circle of radius $\ell\in(0,R)$ at height $|z_0|<H$, the material evolution $X(t,\theta)=(\ell\cos(\theta+\Omega_0t),\ell\sin(\theta+\Omega_0t),z_0)$ has circulation $2\pi\Omega_0\ell^2$. Its Bernoulli function is
$$B=c^2\log(\rho_c/\rho_{\rm ref})+\Omega_0^2r^2.$$
It is constant along each circular streamline but varies between radii, since $\operatorname{curl}u=(0,0,2\Omega_0)\ne0$. This is a conditional prediction of the stated smooth barotropic model, not an empirical claim about viscous flow.

Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be a nonempty open interval containing $0$, let $B\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ be a nonempty bounded open reference body with $C^1$ boundary, and let $\mathcal U$ be an open neighborhood of $\overline B$. A smooth motion is a map $\chi\in C^2(I\times\mathcal U;\mathbb R^3)$ such that each $\chi_t(a):=\chi(t,a)$ is an orientation-preserving $C^2$ diffeomorphism onto its image; when labels are initially the current positions, $\chi_0(a)=a$. Set $\Omega_t=\chi_t(B)$. For $x\in\chi_t(\mathcal U)$ its inverse label map is $A(t,x)=\chi_t^{-1}(x)$, and its Eulerian velocity is $u(t,x)=\partial_t\chi(t,A(t,x))$. Position and material-label coordinates have units $\mathrm m$, time has units $\mathrm s$, and velocity has units $\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$. The velocity gradient is $L=\nabla u$, the rate-of-strain tensor is $D=(L+L^{\mathsf T})/2$, the spin is $W=(L-L^{\mathsf T})/2$, and the dilatation is $\theta=\operatorname{tr}D=\operatorname{tr}L$; all have units $\mathrm{s^{-1}}$. The material derivative is $D_t=\partial_t+u\cdot\nabla$, acting componentwise on tensor fields, with units $\mathrm{s^{-1}}$ on dimensionless fields. Matrix contraction is $S:T=\operatorname{tr}(S^{\mathsf T}T)$, with Frobenius norm $|S|=(S:S)^{1/2}$. These definitions are the mathematical motion and kinematics used below.

Write $\mathrm{Sym}_0(3)=\{D\in M_3(\mathbb R):D^{\mathsf T}=D,\operatorname{tr}D=0\}$. The generalized Newtonian branch is incompressible, so $\theta=0$ and $D\in\mathrm{Sym}_0(3)$. Define the shear-rate scalar $\dot\gamma=(2D:D)^{1/2}$, with units $\mathrm{s}^{-1}$, and let $\eta(\dot\gamma)$ be a finite nonnegative viscosity with units $\mathrm{Pa\,s}$. The deviatoric stress is $\tau=2\eta(\dot\gamma)D$, in $\mathrm{Pa}$; no pressure term is included.

Two named viscosity choices are the Carreau form

$$
\eta_C(\dot\gamma)=\eta_\infty+(\eta_0-\eta_\infty)\bigl(1+(\lambda\dot\gamma)^2\bigr)^{(n-1)/2},
$$

with $\eta_0\ge\eta_\infty\ge0$ in $\mathrm{Pa\,s}$, $\lambda\ge0$ in $\mathrm{s}$, and dimensionless $n>0$, and the regularized power form

$$
\eta_R(\dot\gamma)=m(\varepsilon^2+\dot\gamma^2)^{(n-1)/2},
$$

with $m>0$ in $\mathrm{Pa\,s^n}$, $\varepsilon>0$ in $\mathrm{s}^{-1}$, and dimensionless $n>0$. For comparison, the unregularized power form $\eta_U=m\dot\gamma^{\,n-1}$ is defined only for $\dot\gamma>0$; its stress is extended by $\tau=0$ at $D=0$. When $0<n<1$, this viscosity diverges as $\dot\gamma\downarrow0$, although the extended stress may remain continuous.

For the Bingham branch use the Frobenius norm just defined, $\mu_p\ge0$ in $\mathrm{Pa\,s}$, and yield parameter $\tau_y\ge0$ in $\mathrm{Pa}$. Its set-valued deviatoric stress graph on $\mathrm{Sym}_0(3)$ is

$$
\mathcal B(D)=\begin{cases}\{2\mu_pD+\tau_yD/|D|\},&D\ne0,\\\{S\in\mathrm{Sym}_0(3):|S|\le\tau_y\},&D=0.\end{cases}
$$

The value at rest is therefore a whole stress ball when $\tau_y>0$. The chosen Frobenius normalization fixes the numerical convention for $\tau_y$; a source using a differently normalized second invariant requires a corresponding parameter conversion.

For the conformation branch, $C(t)$ is a dimensionless symmetric positive-definite $3\times3$ tensor, $G>0$ is a modulus in $\mathrm{Pa}$, $\lambda>0$ is a relaxation time in $\mathrm{s}$, and $\eta_s\ge0$ is a solvent viscosity in $\mathrm{Pa\,s}$. Along an incompressible trajectory, adopt

$$D_tC-LC-CL^{\mathsf T}=-(C-I)/\lambda,\qquad \tau_p=G(C-I),\qquad \tau_s=2\eta_sD,\qquad w(C)=\frac G2\bigl(\operatorname{tr}C-\log\det C-3\bigr).$$

Here $\tau_p,\tau_s$ are polymer and solvent stresses in $\mathrm{Pa}$, and $w$ is a stored-energy density in $\mathrm{J\,m^{-3}}$. The determinant in this formula is positive for symmetric positive-definite $C$, by the finite-dimensional real spectral theorem and determinant multiplicativity. These are mathematical constitutive definitions and adopted model equations. They assert neither empirical validity for a particular material nor existence of a solution to a fluid partial differential equation.

Since $Y(0)=C_0$, the fundamental theorem of calculus gives $Y(t)=C_0+\frac1\lambda\int_0^t e^{s/\lambda}Z(s)^{-1}Z(s)^{-\mathsf T}\,ds$. Let $D\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^n$ be open, let $F:D\to\mathbb R^n$ be continuous and locally Lipschitz in the state variable, and let $(t_0,x_0)\in D$. Then a unique local solution of the IVP exists on some interval around the initial time. More quantitatively, if $h,r>0$ make

$$[t_0-h,t_0+h]\times\overline B(x_0,r)\subseteq D,$$

if $\|F\|_2\le M$ and $F$ has state-Lipschitz constant $L$ on this cylinder, and if $hM\le r$ and $Lh<1$, then there is exactly one solution on $[t_0-h,t_0+h]$ through $(t_0,x_0)$ whose graph lies in the cylinder. Any two solutions through the same initial data agree on every common subinterval containing $t_0$.

In particular, a unique local solution exists on an interval around the initial time.

1. $(\mathbb{R}, d_{\mathbb{R}})$ with the usual metric $d_{\mathbb{R}}(x,y) = |x-y|$
   ([[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]]) is a complete metric space
   ([[def-complete-metric-space]]).
2. Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$ and let $d_2$ be the Euclidean metric on
   $\mathbb{R}^n$ ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). Then $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ is complete.

**The hypothesis $n \ge 1$ is inherited and is not decoration.**
[[lem-metrics-on-rn]] defines $\mathbb{R}^n$ and its three metrics only for
$n \ge 1$, because at $n = 0$ the metric $d_\infty$ would be a maximum over the
empty index set. Every statement about $\mathbb{R}^n$ in this library carries the
hypothesis, and this one does too.

Let $m \in \mathbb{N}$ with $m \ge 1$ and let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a < b$.

1. **Fundamental theorem, second part, in $\mathbb{R}^{m}$.** Let
   $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ be differentiable at every point of $[a,b]$ as
   a function on $[a,b]$ ([[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]]), and
   suppose $f' : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ is integrable. Then
   $$\int_a^b f' \;=\; f(b) - f(a).$$
2. **A bounded derivative gives a Lipschitz function.** Let
   $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ be continuous on $[a,b]$ and differentiable at
   every point of $(a,b)$, and let $M \ge 0$ satisfy
   $\lVert f'(t)\rVert_2 \le M$ for every $t \in (a,b)$. Then
   $$\lVert f(t) - f(s)\rVert_2 \;\le\; M\,|t-s| \qquad \text{for all } s,t \in [a,b],$$
   that is, $f$ is Lipschitz with constant $M$ as a map
   $([a,b], d_{\mathbb{R}}) \to (\mathbb{R}^{m}, d_2)$
   ([[def-lipschitz-holder-contraction]], [[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]],
   [[lem-metrics-on-rn]]).

Let $n\ge1$, let $D\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^n$ be open, let $F:D\to\mathbb R^n$ be continuous, let $(t_0,x_0)\in D$, let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be order-convex with at least two elements, and let $x:I\to\mathbb R^n$ be continuous with $t_0\in I$ and $(t,x(t))\in D$. A curve solves the IVP if and only if it satisfies the associated Volterra integral equation. Explicitly, the equation is

$$x(t)=x_0+\int_{t_0}^{t}F(s,x(s))\,ds\qquad(t\in I).$$

The integral is oriented, so the assertion applies on either side of $t_0$.

Every Cauchy sequence of reals converges to a real ([[def-real-limit]]).

More carefully, this is a statement about the *axioms*: in a complete ordered
field, that is in an ordered field with the least-upper-bound property
([[def-complete-ordered-field]]), every Cauchy sequence converges. The proof
below uses nothing about $\mathbb{R}$ except that property, through
[[thm-bolzano-weierstrass]].

**This library already knows the conclusion by a different route.**
It is proved on the Cauchy-construction page, where
$\mathbb{R}$ is built out of Cauchy sequences of rationals and completeness is
read off the construction. That proof is about a particular construction; this
one is about the axioms, and it is what tells us the statement holds in *any*
complete ordered field, however it was obtained.

before.claim: Write each component as a finite sum $F_i(x)=\sum_{\alpha\in E_i}c_{i\alpha}x^\alpha$. On any bounded coordinate box, for each exponent $q\ge1$ the identity $a^q-b^q=(a-b)\sum_{j=0}^{q-1}a^{q-1-j}b^j$ bounds the difference of each monomial at two points by a finite constant times their Euclidean distance; telescoping over the $N$ factors and summing the finitely many monomials proves that $F$ is locally Lipschitz there. It is also continuous, so [F1] applies at every state.

Put $R_+=\max(1,R)$ and $M_R=\bigl(\sum_{i=1}^N(\sum_{\alpha\in E_i}|c_{i\alpha}|R_+^{|\alpha|})^2\bigr)^{1/2}$. Since $|x_j(t)|\le R$ for each coordinate, the finite polynomial sums give $\|F(x(t))\|_2\le M_R$ for all $t<T_*$.

For $0\le s<t<T_*$, apply [F3] to $x|_{[s,t]}$ to obtain $\|x(t)-x(s)\|_2\le M_R(t-s)$. Hence $x(t)$ is Cauchy as $t\uparrow T_*$; for example, the sequence $t_n=T_*(1-1/n)$ for $n\ge2$ is Cauchy after applying this bound. By [F2] it converges to some $x_*\in\mathbb R^N$. For any $t<T_*$ and all sufficiently large $n$ with $t_n\ge t$, the same bound gives $\|x(t)-x_*\|_2\le M_R(t_n-t)+\|x(t_n)-x_*\|_2$; letting $n\to\infty$ yields $\|x(t)-x_*\|_2\le M_R(T_*-t)$, so $x(t)\to x_*$. The closed-ball bound passes to the limit, hence $\|x_*\|_2\le R$.
By step 1.1 the polynomial field is locally Lipschitz near $x_*$. Apply [F1] to the IVP at $(T_*,x_*)$ to obtain a local solution $y$ on an open interval about $T_*$.

By [F4], $x(t)=x_0+\int_0^tF(x(s))\,ds$ for $t<T_*$ and $y(t)=x_*+\int_{T_*}^tF(y(s))\,ds$ near $T_*$. The limit in step 3.1 and continuity of $F$ extend the first identity to $t=T_*$. Define $\widetilde x=x$ before $T_*$ and $\widetilde x=y$ from $T_*$ onward, assigning the common value $x_*$ at $T_*$. The joined curve is continuous and the two integral identities add to its Volterra equation on $[0,T_*+\epsilon)$ for some $\epsilon>0$; [F4] therefore makes it a $C^1$ solution of the same ODE extending $x$.
The extension in step 5.1 agrees with the original curve at every $t<T_*$ and is defined beyond $T_*$. This proves the statement.

before.quote: For an integer $d\in\{1,2,3\}$, let $Q_d=\mathbb R^d/(2\pi\mathbb Z)^d$ carry the probability measure obtained by pushing normalized Haar measure on $\mathbb T^d=\mathbb R^d/\mathbb Z^d$ forward under $y\mapsto x=2\pi y$; in coordinates this is $(2\pi)^{-d}dx$, and the characters are $e_k(x)=e^{ik\cdot x}$. For $q:Q_d\to\mathbb R^N$ and $k\in\mathbb Z^d$, set $\widehat q(k)=\int_{Q_d}q(x)e^{-ik\cdot x}\,d\mu(x)$, componentwise, so real fields have $\widehat q(-k)=\overline{\widehat q(k)}$. Put $w_k=(1+|k|^2)^{1/2}$. For any $s\in\mathbb R$, define $H^s(Q_d;\mathbb R^N)$ as the completion of finite real trigonometric polynomials in the norm $\|q\|_{H^s}^2=\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z^d}w_k^{2s}|\widehat q(k)|^2$. The completion is identified with its weighted coefficient space using finite symmetric cutoffs. If $s\ge0$, it has a unique $L^2$ representative; for $s<0$ no $L^2$ representative is asserted.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $n\ge1$
and let $e_k(x)=\exp(2\pi i\,k\cdot x)$, $k\in\mathbb Z^n$, be the coordinate
characters on $\mathbb T^n$
([[def-the-one-dimensional-torus-and-normalized-haar-integral]],
[[def-fourier-coefficients-and-trigonometric-polynomials]]). Then:

1. $(e_k)_{k\in\mathbb Z^n}$ is an orthonormal family in the complex Hilbert
   space $L^2(\mathbb T^n)$;
2. it is an orthonormal basis: its closed linear span is $L^2(\mathbb T^n)$;
3. consequently the Fourier expansion
   $f=\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z^n}\widehat f(k)e_k$ and Parseval's identity
   $$\|f\|_2^2=\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z^n}|\widehat f(k)|^2,\qquad \langle f,g\rangle=\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z^n}\widehat f(k)\overline{\widehat g(k)}$$
   hold for all $f,g\in L^2(\mathbb T^n)$, in the finite-subset-net sense; and
4. the Fourier coefficient map is a surjective linear isometry of
   $L^2(\mathbb T^n)$ onto $\ell^2(\mathbb Z^n,\mathbb C)$.

No Hilbert tensor-product identification is used anywhere.

Assume Countable Choice and fix $d\in\{1,2,3\}$. For a vector Fourier coefficient $a(k)\in\mathbb C^d$, define $(Pa)(0)=a(0)$ and $(Pa)(k)=P_ka(k)$ for $k
e0$, where $P_k=I-kk^{\mathsf T}/|k|^2$. For a tensor field $F=(F_{ij})_{i,j=1}^d$ with coefficients in any $H^s(Q_d)$, define the scalar pressure map $Q$ by $\widehat{QF}(0)=0$ and $\widehat{QF}(k)=-\sum_{i,j=1}^d k_i k_j|k|^{-2}\widehat F_{ij}(k)$ for $k
e0$. These formulas define real-preserving bounded maps on every $H^s$, $s\in\mathbb R$; $P$ is an orthogonal projection and commutes with derivatives. With $(\operatorname{div}F)_i=\sum_j\partial_jF_{ij}$, they satisfy $
abla QF=-(I-P)\operatorname{div}F$ as Fourier distributions.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $d\in\{1,2,3\}$ and use $H^\sigma(Q_d)$ with the normalized measure and weights in the Definition. For every integer $j\ge0$ and $\sigma>j+d/2$, each scalar $q\in H^\sigma(Q_d)$ has a $C^j$ representative and $\|q\|_{C^j}\le C_{d,\sigma,j}\|q\|_{H^\sigma}$. For every $\sigma>d/2$, pointwise multiplication extends uniquely from trigonometric polynomials to a continuous bilinear map $H^\sigma\times H^\sigma\to H^\sigma$ satisfying $\|fg\|_{H^\sigma}\le C_{d,\sigma}\|f\|_{H^\sigma}\|g\|_{H^\sigma}$. The assertions extend componentwise to finite-dimensional vector and tensor fields.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $d\in\{1,2,3\}$, let $m\ge s\ge4$ be integers, let $f,g\in C^\infty(Q_d;\mathbb R)$, and define $\Lambda^m$ by $\widehat{\Lambda^m q}(k)=w_k^m\widehat q(k)$. For each coordinate $j$,
$$\|[\Lambda^m,f]\partial_jg\|_{L^2}\le C_{d,m,s}\bigl(\|f\|_{H^m}\|g\|_{H^s}+\|f\|_{H^s}\|g\|_{H^m}\bigr),$$
where $[\Lambda^m,f]h=\Lambda^m(fh)-f\Lambda^mh$.

Let $D\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^n$ be open, let $F:D\to\mathbb R^n$ be continuous and locally Lipschitz in the state variable, and let $(t_0,x_0)\in D$. Then a unique local solution of the IVP exists on some interval around the initial time. More quantitatively, if $h,r>0$ make

$$[t_0-h,t_0+h]\times\overline B(x_0,r)\subseteq D,$$

if $\|F\|_2\le M$ and $F$ has state-Lipschitz constant $L$ on this cylinder, and if $hM\le r$ and $Lh<1$, then there is exactly one solution on $[t_0-h,t_0+h]$ through $(t_0,x_0)$ whose graph lies in the cylinder. Any two solutions through the same initial data agree on every common subinterval containing $t_0$.

In particular, a unique local solution exists on an interval around the initial time.

Let $N\ge1$, let $F:\mathbb R^N\to\mathbb R^N$ be a polynomial map, and let $T_*>0$. If $x\in C^1([0,T_*),\mathbb R^N)$ solves $x'(t)=F(x(t))$ and there is $R\ge0$ such that $\|x(t)\|_2\le R$ for every $0\le t<T_*$, then there are $\epsilon>0$ and a solution $\widetilde x\in C^1([0,T_*+\epsilon),\mathbb R^N)$ of the same ODE with $\widetilde x(t)=x(t)$ for $0\le t<T_*$. Thus a finite right endpoint of a bounded finite-dimensional polynomial ODE trajectory is extendible.

Every bounded sequence of reals has a convergent subsequence: if $(x_k)$ is a
sequence of reals and there is $M \in \mathbb{R}$ with $|x_k| \le M$ for every
$k \in \mathbb{N}$ ([[def-sequence]]), then there is a strictly increasing
$n : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ and a real $L$ with $x_{n_j} \to L$.

Equivalently: the subsequential limit set of a bounded sequence is nonempty
([[def-subsequential-limit]]).

The theorem is the exact repair of the false claim that a bounded sequence
converges. A bounded
sequence need not converge, and the alternating sequence is the standing witness;
what boundedness does force is that *some* subsequence converges. The converse of
the theorem is false, and badly so: a sequence with a convergent subsequence need
not be bounded.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.
