Assume Countable Choice. Let $d\in\{1,2,3\}$, $T>0$, and $Q_d=\mathbb R^d/(2\pi\mathbb Z)^d$ with normalized measure $d\mu=(2\pi)^{-d}dx$. For $z:Q_d\to\mathbb R^M$, use componentwise Fourier coefficients $\widehat z(k)=\int_{Q_d}z(x)e^{-ik\cdot x}\,d\mu(x)$, weights $w_k=(1+|k|^2)^{1/2}$, and the weighted coefficient completion norm $\|z\|_{H^s}^2=\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z^d}w_k^{2s}|\widehat z(k)|^2$; the normalized Fourier isometry gives $\|z\|_2^2=\sum_k|\widehat z(k)|^2$, where $\|z\|_2=(\int_{Q_d}|z|^2\,d\mu)^{1/2}$ and the pointwise component norm is Euclidean. In particular, $H^0=L^2$. For a map $z:[0,T]\times Q_d\to\mathbb R^M$, smooth on the closed cylinder means that for every $m\in\mathbb N_0$ and spatial multi-index $\alpha$, $\partial_t^m\partial_x^\alpha z$ exists on $(0,T)\times Q_d$ and extends continuously to $[0,T]\times Q_d$; spatial derivatives are those of its periodic lift. For a spatial vector field define $\operatorname{div}z=\sum_{j=1}^d\partial_jz_j$ and $\Delta z=\sum_{j=1}^d\partial_j^2z$. Write $\nabla z$ for the spatial Jacobian and $\|\nabla z(t)\|_\infty=\sup_{x\in Q_d}|\nabla z(t,x)|_F$, where $|\cdot|_F$ is the Euclidean Frobenius matrix norm. Let $P$ be the coefficientwise vector multiplier with $P_0=I$ and $P_k=I-kk^{\mathsf T}/|k|^2$ for $k\ne0$. The equations below hold pointwise on $(0,T)\times Q_d$ and at the time endpoints by continuous extension.

(i) If $\nu\ge0$ and $u,v\in C^\infty([0,T]\times Q_d;\mathbb R^d)$ satisfy, for each $z\in\{u,v\}$,
$$z_t+P((z\cdot\nabla)z)=\nu\Delta z,\qquad \operatorname{div}z=0,$$
then for every $t\in[0,T]$, with $w=u-v$,
$$\|w(t)\|_2^2\le\|w(0)\|_2^2\exp\!\left(2\int_0^t\|\nabla v(\tau)\|_\infty\,d\tau\right).$$

(ii) Let $N\ge1$ and, for $1\le j\le d$, let $A_j:\mathbb R^N\to\mathbb R^{N\times N}$ be a fixed real-linear map whose image consists of symmetric matrices. If $q,r\in C^\infty([0,T]\times Q_d;\mathbb R^N)$ satisfy, for each $z\in\{q,r\}$,
$$z_t+\sum_{j=1}^dA_j(z)\partial_jz=0,$$
then for every $t\in[0,T]$,
$$\|q(t)-r(t)\|_2^2\le\|q(0)-r(0)\|_2^2\exp\!\left(C_{d,N,A}\int_0^t(\|\nabla q(\tau)\|_\infty+\|\nabla r(\tau)\|_\infty)\,d\tau\right),$$
where $C_{d,N,A}$ depends only on $d,N$ and the operator norms of the finitely many maps $A_j$. For either pair $(z_1,z_2)=(u,v)$ or $(q,r)$, put $w=z_1-z_2$. Let $\Gamma\ge0$ be any uniform rate for which the corresponding squared $L^2$ estimate above gives $\|w(t)\|_2^2\le\|w(0)\|_2^2e^{\Gamma t}$. If $s\ge1$ and $\max_{t\in[0,T]}\max(\|z_1(t)\|_{H^s},\|z_2(t)\|_{H^s})\le M$ for some $M\ge0$, define
$$B_s(M)=\begin{cases}1,&s=1,\\(2M)^{(s-1)/s},&s>1.\end{cases}$$
Then for every $t\in[0,T]$,
$$\|w(t)\|_{H^{s-1}}\le B_s(M)\|w(0)\|_2^{1/s}e^{\Gamma t/(2s)}.$$
These are conditional estimates for already given smooth maps on the stated cylinder and assert no existence theorem. All quantities are mathematical and no physical units are assigned to $\nu$.

For $\alpha=(\alpha_1,\ldots,\alpha_d)\in\mathbb N_0^d$, write $|\alpha|=\sum_j\alpha_j$ and $\partial^\alpha=\partial_1^{\alpha_1}\cdots\partial_d^{\alpha_d}$. Give $C^\infty(Q_d;\mathbb R)$ the Fr'echet topology generated by $p_m(\phi)=\max_{|\alpha|\le m}\|\partial^\alpha\phi\|_\infty$, for $m\in\mathbb N_0$, where the derivatives are those of the smooth periodic lift to $\mathbb R^d$. A periodic distribution is a continuous real-linear functional on this test space, extended complex-linearly to complex-valued tests. For such a distribution $S$, define $\widehat S(k)=\langle S,e^{-ik\cdot x}angle$ for $e_k(x)=e^{ik\cdot x}$ and define its mean to be $\widehat S(0)=\langle S,1angle$. For an integrable function $g$, the pairing is $\langle g,\phiangle=\int_{Q_d}g\phi\,d\mu$. Define distributional derivatives by $\langle\partial_jS,\phiangle=-\langle S,\partial_j\phiangle$. For a smooth scalar test, $
abla\phi=(\partial_1\phi,\ldots,\partial_d\phi)$ and $\Delta\phi=\sum_j\partial_j^2\phi$; for a smooth vector field $v$, $\operatorname{div}v=\sum_j\partial_jv_j$, $(v\otimes v)_{ij}=v_iv_j$, and $(v\cdot
abla)v_i=\sum_jv_j\partial_jv_i$. In particular, $\operatorname{div}u=0$ distributionally means $-\int_{Q_d}u\cdot
abla\phi\,d\mu=0$ for every real test function $\phi$. Equality of periodic distributions means equality on every such test function. Assume Countable Choice. Let $d\in\{1,2,3\}$, let $s>d/2+1$, and let $u\in H^s(Q_d;\mathbb R^d)$ satisfy $\operatorname{div}u=0$ in this sense. Then $u\otimes u\in H^s$, the mean-zero scalar $\pi=Q(u\otimes u)$ belongs to $H^s$, and in $H^{s-1}$,
$$P(u\cdot
abla u)=u\cdot
abla u+
abla\pi.$$
Among mean-zero periodic distributions $\widetilde\pi$ for which this identity holds as an equality of periodic distributions, this pressure is unique. The formula is a torus pressure recovery result and asserts no wall pressure regularity.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $d\in\{1,2,3\}$, $T>0$, and $Q_d=\mathbb R^d/(2\pi\mathbb Z)^d$ with normalized measure $d\mu=(2\pi)^{-d}dx$. For $z:Q_d\to\mathbb R^M$, use componentwise Fourier coefficients $\widehat z(k)=\int_{Q_d}z(x)e^{-ik\cdot x}\,d\mu(x)$, weights $w_k=(1+|k|^2)^{1/2}$, and the weighted coefficient completion norm $\|z\|_{H^s}^2=\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z^d}w_k^{2s}|\widehat z(k)|^2$; the normalized Fourier isometry gives $\|z\|_2^2=\sum_k|\widehat z(k)|^2$, where $\|z\|_2=(\int_{Q_d}|z|^2\,d\mu)^{1/2}$ and the pointwise component norm is Euclidean. In particular, $H^0=L^2$. For a map $z:[0,T]\times Q_d\to\mathbb R^M$, smooth on the closed cylinder means that for every $m\in\mathbb N_0$ and spatial multi-index $\alpha$, $\partial_t^m\partial_x^\alpha z$ exists on $(0,T)\times Q_d$ and extends continuously to $[0,T]\times Q_d$; spatial derivatives are those of its periodic lift. For a spatial vector field define $\operatorname{div}z=\sum_{j=1}^d\partial_jz_j$ and $\Delta z=\sum_{j=1}^d\partial_j^2z$. Write $\nabla z$ for the spatial Jacobian and $\|\nabla z(t)\|_\infty=\sup_{x\in Q_d}|\nabla z(t,x)|_F$, where $|\cdot|_F$ is the Euclidean Frobenius matrix norm. Let $P$ be the coefficientwise vector multiplier with $P_0=I$ and $P_k=I-kk^{\mathsf T}/|k|^2$ for $k\ne0$. The equations below hold pointwise on $(0,T)\times Q_d$ and at the time endpoints by continuous extension.

(i) If $\nu\ge0$ and $u,v\in C^\infty([0,T]\times Q_d;\mathbb R^d)$ satisfy, for each $z\in\{u,v\}$,
$$z_t+P((z\cdot\nabla)z)=\nu\Delta z,\qquad \operatorname{div}z=0,$$
then for every $t\in[0,T]$, with $w=u-v$,
$$\|w(t)\|_2^2\le\|w(0)\|_2^2\exp\!\left(2\int_0^t\|\nabla v(\tau)\|_\infty\,d\tau\right).$$

(ii) Let $N\ge1$ and, for $1\le j\le d$, let $A_j:\mathbb R^N\to\mathbb R^{N\times N}$ be a fixed real-linear map whose image consists of symmetric matrices. If $q,r\in C^\infty([0,T]\times Q_d;\mathbb R^N)$ satisfy, for each $z\in\{q,r\}$,
$$z_t+\sum_{j=1}^dA_j(z)\partial_jz=0,$$
then for every $t\in[0,T]$,
$$\|q(t)-r(t)\|_2^2\le\|q(0)-r(0)\|_2^2\exp\!\left(C_{d,N,A}\int_0^t(\|\nabla q(\tau)\|_\infty+\|\nabla r(\tau)\|_\infty)\,d\tau\right),$$
where $C_{d,N,A}$ depends only on $d,N$ and the operator norms of the finitely many maps $A_j$. For either pair $(z_1,z_2)=(u,v)$ or $(q,r)$, put $w=z_1-z_2$. Let $\Gamma\ge0$ be any uniform rate for which the corresponding squared $L^2$ estimate above gives $\|w(t)\|_2^2\le\|w(0)\|_2^2e^{\Gamma t}$. If $s\ge1$ and $\max_{t\in[0,T]}\max(\|z_1(t)\|_{H^s},\|z_2(t)\|_{H^s})\le M$ for some $M\ge0$, define
$$B_s(M)=\begin{cases}1,&s=1,\\(2M)^{(s-1)/s},&s>1.\end{cases}$$
Then for every $t\in[0,T]$,
$$\|w(t)\|_{H^{s-1}}\le B_s(M)\|w(0)\|_2^{1/s}e^{\Gamma t/(2s)}.$$
These are conditional estimates for already given smooth maps on the stated cylinder and assert no existence theorem. All quantities are mathematical and no physical units are assigned to $\nu$.

Completeness of the coefficient space [F1] yields a limit $u\in\bigcap_{m\ge s}C([0,T],H^m)$; finite sums show $\sup_t\|u(t)\|_{H^m}\le\sup_N\sup_t\|u_N(t)\|_{H^m}$, and coefficientwise limits preserve reality, divergence-free constraints, and $u(0)=u_0$.

Since $d\le3$ and $s\ge4$, we have $s>d/2+1$. The pressure recovery statement [F9] therefore applies to the smooth divergence-free field from step 11.1 and yields the unique mean-zero $\pi=Q(u\otimes u)$ with $P(u\cdot
abla u)=u\cdot
abla u+
abla\pi$. Substitution into the projected equation gives $u_t+(u\cdot
abla)u=-
abla\pi+
u\Delta u$.

Let $u,v$ be any two smooth solutions with the same initial datum and viscosity. They satisfy the hypotheses of [F10], so $\|u(t)-v(t)\|_2^2\le0\cdot\exp(2\int_0^t\|\nabla v(s)\|_\infty ds)=0$ for each $t\in[0,T]$. Thus $u=v$ throughout the interval. before.claim: Write Fourier coefficients with kernel $e^{-ik\cdot x}$. For each $k\in\mathbb Z^d$, the PDE is the finite-dimensional ODE $\dot{\widehat z}=-i\rho_* k\cdot\widehat v$, $\dot{\widehat v}=-i(c_*^2/\rho_*)k\widehat z$. For $k\ne0$, differentiating the first equation and substituting the second gives $\ddot{\widehat z}+c_*^2|k|^2\widehat z=0$. With $\omega_k=c_*|k|$, its unique solution is $\widehat z(t,k)=\widehat z_0(k)\cos(\omega_kt)-i\rho_*(k\cdot\widehat v_0(k))\sin(\omega_kt)/\omega_k$, and integrating the second mode equation gives $\widehat v(t,k)=\widehat v_0(k)-i(c_*^2/\rho_*)k\int_0^t\widehat z(s,k)\,ds$. At $k=0$ both coefficients are constant.

Differentiation of these formulas recovers both mode equations and their initial coefficients. For each $k$, differentiating $E_k=|\widehat v|^2+(c_*^2/\rho_*^2)|\widehat z|^2$ gives zero: the two cross terms are $-i(c_*^2/\rho_*)[(k\widehat z)\cdot\overline{\widehat v}+(k\cdot\widehat v)\overline{\widehat z}]$, whose bracket is real, so its real part vanishes. Thus $E_k(t)=E_k(0)$ for every mode. The mode formulas also preserve conjugate symmetry because their coefficients at $-k$ are conjugates of those at $k$.

Multiplying $E_k(t)=E_k(0)$ by $(1+|k|^2)^m$ and summing over $k$ proves the stated conserved weighted energy by Parseval [F2]. Since the initial data are smooth, these sums are finite for every integer $m$; therefore the coefficient families remain in every $H^m$, uniformly for all time.

Fourier synthesis [F2], under the stated Countable Choice assumption [A1], now defines real fields $z(t),v(t)$. The uniform $H^m$ bounds and embeddings [F3] imply convergence of the Fourier series with every spatial derivative, locally uniformly in time. The mode equations pass through these convergent series and give the PDE. Write $q=(z,v)$ and let $\mathcal L$ be the constant-coefficient first-order spatial operator in that system; recursively $\partial_t^nq=\mathcal L^nq$, which is a finite sum of spatial derivatives of order at most $n$. Thus all mixed derivatives are continuous, so $q\in C^\infty(\mathbb R\times\mathbb T^d)$.

For any two smooth solutions with the same data, each Fourier-mode difference solves the same linear ODE with zero initial value. Uniqueness of the finite-dimensional linear ODE gives zero difference at each $k$, and Fourier synthesis then gives equality of the fields. Together with the energy conservation and smooth synthesis above, this proves the global existence, conservation, and uniqueness assertions.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $L_1,L_2,h,
u>0$ and let $\Omega=(\mathbb R/L_1\mathbb Z)	imes(0,h)	imes(\mathbb R/L_2\mathbb Z)$ with periodic coordinates $x,z$ and no-slip walls $y=0,h$. Use product Lebesgue measure $dx\,dy\,dz$, with the quotient coordinates carrying their period-length measures. Suppose $F\in C^\infty([0,h])$ has a smooth odd $2h$-periodic extension to the real line. For $n\ge1$, define $b_n=(2/h)\int_0^hF(y)\sin(n\pi y/h)\,dy$ and
$$V(t,y)=\sum_{n=1}^\infty b_n e^{-
u(n\pi/h)^2t}\sin(n\pi y/h),\qquad t\ge0.$$
Then $u(t,x,y,z)=(V(t,y),0,0)$ is a global smooth real solution, unique among all smooth velocity solutions with the same initial data, of the incompressible periodic-channel system $u_t+u\cdot
abla u+
abla\pi=
u\Delta u$, $\operatorname{div}u=0$, $u|_{y=0,h}=0$, $u(0)=(F(y),0,0)$, with mean-zero pressure $\pi=0$. The same sine series defines a smooth $2h$-periodic function of $y$ on the full real line. For every $t\ge0$, $\|u(t)\|_{L^2(\Omega)}\le e^{-
u(\pi/h)^2t}\|u(0)\|_{L^2(\Omega)}$. This theorem concerns the shear solution and smooth uniqueness for the same full-flow data; it gives no global regularity theorem for perturbed three-dimensional flows.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $d\in\{1,2,3\}$, let $s\ge4$ be an integer, let $
u\ge0$, and let $u_0:\mathbb T^d	o\mathbb R^d$ be smooth, real, and divergence-free, where $\mathbb T^d=(\mathbb R/2\pi\mathbb Z)^d$ has normalized Lebesgue measure and divergence-free means $\sum_{j=1}^d\partial_j(u_0)_j=0$. For a smooth periodic $f$, set $\widehat f(k)=(2\pi)^{-d}\int_{[0,2\pi]^d}f(x)e^{-ik\cdot x}\,dx$, $w_k=(1+|k|^2)^{1/2}$, and $\|f\|_{H^m}^2=\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z^d}w_k^{2m}|\widehat f(k)|^2$. Define the Leray multiplier by $P_0=I$ and $P_k=I-kk^{\mathsf T}/|k|^2$ for $k
e0$. Then there is $T>0$, depending only on $d$, $s$, and $\|u_0\|_{H^s}$ and independent of $
u$ and all higher Sobolev norms of $u_0$, and a unique smooth real field $u:[0,T]	imes\mathbb T^d	o\mathbb R^d$ satisfying
$$u(0,\cdot)=u_0,\qquad \partial_tu+P((u\cdot
abla)u)=
u\Delta u,\qquad \operatorname{div}u=0.$$
The same time $T$ works for every integer Sobolev order $m\ge s$, and $\sup_{0\le t\le T}\|u(t)\|_{H^m}<\infty$ for each such $m$. There is a unique smooth mean-zero scalar field $\pi$ for which the equivalent full equation $\partial_tu+(u\cdot

For positive density $\rho>0$, define the polytropic pressure $p(\rho)=\kappa\rho^\gamma$, sound speed $c(\rho)=\sqrt{p'(\rho)}=\sqrt{\kappa\gamma}\,\rho^a$, and sound-speed variable $r=c/a$. u\le1$, smooth solutions $u^
u$ of the periodic Navier–Stokes equation and $v=u^0$ of periodic Euler with the same initial data. For every $t\in[0,T]$,
$$\|u^
u(t)-v(t)\|_{L^2}\le
u\int_0^t\exp\!\left(\int_s^t\|
abla v(	au)\|_{L^\infty}\,d	auight)\|\Delta v(s)\|_{L^2}\,ds.$$
Consequently the $L^2$ error is $O(
u)$ uniformly on $[0,T]$ as $
u\downarrow0$. For each integer $m\ge s$, the same local construction supplies a uniform $H^m$ bound for this family, independent of $
u$; therefore the $H^{s-1}$ error is $O(
u^{1/s})$. The result is confined to a fixed periodic domain and this common local smooth interval; it asserts no wall inviscid limit or boundary-layer estimate.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $d\in\{1,2,3\}$, $\rho_*>0$, $c_*>0$, and let $z_0:\mathbb T^d\to\mathbb R$ and $v_0:\mathbb T^d\to\mathbb R^d$ be smooth periodic data on the normalized torus $\mathbb T^d=(\mathbb R/2\pi\mathbb Z)^d$. Use normalized measure $d\mu=(2\pi)^{-d}dx$, coefficients $\widehat f(k)=\int f(x)e^{-ik\cdot x}\,d\mu(x)$, weights $w_k=(1+|k|^2)^{1/2}$, and componentwise norms $\|f\|_{H^m}^2=\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z^d}w_k^{2m}|\widehat f(k)|^2$. The constant-coefficient tangent system
$$z_t+\rho_*\operatorname{div}v=0,\qquad v_t+(c_*^2/\rho_*)\nabla z=0,\qquad (z,v)|_{t=0}=(z_0,v_0)$$
has a unique real $C^\infty$ solution $(z,v)$ on $\mathbb R\times\mathbb T^d$. For every integer $m\ge0$, the weighted energy $\|v(t)\|_{H^m}^2+(c_*^2/\rho_*^2)\|z(t)\|_{H^m}^2$ is constant for all $t\in\mathbb R$. This is the exact linear tangent model; it does not assert equality with a finite-amplitude nonlinear fluid evolution.

$$u_t+(u\cdot\nabla)u=-\nabla\pi+\nu\Delta u,\qquad \operatorname{div}u=0,$$

$$u_\lambda(t,x)=\lambda u(\lambda^2t,\lambda x),\qquad \pi_\lambda(t,x)=\lambda^2\pi(\lambda^2t,\lambda x)$$
solves the same system with the same viscosity on $\mathbb R^d$ or on the torus of period $\ell/\lambda$, respectively, for $0\le t\le T/\lambda^2$. On the torus, use the Fourier Leray multiplier $P_0=I$, $P_\xi=I-\xi\xi^{\mathsf T}/|\xi|^2$ for $\xi\ne0$; the projected equation is preserved as well because $P_{\lambda\xi}=P_\xi$. $$u_{\alpha,\beta}(t,x)=\alpha u(\alpha\beta t,\beta x),\qquad \pi_{\alpha,\beta}(t,x)=\alpha^2\pi(\alpha\beta t,\beta x)$$
solves the same equation on the correspondingly scaled domain and time interval $0\le t\le T/(\alpha\beta)$. These transformations are equation symmetries; on a torus they transform its period.

Let $p$ be differentiable at the positive reference density $\rho_*$, with pressure measured in Pa and $p'(\rho_*)>0$ in m$^2$/s$^2$, and sound speed $c_*=\sqrt{p'(\rho_*)}$. For the linear acoustic tangent system $\delta\rho_t+\rho_*\operatorname{div}v_{\rm phys}=0$, $(v_{\rm phys})_t+(c_*^2/\rho_*)\nabla_X\delta\rho=0$, where $\delta\rho$ has units kg/m$^3$, the scales $X=Lx$, $t_{\rm phys}=(L/U)t$, $\delta\rho=\rho_*\delta\rho'$, and $v_{\rm phys}=Uv$ give the momentum coefficient $Ma^{-2}$, where $Ma=U/c_*$. Both $Re$ and $Ma$ are dimensionless. These are chain-rule identities and assert no continuum limit or empirical similarity.

statement.

> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

The physical density $\rho_{\mathrm{phys}}$ is measured in kilograms per cubic metre, velocity $u_{\mathrm{phys}}$ in metres per second, and pressure $p_{\mathrm{phys}}$ in pascals. $$\partial_t\rho_{\mathrm{phys}}+\nabla_X\cdot(\rho_{\mathrm{phys}}u_{\mathrm{phys}})=0,\qquad \partial_tu_{\mathrm{phys}}+(u_{\mathrm{phys}}\cdot\nabla_X)u_{\mathrm{phys}}+\rho_{\mathrm{phys}}^{-1}\nabla_X\!\left(\kappa_{\mathrm{phys}}\rho_{\mathrm{phys}}^\gamma\right)=0,$$
where the same fixed $\kappa_{\mathrm{phys}}$ and $\gamma$ apply throughout the flow. Set $x=X/L\in\mathbb T^d=(\mathbb R/(2\pi\mathbb Z))^d$, $\tau=tU_*/L$, $R=\rho_{\mathrm{phys}}/\rho_*$, $V=u_{\mathrm{phys}}/U_*$, $P=p_{\mathrm{phys}}/(\rho_*U_*^2)$, and $\bar\kappa=\kappa_{\mathrm{phys}}\rho_*^{\gamma-1}/U_*^2>0$. after.claim: Let $\widetilde\Omega=\mathbb R\times(0,h)\times\mathbb R$ and $\Lambda=\{(mL_x,0,nL_z):m,n\in\mathbb Z\}$. For $U=U_P$ in the Poiseuille case and $U=U_C$ in the Couette case, define the lifted material map for each $t$ by $\widetilde\chi^U_t(x,y,z)=(x+tU(y),y,z)$. Both profiles are smooth, so this map is $C^\infty$; its inverse is $(x-tU(y),y,z)$. It maps $\widetilde\Omega$ onto itself, fixes the $y$ coordinate, and obeys $\widetilde\chi^U_t(a+\lambda)=\widetilde\chi^U_t(a)+\lambda$ for every $\lambda\in\Lambda$. Its Jacobian matrix is $\begin{pmatrix}1&tU'(y)&0\\0&1&0\\0&0&1\end{pmatrix}$, with determinant $1>0$. Since $y$ is unchanged, $\partial_t\widetilde\chi^U_t=(U(y),0,0)=\widetilde u(t,\widetilde\chi^U_t(x,y,z))$, so each map descends to the periodic channel and has the example's velocity as its Eulerian velocity. Thus both profiles meet the material-motion hypothesis of [F1].

In the Poiseuille case, $U_P(0)=U_P(h)=0$ and $U_P''=-G/\eta$. Thus $(\operatorname{div}\sigma)_x+\rho b_x=\eta U_P''+G=0$, and the other momentum components vanish, proving the steady equations and no-slip compatibility. Direct integration gives $Q_P=\int_0^hU_P(y)\,dy=Gh^3/(12\eta)$ and $\omega_{P,z}=-U_P'=-G(h-2y)/(2\eta)$.

In the Couette case, $U_C(0)=0$, $U_C(h)=V$, and $U_C''=0$, so the momentum equation holds with constant pressure and no body force; the velocity traces equal the stated wall velocities. Direct integration gives $Q_C=\int_0^hU_C(y)\,dy=Vh/2$ and $\omega_{C,z}=-U_C'=-V/h$.

By the defined squared norm $|D|^2=D:D$, for either profile $|D|^2=(U')^2/2$, hence viscous dissipation per unit streamwise/spanwise wall area is $\eta\int_0^h(U')^2\,dy$. In the Poiseuille case this is $\frac{G^2}{4\eta}\int_0^h(h-2y)^2\,dy=G^2h^3/(12\eta)$, while body-force power is $\int_0^h\rho(G/\rho)U_P\,dy=GQ_P=G^2h^3/(12\eta)$; stationary-wall power is zero. This agrees with the stationary no-slip case of [F1].

In the Couette case viscous dissipation per unit wall area is $\eta\int_0^h(V/h)^2\,dy=\eta V^2/h$. At the top wall $n=(0,1,0)$ and $\sigma n$ has tangential component $\eta(V/h)(1,0,0)$, so wall power per unit area is $g\cdot\sigma n=\eta V^2/h$; the lower wall has $g=0$. This agrees with the tangential no-slip case of [F1]. Finally, a purported periodic pressure $p_0-Gx$ changes by $-GL_x$ under $x\mapsto x+L_x$, so it is not single-valued on $\Omega$ when $G>0$; the body-force formulation in the Example avoids that incompatibility.

For either profile $u=(U(y),0,0)$, $\operatorname{div}u=0$, $\partial_tu=0$ and $(u\cdot\nabla)u=U(y)\partial_xu=0$. The only nonzero entries of $D$ are $D_{xy}=D_{yx}=U'/2$, so the only nonzero viscous shear entries are $\sigma_{xy}=\sigma_{yx}=\eta U'$, and $(\operatorname{div}\sigma)_x=-\partial_xp+\eta U''$.

The conductivity law is tensor-valued and may be anisotropic; no restriction $K=kI_3$ is imposed. after.claim: Fix an admissible reference region $V$ and write $J(t,a)=\det D_a\chi(t,a)$. Change of variables gives $\int_{\chi_t(V)}\rho u\,dx=\int_V\rho u(t,\chi(t,a))J(t,a)\,da$. From $\partial_t\chi=u\circ\chi$ and Jacobi's determinant formula, $\partial_tJ=J(\operatorname{div}u)(t,\chi)=0$. Differentiating the changed integral by the chain rule therefore yields $\frac{d}{dt}\int_{\chi_t(V)}\rho u\,dx=\int_{\chi_t(V)}\rho(\partial_tu+(u\cdot\nabla)u)\,dx$.

The image $\chi_t(V)$ is a bounded $C^1$ domain and the adopted Newtonian stress [F3] is $C^1$ up to its boundary by the stated field regularity. Apply [F4] to each row of $\sigma$ to replace its traction resultant by $\int_{\chi_t(V)}\operatorname{div}\sigma\,dx$. Substitution of step 1.1 into [A1] gives $\int_{\chi_t(V)}R(t,x)\,dx=0$ for every such $V$, where $R:=\rho(\partial_tu+(u\cdot\nabla)u)-\rho b-\operatorname{div}\sigma$ is continuous. The hypotheses of [F4] hold by the stated regularity, the $C^2$ motion and [A2].

Fix $t$ and $x_0\in\Omega_t$. For all sufficiently small $r>0$, the closed ball $\overline{B_r(x_0)}$ lies in $\Omega_t$; because $\chi_t$ is a $C^2$ diffeomorphism, $V:=\chi_t^{-1}(B_r(x_0))$ is a bounded open reference region with $C^1$ boundary. Both contradict the zero integral, so $R_i(t,x_0)=0$ for each component. Thus $R=0$ throughout $\Omega_t$, which is the claimed local momentum equation.

Assume Countable Choice. For any open $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$,
$n\ge1$, any $1\le p\le\infty$ and any
$\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$, extension by zero
$$E_0u(x)=u(x)\ \ (x\in\Omega),\qquad E_0u(x)=0\ \ (x\notin\Omega),$$
acted on representatives, sends $W_0^{1,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ linearly into
$W^{1,p}(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb K)$. For every $u\in W_0^{1,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$
and every coordinate direction $i$, the class $D_i(E_0u)$ is the zero
extension of the class $D_iu$, and every $L^p$ component norm is preserved:
$$\|E_0u\|_{L^p(\mathbb R^n)}=\|u\|_{L^p(\Omega)},\qquad \|D_i(E_0u)\|_{L^p(\mathbb R^n)}=\|D_iu\|_{L^p(\Omega)},$$
so that $\|E_0u\|_{W^{1,p}(\mathbb R^n)}=\|u\|_{W^{1,p}(\Omega)}$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice, used to invoke the published real and complex
$L^p$ completeness results through their Countable-Choice interface. Let
$\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, $n\ge1$, let $k\in\mathbb N_0$,
$1\le p\le\infty$, and $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$. Then
$W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$, equipped with the displayed norm of
[[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]], is a complete normed space over
$\mathbb K$.

Both endpoints $p=1$ and $p=\infty$ are included, as is $k=0$, where the
assertion reduces to the completeness of $L^p$. If $\Omega=\varnothing$, then
$W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ is the zero space and the assertion is trivial.
The Axiom of Choice is used only to derive Countable Choice for the two
published completeness interfaces; no other selection is made. Representative
selection inside the finitely many coordinate classes is finite and
choice-free.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $n\ge1$
and let $e_k(x)=\exp(2\pi i\,k\cdot x)$, $k\in\mathbb Z^n$, be the coordinate
characters on $\mathbb T^n$
([[def-the-one-dimensional-torus-and-normalized-haar-integral]],
[[def-fourier-coefficients-and-trigonometric-polynomials]]). Then:

1. $(e_k)_{k\in\mathbb Z^n}$ is an orthonormal family in the complex Hilbert
   space $L^2(\mathbb T^n)$;
2. it is an orthonormal basis: its closed linear span is $L^2(\mathbb T^n)$;
3. consequently the Fourier expansion
   $f=\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z^n}\widehat f(k)e_k$ and Parseval's identity
   $$\|f\|_2^2=\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z^n}|\widehat f(k)|^2,\qquad \langle f,g\rangle=\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z^n}\widehat f(k)\overline{\widehat g(k)}$$
   hold for all $f,g\in L^2(\mathbb T^n)$, in the finite-subset-net sense; and
4. the Fourier coefficient map is a surjective linear isometry of
   $L^2(\mathbb T^n)$ onto $\ell^2(\mathbb Z^n,\mathbb C)$.

No Hilbert tensor-product identification is used anywhere.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space, let $p,q\in[1,\infty]$ be
conjugate exponents, and let $f,g$ be measurable real-valued functions.

1. If $1\le p<\infty$ and $q<\infty$ with $f\in\mathcal L^p(\mu)$ and
   $g\in\mathcal L^q(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_p\|g\|_q.$$
2. If $p=1$ and $q=\infty$ with $f\in\mathcal L^1(\mu)$ and
   $g\in L^\infty(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_1\|g\|_\infty.$$
3. If $p=\infty$ and $q=1$ with $f\in L^\infty(\mu)$ and
   $g\in\mathcal L^1(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_\infty\|g\|_1.$$

In every case the right-hand side is finite, so $fg$ is integrable.

Let $H,V,H^{-r}$ be the spaces of Periodic solenoidal Fourier spaces, let
$T>0$, and identify time-dependent functions that agree almost everywhere.
A map $u:[0,T]\to H$ is in $C_w([0,T];H)$ when
$t\mapsto (u(t),h)_H$ is continuous for each fixed $h\in H$. A map
$u:(0,T)\to X$ into a separable Hilbert space $X$ is strongly measurable
when it is an almost-everywhere pointwise limit of measurable simple
$X$-valued maps. For $1\le p<\infty$, $L^p(0,T;X)$ consists of strongly
measurable maps with $\int_0^T\|u(t)\|_X^pdt<\infty$; $L^\infty(0,T;X)$
uses the essential supremum norm. In this page, $L^p_{\rm loc}(0,\infty;X)$
means membership on every finite interval $(0,T)$. These conventions also
apply with $X=V$ and $X=H^{-r}$.

For a distribution $u\in\mathcal D'(\Omega)$ in the convention of [[def-distribution]] and a multi-index $\alpha\in\mathbb N_0^n$, its **distributional derivative** is
$$\langle\partial^\alpha u,\varphi\rangle=(-1)^{|\alpha|}\langle u,\partial^\alpha\varphi\rangle\qquad(\varphi\in\mathcal D(\Omega)).$$
The test derivative is a continuous linear endomorphism by [[thm-test-function-operations-are-continuous]]. Its composition with $u$, multiplied by the indicated sign, is therefore a continuous complex-linear functional, so this definition produces a distribution. The pairing is bilinear, with no complex conjugation. For $\alpha=0$ the operation is the identity; for one coordinate derivative its sign is minus. Every derivative of the zero distribution is zero, including on the empty domain. No choice axiom enters this construction. Compatibility with classical derivatives requires an integration-by-parts argument where it is used; it is not part of the definition.

Let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^3$ be a nonempty bounded open set. Let
$C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb R^3)$ denote smooth compactly supported vector
fields and set
$$D_\sigma(\Omega)=\{a\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb R^3):\operatorname{div}a=0\}.$$
Let $H$ be the closure of $D_\sigma(\Omega)$ in
$L^2(\Omega;\mathbb R^3)$, and let $V$ be its closure in
$H_0^1(\Omega;\mathbb R^3)$, where $H_0^1$ is the $H^1$ closure of
$C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb R^3)$ and weak derivatives define the $H^1$
norm. Use $\|a\|_H=\|a\|_2$ and
$\|a\|_V^2=\|a\|_2^2+\|\nabla a\|_2^2$. Each $V$ element has zero
extension in $H^1(\mathbb R^3)$ and distributional divergence zero. This
closure definition does not identify $V$ with every divergence-free member
of $H_0^1(\Omega;\mathbb R^3)$ on an arbitrary open set, and it makes no
pointwise boundary trace assertion.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. For every nonempty bounded open
$\Omega\subset\mathbb R^3$, the closure spaces $H,V$ of
Bounded no-slip solenoidal closure spaces are separable Hilbert spaces, with
$V\hookrightarrow H$ continuous and dense. There is a countable sequence
$e_j\in D_\sigma(\Omega)$ that is orthonormal in $H$ and whose finite linear
span is dense in both $H$ and $V$. No Stokes eigenfunction regularity or
identification of $V$ with a larger solenoidal space is asserted.

Assume Countable Choice. For any open $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$,
$n\ge1$, any $1\le p\le\infty$ and any
$\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$, extension by zero
$$E_0u(x)=u(x)\ \ (x\in\Omega),\qquad E_0u(x)=0\ \ (x\notin\Omega),$$
acted on representatives, sends $W_0^{1,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ linearly into
$W^{1,p}(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb K)$. For every $u\in W_0^{1,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$
and every coordinate direction $i$, the class $D_i(E_0u)$ is the zero
extension of the class $D_iu$, and every $L^p$ component norm is preserved:
$$\|E_0u\|_{L^p(\mathbb R^n)}=\|u\|_{L^p(\Omega)},\qquad \|D_i(E_0u)\|_{L^p(\mathbb R^n)}=\|D_iu\|_{L^p(\Omega)},$$
so that $\|E_0u\|_{W^{1,p}(\mathbb R^n)}=\|u\|_{W^{1,p}(\Omega)}$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to \mathbb C$ belong to
$L^1(\mu \times \nu)$. Then:

1. for $\mu$-almost every $x$, the section $f_x$ belongs to $L^1(\nu)$;
2. for $\nu$-almost every $y$, the section $f^y$ belongs to $L^1(\mu)$;
3. after assigning the value $0$ on the exceptional parameter sets, the
   section-integral functions are integrable; and
4. the three integrals agree:
$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

$$F(x):=\int_a^x f(t)\,dt\qquad(a\le x\le b).$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space, let $p,q\in[1,\infty]$ be
conjugate exponents, and let $f,g$ be measurable real-valued functions.

1. If $1\le p<\infty$ and $q<\infty$ with $f\in\mathcal L^p(\mu)$ and
   $g\in\mathcal L^q(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_p\|g\|_q.$$
2. If $p=1$ and $q=\infty$ with $f\in\mathcal L^1(\mu)$ and
   $g\in L^\infty(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_1\|g\|_\infty.$$
3. If $p=\infty$ and $q=1$ with $f\in L^\infty(\mu)$ and
   $g\in\mathcal L^1(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_\infty\|g\|_1.$$

In every case the right-hand side is finite, so $fg$ is integrable.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. For every nonempty bounded open
$\Omega\subset\mathbb R^3$, the closure spaces $H,V$ of
Bounded no-slip solenoidal closure spaces are separable Hilbert spaces, with
$V\hookrightarrow H$ continuous and dense. There is a countable sequence
$e_j\in D_\sigma(\Omega)$ that is orthonormal in $H$ and whose finite linear
span is dense in both $H$ and $V$. No Stokes eigenfunction regularity or
identification of $V$ with a larger solenoidal space is asserted.

statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

before.quote:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^3$ be a nonempty bounded open set. Let
$C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb R^3)$ denote smooth compactly supported vector
fields and set
$$D_\sigma(\Omega)=\{a\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb R^3):\operatorname{div}a=0\}.$$
Let $H$ be the closure of $D_\sigma(\Omega)$ in
$L^2(\Omega;\mathbb R^3)$, and let $V$ be its closure in
$H_0^1(\Omega;\mathbb R^3)$, where $H_0^1$ is the $H^1$ closure of
$C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb R^3)$ and weak derivatives define the $H^1$
norm. Use $\|a\|_H=\|a\|_2$ and
$\|a\|_V^2=\|a\|_2^2+\|\nabla a\|_2^2$. Each $V$ element has zero
extension in $H^1(\mathbb R^3)$ and distributional divergence zero. This
closure definition does not identify $V$ with every divergence-free member
of $H_0^1(\Omega;\mathbb R^3)$ on an arbitrary open set, and it makes no
pointwise boundary trace assertion.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space, let $p,q\in[1,\infty]$ be
conjugate exponents, and let $f,g$ be measurable real-valued functions.

1. If $1\le p<\infty$ and $q<\infty$ with $f\in\mathcal L^p(\mu)$ and
   $g\in\mathcal L^q(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_p\|g\|_q.$$
2. If $p=1$ and $q=\infty$ with $f\in\mathcal L^1(\mu)$ and
   $g\in L^\infty(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_1\|g\|_\infty.$$
3. If $p=\infty$ and $q=1$ with $f\in L^\infty(\mu)$ and
   $g\in\mathcal L^1(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_\infty\|g\|_1.$$

In every case the right-hand side is finite, so $fg$ is integrable.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to \mathbb C$ belong to
$L^1(\mu \times \nu)$. Then:

1. for $\mu$-almost every $x$, the section $f_x$ belongs to $L^1(\nu)$;
2. for $\nu$-almost every $y$, the section $f^y$ belongs to $L^1(\mu)$;
3. after assigning the value $0$ on the exceptional parameter sets, the
   section-integral functions are integrable; and
4. the three integrals agree:
$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice (The Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$)).

Let $a<b$ and let $f\in L^1([a,b])$. Fix a measurable integrable representative, also denoted by $f$, if $L^1([a,b])$ is interpreted as a space of almost-everywhere equivalence classes. Define
$$F(x):=\int_a^x f(t)\,dt\qquad(a\le x\le b).$$
Then there is a measurable set $E\subseteq(a,b)$ whose complement in $(a,b)$ has Lebesgue measure zero such that $F$ is differentiable at every $x\in E$ and
$$F'(x)=f(x)\qquad(x\in E).$$
The primitive $F$ is independent of the chosen representative; the almost-everywhere derivative identity holds for every fixed measurable integrable representative.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

$\Omega\subset\mathbb R^3$, the closure spaces $H,V$ of
Bounded no-slip solenoidal closure spaces are separable Hilbert spaces, with
$V\hookrightarrow H$ continuous and dense. There is a countable sequence
$e_j\in D_\sigma(\Omega)$ that is orthonormal in $H$ and whose finite linear
span is dense in both $H$ and $V$. No Stokes eigenfunction regularity or
identification of $V$ with a larger solenoidal space is asserted.

$u:(0,T)\to X$ into a separable Hilbert space $X$ is strongly measurable
when it is an almost-everywhere pointwise limit of measurable simple
$X$-valued maps. For $1\le p<\infty$, $L^p(0,T;X)$ consists of strongly
measurable maps with $\int_0^T\|u(t)\|_X^pdt<\infty$; $L^\infty(0,T;X)$
uses the essential supremum norm. In this page, $L^p_{\rm loc}(0,\infty;X)$
means membership on every finite interval $(0,T)$. These conventions also
apply with $X=V$ and $X=H^{-r}$.

Assume Countable Choice and let $V$ be the separable real Hilbert space supplied by the bounded solenoidal basis
result above. Its continuous real-linear dual $V^*$,
with norm $\|\ell\|_{V^*}=\sup_{\|v\|_V\le1}|\ell(v)|$, is a separable real
Hilbert space. The Riesz map
$$J:V\to V^*,\qquad Jw(v)=(w,v)_V$$
is a surjective linear isometry.

details.actual_current_public_excerpt:
Let $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$, let $H$ be a Hilbert space over
$\mathbb K$, let $X$ be a separable Hilbert space over $\mathbb K$, and let
$T>0$. Define $C_w([0,T];H)$ to be the set of actual maps $u:[0,T]\to H$
such that $t\mapsto (u(t),h)_H$ is continuous for every fixed $h\in H$;
membership here is pointwise and is not an almost-everywhere equivalence
class. A map $u:(0,T)\to X$ is strongly measurable if it is an almost-everywhere
pointwise limit of measurable simple $X$-valued maps. For $1\le p<\infty$,
$L^p(0,T;X)$ consists of almost-everywhere equivalence classes of strongly
measurable maps with $\int_0^T\|u(t)\|_X^pdt<\infty$; $L^\infty(0,T;X)$
consists of such classes with finite essential supremum norm. In this page,
$L^p_{\rm loc}(0,\infty;X)$ means membership on every finite interval
$(0,T)$. These conventions apply to any of the periodic spaces $H,V,H^{-r}$
and to the bounded-domain Hilbert spaces $H,V$ whenever the target space $X$
is separable.

If two maps in $C_w([0,T];H)$ agree almost everywhere on $(0,T)$, they agree
at every $t\in[0,T]$. Consequently, a Bochner equivalence class has at most
one weakly continuous representative; whenever it has one, all pointwise
values associated with that class mean the values of this unique representative.

$\mathbb T_L^d=(\mathbb R/L\mathbb Z)^d$ carry normalized Lebesgue measure
$L^{-d}dx$. For $k\in\mathbb Z^d$ put
$\kappa_k=2\pi k/L$ and $e_k(x)=\exp(i\kappa_k\cdot x)$. For a complex
scalar or vector $L^2$ class $f$, let
$\widehat f(k)=L^{-d}\int_{[0,L]^d}f(x)e^{-i\kappa_k\cdot x}\,dx$;
real fields are the classes satisfying
$\widehat f(-k)=\overline{\widehat f(k)}$. Define
$H^s(\mathbb T_L^d)$ by
$$\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z^d}(1+L^2|\kappa_k|^2)^s|\widehat f(k)|^2<\infty,$$
for $s\ge0$, with the square root of this sum as norm; the weight is dimensionless. The
real solenoidal spaces are
$$H=\{u\in L^2(\mathbb T_L^d;\mathbb R^d): k\cdot\widehat u(k)=0\text{ for every }k\ne0\},\qquad V=H\cap H^1(\mathbb T_L^d;\mathbb R^d).$$
The zero Fourier mode is unrestricted. The orthogonal solenoidal projection
$P$ has multiplier $P_0=I$ and
$P_k=I-\kappa_k\kappa_k^{\mathsf T}/|\kappa_k|^2$ for $k\ne0$; the
for integer $N\ge0$, rectangular truncation $\Pi_N$ keeps precisely $|k|_\infty\le N$. A weak
derivative in coordinate $j$ has Fourier coefficient $i\kappa_{k,j}\widehat f(k)$.
For $r>0$, $H^{-r}$ is the completion of finite Fourier coefficient sequences
in the norm squared $\sum_k(1+L^2|\kappa_k|^2)^{-r}|\widehat f(k)|^2$.

Let $d\ge2$, $L>0$, $\nu>0$, $u_0\in H$, and use the spaces and weak-time
conventions of Periodic solenoidal Fourier spaces and
Weak time continuity and energy spaces. A **global unforced periodic Leray–Hopf
solution** with data $(\nu,u_0)$ is a map
$u\in C_w([0,\infty);H)\cap L^\infty(0,\infty;H)\cap L^2_{\rm loc}(0,\infty;V)$
such that $u(0)=u_0$ in $H$, $\|u(t)-u_0\|_H\to0$ as $t\downarrow0$, and for
every smooth real periodic divergence-free test field
$\phi:[0,\infty)\times\mathbb T_L^d\to\mathbb R^d$ compactly supported in
time,
$$\int_0^\infty\!\big[(u,\partial_t\phi)+(u\otimes u,\nabla\phi)-\nu(\nabla u,\nabla\phi)\big]dt+(u_0,\phi(0))=0.$$
It must also satisfy, for every $t\ge0$,
$$\|u(t)\|_2^2+2\nu\int_0^t\|\nabla u(s)\|_2^2ds\le\|u_0\|_2^2,$$
and there must be a full-measure set $S\subset(0,\infty)$ such that for
every $s\in S\cup\{0\}$ and every $t\ge s$,
$$\|u(t)\|_2^2+2\nu\int_s^t\|\nabla u(\tau)\|_2^2d\tau\le\|u(s)\|_2^2.$$
For a matrix field $A$, $(\operatorname{div}A)_i=\sum_j\partial_jA_{ij}$. The tensor pairing means $(u\otimes u):\nabla\phi=\sum_{i,j}u_i u_j\partial_j\phi_i$;
the gradient pairing means $\nabla u:\nabla\phi=\sum_{i,j}\partial_j u_i\partial_j\phi_i$.
All derivatives in the weak identity are distributional; the definition
asserts neither uniqueness nor smoothness.

Let $d\ge2$, $L>0$, and $T>0$. Let $z_n:[0,T]\to H$ be continuous
finite-Fourier-sum curves such that, for constants $A,B<\infty$,
$$\sup_{n,t}\|z_n(t)\|_H\le A,\qquad \sup_n\int_0^T\|\nabla z_n(t)\|_2^2dt\le B,$$
and for each $k\in\mathbb Z^d$ there is $C_k<\infty$ with
$|\widehat z_n(k,t)-\widehat z_n(k,s)|\le C_k|t-s|$ for all $n,s,t$.
Then some subsequence converges uniformly in each Fourier coefficient to
$z\in C_w([0,T];H)\cap L^2(0,T;V)$, with
$\sup_t\|z(t)\|_H\le A$ and $\int_0^T\|\nabla z\|_2^2dt\le B$; it also
converges strongly to $z$ in $L^2(0,T;H)$ and, after a further subsequence,
strongly in $H$ for almost every $t$.

Let $d\ge2$, $L>0$, $r>d/2+1$, and $a\in L^2(\mathbb T_L^d;\mathbb R^d)$.
For the Fourier projection $P$ and divergence convention of
Periodic solenoidal Fourier spaces, the distribution $P\operatorname{div}(a\otimes a)$ belongs to $H^{-r}$ and satisfies
$$\|P\operatorname{div}(a\otimes a)\|_{H^{-r}}\le C(d,L,r)\|a\|_2^2.$$
Here $(a\otimes a)_{ij}=a_i a_j$ and
$(\operatorname{div}A)_i=\sum_j\partial_jA_{ij}$. The estimate uses no
three-dimensional singular-integral bound.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Let $D\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^n$ be open, let $F:D\to\mathbb R^n$ be continuous and locally Lipschitz in the state variable, and let $(t_0,x_0)\in D$. Then a unique local solution of the IVP exists on some interval around the initial time. More quantitatively, if $h,r>0$ make

$$[t_0-h,t_0+h]\times\overline B(x_0,r)\subseteq D,$$

if $\|F\|_2\le M$ and $F$ has state-Lipschitz constant $L$ on this cylinder, and if $hM\le r$ and $Lh<1$, then there is exactly one solution on $[t_0-h,t_0+h]$ through $(t_0,x_0)$ whose graph lies in the cylinder. Any two solutions through the same initial data agree on every common subinterval containing $t_0$.

In particular, a unique local solution exists on an interval around the initial time.

before.claim:
For $N\ge1$, let $X_N=\operatorname{ran}\Pi_N\cap H$ and solve in this finite-dimensional real space
$$\partial_tu_N+\Pi_NP\operatorname{div}(u_N\otimes u_N)=\nu\Delta u_N,\qquad u_N(0)=\Pi_Nu_0.$$
Choose real orthonormal coordinates on $X_N$, whose finite Fourier coefficients satisfy the real conjugation and solenoidal conditions. The right side preserves this real space and is a polynomial vector field $F_N:\mathbb R^m\to\mathbb R^m$. It is continuous on the open time-state domain $\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^m$; its derivative is bounded on each closed coefficient ball, so integration along line segments gives a Lipschitz bound there. Thus [F6] gives a unique local solution through the projected initial value. Pairing with $u_N$ removes $P,\Pi_N$ by orthogonality, and periodic integration by parts gives $\int (u_N\cdot\nabla)u_N\cdot u_N=\int\operatorname{div}(u_N|u_N|^2/2)=0$. Thus
$$\|u_N(t)\|_2^2+2\nu\int_s^t\|\nabla u_N\|_2^2d\tau=\|u_N(s)\|_2^2$$
on every local existence interval. [given, F1, F6, algebra]

By the overlap uniqueness in [F6], all local solutions through the initial data glue on their interval union to one maximal solution. The energy identity bounds its coordinates in the fixed finite-dimensional real space $X_N$ for all nonnegative times of existence. The polynomial vector field is bounded on that closed coefficient ball, so the coordinate curve is uniformly Lipschitz in time. before.quote:
Assume Countable Choice. Let $d\ge2$, $L>0$, $\nu>0$, and $u_0\in H$ for the periodic solenoidal
Fourier spaces defined above. Then there
exists a global unforced periodic Leray–Hopf solution with data $(\nu,u_0)$
under the definition above. This is an existence assertion; it asserts no
uniqueness or global smoothness.

Let $d\ge2$ be an integer, and let $L>0$ be the numerical period in a fixed
length unit. Let
$\mathbb T_L^d=(\mathbb R/L\mathbb Z)^d$ carry normalized Lebesgue measure
$L^{-d}dx$. For $k\in\mathbb Z^d$ put
$\kappa_k=2\pi k/L$ and $e_k(x)=\exp(i\kappa_k\cdot x)$. For a complex
scalar or vector $L^2$ class $f$, let
$\widehat f(k)=L^{-d}\int_{[0,L]^d}f(x)e^{-i\kappa_k\cdot x}\,dx$;
real fields are the classes satisfying
$\widehat f(-k)=\overline{\widehat f(k)}$. Define
$H^s(\mathbb T_L^d)$ by
$$\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z^d}(1+L^2|\kappa_k|^2)^s|\widehat f(k)|^2<\infty,$$
for $s\ge0$, with the square root of this sum as norm; the weight is dimensionless. The
real solenoidal spaces are
$$H=\{u\in L^2(\mathbb T_L^d;\mathbb R^d): k\cdot\widehat u(k)=0\text{ for every }k\ne0\},\qquad V=H\cap H^1(\mathbb T_L^d;\mathbb R^d).$$
The zero Fourier mode is unrestricted. The orthogonal solenoidal projection
$P$ has multiplier $P_0=I$ and
$P_k=I-\kappa_k\kappa_k^{\mathsf T}/|\kappa_k|^2$ for $k\ne0$; the
for integer $N\ge0$, rectangular truncation $\Pi_N$ keeps precisely $|k|_\infty\le N$. A weak
derivative in coordinate $j$ has Fourier coefficient $i\kappa_{k,j}\widehat f(k)$.
For $r>0$, $H^{-r}$ is the completion of finite Fourier coefficient sequences
in the norm squared $\sum_k(1+L^2|\kappa_k|^2)^{-r}|\widehat f(k)|^2$.

For open $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$, a **distribution** is a continuous complex-linear map $u:\mathcal D(\Omega)\to\mathbb C$, with the test-function topology of [[def-test-function-topology]]. Their vector space is denoted $\mathcal D'(\Omega)$. Write $\langle u,\varphi\rangle=u(\varphi)$; the pairing is linear in both arguments, with no conjugation.

Continuity means continuity for that topology: for each $\varepsilon>0$ the set $\{|u(\varphi)|<\varepsilon\}$ contains a zero-neighborhood. By linearity this suffices at every point. Sums and scalar multiples remain continuous and linear, so the indicated collection is a complex vector space. If $\Omega=\varnothing$, its test space is zero and its distribution space is zero as well. The finite-order estimate and the sequential criterion are established separately; neither substitutes for continuity in this definition.

For a distribution $u\in\mathcal D'(\Omega)$ in the convention of [[def-distribution]] and a multi-index $\alpha\in\mathbb N_0^n$, its **distributional derivative** is
$$\langle\partial^\alpha u,\varphi\rangle=(-1)^{|\alpha|}\langle u,\partial^\alpha\varphi\rangle\qquad(\varphi\in\mathcal D(\Omega)).$$
The test derivative is a continuous linear endomorphism by [[thm-test-function-operations-are-continuous]]. Its composition with $u$, multiplied by the indicated sign, is therefore a continuous complex-linear functional, so this definition produces a distribution. The pairing is bilinear, with no complex conjugation. For $\alpha=0$ the operation is the identity; for one coordinate derivative its sign is minus. Every derivative of the zero distribution is zero, including on the empty domain. No choice axiom enters this construction. Compatibility with classical derivatives requires an integration-by-parts argument where it is used; it is not part of the definition.

For open $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$, write $f\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega)$ when $f:\Omega\to\mathbb C$ is Lebesgue measurable and $\int_K|f|<\infty$ for every compact $K\subseteq\Omega$. This extends [[def-locally-integrable-function-on-r-n]]: equivalently, require integrability on every ball whose closure is a compact subset of $\Omega$. Such balls finitely cover each compact $K$, and conversely their closures are compact; on all of $\mathbb R^n$, any ball lies in a larger compact closed ball.

For a test $\varphi$ as in [[def-test-function-space-d-of-an-open-set]], define the **regular functional**

$$\langle u_f,\varphi\rangle=\int_\Omega f(x)\varphi(x)\,dx.$$

This is well-defined since $|\int f\varphi|\le\sup_K|\varphi|\int_K|f|$ for $K=\operatorname{supp}\varphi$. It is complex-linear in $f$ and in $\varphi$ and depends only on the almost-everywhere class of $f$. For an empty support the integral is zero. The subsequent embedding theorem establishes continuity, so that this is a distribution, and injectivity modulo almost-everywhere equality. That theorem states the Countable Choice cost of its injectivity proof; no choice is needed to define the displayed pairing.

$$\widehat\pi(k,t)=-\sum_{a,b=1}^d\frac{\kappa_{k,a}\kappa_{k,b}}{|\kappa_k|^2}\widehat T_{ab}(k,t),\qquad \widehat\pi(0,t)=0.$$
The coefficients are bounded in $k$ by $C_d\|u(t)\|_2^2$. For a smooth spacetime test $\phi$, repeated spatial integration by parts makes $\widehat\phi(k,t)$ decay faster than any power of $|k|$, uniformly with each time derivative on its compact support. Therefore $\langle\pi,\phi\rangle=\int\sum_k\widehat\pi(k,t)\widehat\phi(-k,t)dt$ converges absolutely and is bounded by a finite test seminorm; it defines a spacetime distribution with zero spatial mean.

At each nonzero frequency, the Fourier multiplier identity gives $i\kappa_k\widehat\pi(k)=- (I-P_k)\,i\sum_b\kappa_{k,b}\widehat T_{\cdot b}(k)$; the zero-frequency identity is also valid because both sides vanish. The weak identity in [F1] is exactly $\partial_tu+P\operatorname{div}T-
u\Delta u=0$ after testing against solenoidal fields. Adding the displayed gradient identity yields $\partial_tu+\operatorname{div}T+
abla\pi-
u\Delta u=0$ for every smooth periodic vector test, which is the claimed equation.

If $\pi_1,\pi_2$ are two such mean-zero distributions, the difference has zero spatial gradient. Its $k$th Fourier coefficient therefore vanishes for every $k\ne0$, since $i\kappa_k\ne0$; its zero coefficient vanishes by the mean-zero normalization. All Fourier coefficients of the difference are zero, so Fourier completeness implies $\pi_1=\pi_2$.

before.quote:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^3$ be a nonempty bounded open set. Let
$C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb R^3)$ denote smooth compactly supported vector
fields and set
$$D_\sigma(\Omega)=\{a\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb R^3):\operatorname{div}a=0\}.$$
Let $H$ be the closure of $D_\sigma(\Omega)$ in
$L^2(\Omega;\mathbb R^3)$, and let $V$ be its closure in
$H_0^1(\Omega;\mathbb R^3)$, where $H_0^1$ is the $H^1$ closure of
$C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb R^3)$ and weak derivatives define the $H^1$
norm. Use $\|a\|_H=\|a\|_2$ and
$\|a\|_V^2=\|a\|_2^2+\|\nabla a\|_2^2$. Each $V$ element has zero
extension in $H^1(\mathbb R^3)$ and distributional divergence zero. This
closure definition does not identify $V$ with every divergence-free member
of $H_0^1(\Omega;\mathbb R^3)$ on an arbitrary open set, and it makes no
pointwise boundary trace assertion.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. For every nonempty bounded open
$\Omega\subset\mathbb R^3$, the closure spaces $H,V$ of
Bounded no-slip solenoidal closure spaces are separable Hilbert spaces, with
$V\hookrightarrow H$ continuous and dense. There is a countable sequence
$e_j\in D_\sigma(\Omega)$ that is orthonormal in $H$ and whose finite linear
span is dense in both $H$ and $V$. No Stokes eigenfunction regularity or
identification of $V$ with a larger solenoidal space is asserted.

Let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^3$ be bounded and open, and let $H,V$ and
$(e_j)_{j\ge1}$ be as in the bounded closure-space and basis results on this
page. The inclusion $V\hookrightarrow H$ is compact. If $\Pi_K$ is the
$H$-orthogonal projection onto $\operatorname{span}(e_1,\ldots,e_K)$, then
there are numbers $\delta_K\downarrow0$ such that
$$\|(I-\Pi_K)a\|_H\le\delta_K\|a\|_V\qquad(a\in V).$$

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^3$ be bounded and
open, and let $H,V$ be the closure spaces defined above. There is a constant $C$ independent of $\Omega$
and $a$ such that every $a\in H_0^1(\Omega;\mathbb R^3)$ satisfies
$$\|a\|_{L^6(\Omega)}\le C\|\nabla a\|_{L^2(\Omega)},\qquad \|a\|_{L^4(\Omega)}\le\|a\|_{L^2(\Omega)}^{1/4}\|a\|_{L^6(\Omega)}^{3/4}.$$
For $T>0$, if $u\in L^\infty(0,T;H)\cap L^2(0,T;V)$, then
$u\in L^{8/3}(0,T;L^4(\Omega))$. Here the time-dependent $L^p$ notation
means strong measurability and integrability of the displayed norm; the
continuous embedding $V\to L^4(\Omega)$ carries strongly measurable
$V$-valued maps to strongly measurable $L^4$-valued maps. Let $V^*$ be the
continuous real-linear dual of $V$ with its operator norm and set
$$b_u(t)(\phi)=-\int_\Omega u_i(t,x)u_j(t,x)\partial_j\phi_i(x)dx,\qquad\phi\in V.$$
Then $b_u(t)\in V^*$, $t\mapsto b_u(t)$ is strongly measurable, and
$b_u\in L^{4/3}(0,T;V^*)$ with
$\|b_u(t)\|_{V^*}\le\|u(t)\|_{L^4(\Omega)}^2.$

Let $H,V,H^{-r}$ be the spaces of Periodic solenoidal Fourier spaces, let
$T>0$, and identify time-dependent functions that agree almost everywhere.
A map $u:[0,T]\to H$ is in $C_w([0,T];H)$ when
$t\mapsto (u(t),h)_H$ is continuous for each fixed $h\in H$. A map
$u:(0,T)\to X$ into a separable Hilbert space $X$ is strongly measurable
when it is an almost-everywhere pointwise limit of measurable simple
$X$-valued maps. For $1\le p<\infty$, $L^p(0,T;X)$ consists of strongly
measurable maps with $\int_0^T\|u(t)\|_X^pdt<\infty$; $L^\infty(0,T;X)$
uses the essential supremum norm. In this page, $L^p_{\rm loc}(0,\infty;X)$
means membership on every finite interval $(0,T)$. These conventions also
apply with $X=V$ and $X=H^{-r}$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to [0,\infty]$ be product-measurable. Then
$x \mapsto \int_Y f_x\,d\nu$ and $y \mapsto \int_X f^y\,d\mu$ are measurable,
and

$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $n\ge1$
and let $e_k(x)=\exp(2\pi i\,k\cdot x)$, $k\in\mathbb Z^n$, be the coordinate
characters on $\mathbb T^n$
([[def-the-one-dimensional-torus-and-normalized-haar-integral]],
[[def-fourier-coefficients-and-trigonometric-polynomials]]). Then:

1. $(e_k)_{k\in\mathbb Z^n}$ is an orthonormal family in the complex Hilbert
   space $L^2(\mathbb T^n)$;
2. it is an orthonormal basis: its closed linear span is $L^2(\mathbb T^n)$;
3. consequently the Fourier expansion
   $f=\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z^n}\widehat f(k)e_k$ and Parseval's identity
   $$\|f\|_2^2=\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z^n}|\widehat f(k)|^2,\qquad \langle f,g\rangle=\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z^n}\widehat f(k)\overline{\widehat g(k)}$$
   hold for all $f,g\in L^2(\mathbb T^n)$, in the finite-subset-net sense; and
4. the Fourier coefficient map is a surjective linear isometry of
   $L^2(\mathbb T^n)$ onto $\ell^2(\mathbb Z^n,\mathbb C)$.

No Hilbert tensor-product identification is used anywhere.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Let $D\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^n$ be open, let $F:D\to\mathbb R^n$ be continuous and locally Lipschitz in the state variable, and let $(t_0,x_0)\in D$. Then a unique local solution of the IVP exists on some interval around the initial time. More quantitatively, if $h,r>0$ make

$$[t_0-h,t_0+h]\times\overline B(x_0,r)\subseteq D,$$

if $\|F\|_2\le M$ and $F$ has state-Lipschitz constant $L$ on this cylinder, and if $hM\le r$ and $Lh<1$, then there is exactly one solution on $[t_0-h,t_0+h]$ through $(t_0,x_0)$ whose graph lies in the cylinder. Any two solutions through the same initial data agree on every common subinterval containing $t_0$.

In particular, a unique local solution exists on an interval around the initial time.

$T>0$, and identify time-dependent functions that agree almost everywhere.

when it is an almost-everywhere pointwise limit of measurable simple
$X$-valued maps. For $1\le p<\infty$, $L^p(0,T;X)$ consists of strongly
measurable maps with $\int_0^T\|u(t)\|_X^pdt<\infty$; $L^\infty(0,T;X)$

details.actual_current_public_excerpt:
Let $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$, let $H$ be a Hilbert space over
$\mathbb K$, let $X$ be a separable Hilbert space over $\mathbb K$, and let
$T>0$. Define $C_w([0,T];H)$ to be the set of actual maps $u:[0,T]\to H$
such that $t\mapsto (u(t),h)_H$ is continuous for every fixed $h\in H$;
membership here is pointwise and is not an almost-everywhere equivalence
class. A map $u:(0,T)\to X$ is strongly measurable if it is an almost-everywhere
pointwise limit of measurable simple $X$-valued maps. For $1\le p<\infty$,
$L^p(0,T;X)$ consists of almost-everywhere equivalence classes of strongly
measurable maps with $\int_0^T\|u(t)\|_X^pdt<\infty$; $L^\infty(0,T;X)$
consists of such classes with finite essential supremum norm. In this page,
$L^p_{\rm loc}(0,\infty;X)$ means membership on every finite interval
$(0,T)$. These conventions apply to any of the periodic spaces $H,V,H^{-r}$
and to the bounded-domain Hilbert spaces $H,V$ whenever the target space $X$
is separable.

If two maps in $C_w([0,T];H)$ agree almost everywhere on $(0,T)$, they agree
at every $t\in[0,T]$. Consequently, a Bochner equivalence class has at most
one weakly continuous representative; whenever it has one, all pointwise
values associated with that class mean the values of this unique representative.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $d\ge2$, $L>0$, $\nu>0$, and $u_0\in H$ for the periodic solenoidal
Fourier spaces defined above. Then there
exists a global unforced periodic Leray–Hopf solution with data $(\nu,u_0)$
under the definition above. This is an existence assertion; it asserts no
uniqueness or global smoothness.
For $f\in L^1[a,b]$, the function $I_f(x)=\int_a^x f$ is absolutely continuous.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice (The Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$)).

Let $a<b$ and let $f\in L^1([a,b])$. Fix a measurable integrable representative, also denoted by $f$, if $L^1([a,b])$ is interpreted as a space of almost-everywhere equivalence classes. Define
$$F(x):=\int_a^x f(t)\,dt\qquad(a\le x\le b).$$
Then there is a measurable set $E\subseteq(a,b)$ whose complement in $(a,b)$ has Lebesgue measure zero such that $F$ is differentiable at every $x\in E$ and
$$F'(x)=f(x)\qquad(x\in E).$$
The primitive $F$ is independent of the chosen representative; the almost-everywhere derivative identity holds for every fixed measurable integrable representative.
If $F,G\in AC[a,b]$, then $FG\in AC[a,b]$.

Assume the Axioms of Countable Choice and Dependent Choice. For $F:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$, the following are equivalent:

1. $F$ is absolutely continuous.
2. $F'$ exists almost everywhere, $F'\in L^1[a,b]$, and
$$F(x)-F(a)=\int_a^xF'(t)\,dt\quad\text{for every }x\in[a,b].$$

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Let $X$ be a set and let $R \subseteq X \times X$ be a binary relation on $X$.
Call $R$ **entire on $X$** when

$$\text{for every } x \in X \text{ there is } y \in X \text{ with } x \mathbin{R} y .$$

The **Axiom of Dependent Choice**, written $\mathrm{DC}$, is the following
statement.

> For every nonempty set $X$, every relation $R$ entire on $X$, and every
> $a \in X$, there is a function $x : \mathbb{N} \to X$ (A function is a relation $f$ with $(a,b) \in f$ and $(a,c) \in f$ implying $b = c$; $f : A \to B$, the value $f(a)$, domain and codomain,
> The natural numbers $\mathbb{N}$ (von Neumann)) with
> $$x_0 = a \qquad \text{and} \qquad x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1} \ \text{ for every } n \in \mathbb{N}.$$

Here a sequence in $X$ means a function from $\mathbb{N}$ to $X$, not necessarily
a real-valued sequence. As everywhere in this library $\mathbb{N}$ contains $0$, and the sequence is
indexed from $0$; the term $x_0$ is the prescribed starting point $a$ and every
later term is related to its predecessor.

**What DC adds to what came before.** Choice function and
The Axiom of Choice select one element from each member of a family that is
fixed in advance, and The Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$) does the same for a family indexed
by $\mathbb{N}$. In both, the family is given before any selection is made. DC is
the principle needed when the $n$-th set to select from is not known until the
first $n$ selections have been made: here the admissible values of $x_{n+1}$ are
exactly the $R$-successors of $x_n$, so the family being chosen from is built
along the choosing. Thus the displayed recursion is directly an instance of
DC; it is not itself an application of the fixed-family formulation of
countable choice. This observation concerns the input to the two axioms and
makes no claim about a nonimplication between them.

**The starting point may be dropped.** The formally weaker statement obtained by
deleting the clause $x_0 = a$ — for every nonempty $X$ and every entire $R$ there
is a sequence with $x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1}$ for all $n$ — is an immediate
consequence of the form above, since $X$ is nonempty and any of its elements may
be taken as $a$. Conversely, assume the start-free form, and fix $X$, $R$ and $a$ as above. Let $P$ be the set of all functions $p:k\to X$ with nonzero $k\in\mathbb N$, $p(0)=a$, and $p(i)\mathbin R p(i+1)$ whenever $i+1<k$. It is a set by Separation inside $\mathcal P(\mathbb N\times X)$ (The power set $\mathcal{P}(x) = \{\, z : z \subseteq x \,\}$, The Cartesian product $A \times B := \{\, z \in \mathcal{P}(\mathcal{P}(A \cup B)) : \exists a \in A\ \exists b \in B\ z = (a,b) \,\}$, The Axiom Schema of Separation: for each formula $\varphi$, $\forall \bar p\,\forall x\,\exists y\,\forall z\,(z \in y \leftrightarrow (z \in x \wedge \varphi(z,\bar p)))$); a natural is the set of its predecessors (On $\mathbb{N}$ the order is membership: $m < n \iff m \in n$). The singleton path $\{(0,a)\}$ lies in $P$.

On $P$ let $p\mathbin S q$ mean that $q$ extends $p$ by exactly one new last entry. This relation is entire: for one particular $p:k\to X$, write $k=j+1$ (Every nonzero natural number is a successor); an $R$-successor $y$ of $p(j)$ exists, and $q=p\cup\{(k,y)\}$ is the required extension. This is existential instantiation for that path, not a simultaneous choice of successors. Start-free DC now supplies a sequence $(p_n)$ with $p_n\mathbin S p_{n+1}$; its first path need not be the singleton path, but every path in $P$ already starts at $a$.

Their graphs are nested. By induction (The principle of mathematical induction), $p_n$ has at least $n+1$ entries: the initial path is nonempty, and every step adds one entry. Hence $x=\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb N}p_n$ is a function with domain $\mathbb N$ and values in $X$. Indeed, nestedness makes all common values agree, every natural index eventually lies in a path, and no path has indices outside $\mathbb N$. Each path starts at $a$, so $x(0)=a$; for any $i$, a sufficiently long path contains both $i$ and $i+1$, giving $x(i)\mathbin R x(i+1)$. Replacement and Union form this union of the sequence of graphs. Thus the start-free and prescribed-start forms are equivalent in ZF. Every use below retains the prescribed-start convention.

**$R$ need not be an order and the terms need not be distinct.** What DC delivers
is a sequence, that is a function $\mathbb{N} \to X$, not a chain in the
order-theoretic sense (Chain in a poset). The relation may be symmetric, and the
sequence may repeat a value or be constant; all that is asserted is
$x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1}$ at every index.

Let $d\ge2$, $L>0$, $\nu>0$, $u_0\in H$, and use the spaces and weak-time
conventions of Periodic solenoidal Fourier spaces and
Weak time continuity and energy spaces. A **global unforced periodic Leray–Hopf
solution** with data $(\nu,u_0)$ is a map
$u\in C_w([0,\infty);H)\cap L^\infty(0,\infty;H)\cap L^2_{\rm loc}(0,\infty;V)$
such that $u(0)=u_0$ in $H$, $\|u(t)-u_0\|_H\to0$ as $t\downarrow0$, and for
every smooth real periodic divergence-free test field
$\phi:[0,\infty)\times\mathbb T_L^d\to\mathbb R^d$ compactly supported in
time,
$$\int_0^\infty\!\big[(u,\partial_t\phi)+(u\otimes u,\nabla\phi)-\nu(\nabla u,\nabla\phi)\big]dt+(u_0,\phi(0))=0.$$
It must also satisfy, for every $t\ge0$,
$$\|u(t)\|_2^2+2\nu\int_0^t\|\nabla u(s)\|_2^2ds\le\|u_0\|_2^2,$$
and there must be a full-measure set $S\subset(0,\infty)$ such that for
every $s\in S\cup\{0\}$ and every $t\ge s$,
$$\|u(t)\|_2^2+2\nu\int_s^t\|\nabla u(\tau)\|_2^2d\tau\le\|u(s)\|_2^2.$$
For a matrix field $A$, $(\operatorname{div}A)_i=\sum_j\partial_jA_{ij}$. The tensor pairing means $(u\otimes u):\nabla\phi=\sum_{i,j}u_i u_j\partial_j\phi_i$;
the gradient pairing means $\nabla u:\nabla\phi=\sum_{i,j}\partial_j u_i\partial_j\phi_i$.
All derivatives in the weak identity are distributional; the definition
asserts neither uniqueness nor smoothness.

before.quote:
Let $d\ge2$ be an integer, and let $L>0$ be the numerical period in a fixed
length unit. Let
$\mathbb T_L^d=(\mathbb R/L\mathbb Z)^d$ carry normalized Lebesgue measure
$L^{-d}dx$. For $k\in\mathbb Z^d$ put
$\kappa_k=2\pi k/L$ and $e_k(x)=\exp(i\kappa_k\cdot x)$. For a complex
scalar or vector $L^2$ class $f$, let
$\widehat f(k)=L^{-d}\int_{[0,L]^d}f(x)e^{-i\kappa_k\cdot x}\,dx$;
real fields are the classes satisfying
$\widehat f(-k)=\overline{\widehat f(k)}$. Define
$H^s(\mathbb T_L^d)$ by
$$\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z^d}(1+L^2|\kappa_k|^2)^s|\widehat f(k)|^2<\infty,$$
for $s\ge0$, with the square root of this sum as norm; the weight is dimensionless. The
real solenoidal spaces are

before.quote:
Assume Countable Choice. Let $d\ge2$, $L>0$, $\nu>0$, and $u_0\in H$ for the periodic solenoidal
Fourier spaces defined above. Then there
exists a global unforced periodic Leray–Hopf solution with data $(\nu,u_0)$
under the definition above. This is an existence assertion; it asserts no
uniqueness or global smoothness.

Let $d\ge2$, $L>0$, and $T>0$. Let $z_n:[0,T]\to H$ be continuous
finite-Fourier-sum curves such that, for constants $A,B<\infty$,
$$\sup_{n,t}\|z_n(t)\|_H\le A,\qquad \sup_n\int_0^T\|\nabla z_n(t)\|_2^2dt\le B,$$
and for each $k\in\mathbb Z^d$ there is $C_k<\infty$ with
$|\widehat z_n(k,t)-\widehat z_n(k,s)|\le C_k|t-s|$ for all $n,s,t$.
Then some subsequence converges uniformly in each Fourier coefficient to
$z\in C_w([0,T];H)\cap L^2(0,T;V)$, with
$\sup_t\|z(t)\|_H\le A$ and $\int_0^T\|\nabla z\|_2^2dt\le B$; it also
converges strongly to $z$ in $L^2(0,T;H)$ and, after a further subsequence,
strongly in $H$ for almost every $t$.

Let $u$ be a global unforced periodic Leray–Hopf solution on $\mathbb T_L^d$
with viscosity $\nu>0$ and initial datum $u_0$. Suppose
$v\in C^\infty([0,T]\times\mathbb T_L^d;\mathbb R^d)$ and
$q\in C^\infty([0,T]\times\mathbb T_L^d)$ satisfy $\operatorname{div}v=0$ and
$\partial_tv+\operatorname{div}(v\otimes v)+\nabla q=\nu\Delta v$, with
$v(0)=u_0$. Then $u(t)=v(t)$ in $H$ for every $t\in[0,T]$. More generally,
for $D(t)=\|u(t)-v(t)\|_2^2$,
$$D(t)\le D(0)+2\int_0^t\|\nabla v(s)\|_\infty D(s)\,ds.$$
This conditional result does not assert existence of such a smooth pair.

before.quote:
Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be open, $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^d$ be open, $\mathcal O\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be the state domain of a conservation system, $n\in\mathbb R^d$ satisfy $|n|=1$, and $s\in\mathbb R$. The planar interface and its two open sides are
$$\Sigma=\{(t,x)\in I\times\Omega:n\cdot x-st=0\},\qquad Q^-=\{n\cdot x-st<0\},\qquad Q^+=\{n\cdot x-st>0\}.$$
A state field is piecewise $C^1$ across $\Sigma$ if on each side it is $C^1$ and, near every point of $\Sigma$, each side field is the restriction of a $C^1$ map from a neighborhood in $I\times\Omega$ into $\mathcal O$. The left and right traces $U_L,U_R:\Sigma\to\mathcal O$ are the restrictions of those extensions to $\Sigma$; they are independent of the chosen extensions because they agree with the same field on their respective open sides. For any state or flux quantity $G$ with these traces, define its jump by $[G]=G_R-G_L$. A planar shock profile is such a piecewise $C^1$ state field with its specified constant interface normal $n$ and speed $s$; the definition does not assert that it solves a conservation system.

Let $d,m\in\mathbb N$, let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an open time interval, let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^d$ be open, and let $\mathcal O\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open and convex. Put $Q=I\times\Omega$. A first-order conservation system on $\mathcal O$ consists of fluxes $F_j\in C^1(\mathcal O;\mathbb R^m)$, $1\leq j\leq d$, and the equation
$$\partial_tU+\sum_{j=1}^d\partial_{x_j}F_j(U)=0.$$
A state field $U:Q\to\mathcal O$ is locally bounded if it is measurable and essentially bounded on every compact subset of $Q$. For an open set $Q$, $g\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(Q)$ means $g$ is measurable and $\int_K|g|<\infty$ for every compact $K\subseteq Q$. Require also $U,F_1(U),\ldots,F_d(U)\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(Q;\mathbb R^m)$. These fields then define regular distributions componentwise. The conservation system holds in distributions on $Q$ when, for every real-valued $\varphi\in C_c^\infty(Q;\mathbb R^m)$,
$$\int_Q\left(U\cdot\partial_t\varphi+\sum_{j=1}^dF_j(U)\cdot\partial_{x_j}\varphi\right)\,dx\,dt=0.$$
This is the test-function meaning of the displayed derivative equation, using the distributional derivative convention in the supplied mathematics. The pairing is bilinear, without complex conjugation.

For an initial-value problem on $(0,T)\times\Omega$, $T>0$, let $U_0:\Omega\to\mathcal O$ be measurable and locally integrable. A test function up to the initial boundary is the restriction of a smooth function defined on a neighborhood of $[0,T)\times\Omega$, with compact support in $[0,T)\times\Omega$; its value at $t=0$ need not vanish. The initial-value weak identity is
$$\int_0^T\!\!\int_\Omega\left(U\cdot\partial_t\varphi+\sum_{j=1}^dF_j(U)\cdot\partial_{x_j}\varphi\right)\,dx\,dt+\int_\Omega U_0(x)\cdot\varphi(0,x)\,dx=0$$
for every such real vector test function. The integral identity is required only when the displayed integrands are locally integrable on the test support.

A convex entropy-flux pair for the system is a function $\eta\in C^2(\mathcal O;\mathbb R)$ that is convex on the convex state domain $\mathcal O$ and functions $q_j\in C^1(\mathcal O;\mathbb R)$ satisfying
$$Dq_j(V)=D\eta(V)\,DF_j(V)\qquad(V\in\mathcal O,\ 1\leq j\leq d),$$
where convexity means $\eta((1-\theta)V+\theta W)\leq(1-\theta)\eta(V)+\theta\eta(W)$ for $V,W\in\mathcal O$ and $\theta\in[0,1]$, and $D\eta,Dq_j$ are row derivatives while $DF_j$ is the Jacobian matrix. For a state field $U$, require $\eta(U),q_1(U),\ldots,q_d(U)\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}$ before using their distributions. The entropy inequality on $Q$ means
$$\partial_t\eta(U)+\sum_{j=1}^d\partial_{x_j}q_j(U)\leq0,$$
with the sign convention that this holds exactly when
$$\int_Q\left(\eta(U)\,\partial_t\psi+\sum_{j=1}^dq_j(U)\,\partial_{x_j}\psi\right)\,dx\,dt\geq0$$
for every nonnegative $\psi\in C_c^\infty(Q)$. With initial data, add $\int_\Omega\eta(U_0)\psi(0,x)\,dx$ and require $\eta(U_0)\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}$. A weak solution satisfying this inequality is entropy-admissible relative to that pair.

For a distribution $u\in\mathcal D'(\Omega)$ in the convention of [[def-distribution]] and a multi-index $\alpha\in\mathbb N_0^n$, its **distributional derivative** is
$$\langle\partial^\alpha u,\varphi\rangle=(-1)^{|\alpha|}\langle u,\partial^\alpha\varphi\rangle\qquad(\varphi\in\mathcal D(\Omega)).$$
The test derivative is a continuous linear endomorphism by [[thm-test-function-operations-are-continuous]]. Its composition with $u$, multiplied by the indicated sign, is therefore a continuous complex-linear functional, so this definition produces a distribution. The pairing is bilinear, with no complex conjugation. For $\alpha=0$ the operation is the identity; for one coordinate derivative its sign is minus. Every derivative of the zero distribution is zero, including on the empty domain. No choice axiom enters this construction. Compatibility with classical derivatives requires an integration-by-parts argument where it is used; it is not part of the definition.

Let $n \ge 1$, **assume the Axiom of Countable Choice**
(The Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$)) and let $T : \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}^n$ be linear
with matrix $A$ (Linear map between vector spaces over the same field,
Every Euclidean linear map has a unique matrix and satisfies $\|Lh\|_2\le K\|h\|_2$ for some $K\ge0$).

1. **Invertible case.** If $\det A \ne 0$, then $T[E]$ is Lebesgue measurable for
   every Lebesgue measurable $E$ and
   $$\lambda_n\big(T[E]\big) \;=\; |\det A|\;\lambda_n(E),$$
   both sides possibly $+\infty$; the product is defined in
   $\overline{\mathbb{R}}$ because $|\det A| > 0$.
2. **Singular case.** If $\det A = 0$, then $T[E]$ is Lebesgue measurable with
   $\lambda_n(T[E]) = 0$ for **every** $E \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$.

**The singular clause is stated as nullity and not as a product.** When
$\det A = 0$ and $\lambda_n(E) = +\infty$ the expression
$|\det A|\,\lambda_n(E)$ is $0\cdot(+\infty)$, which The extended real line $\overline{\mathbb{R}} = \mathbb{R} \cup \{-\infty, +\infty\}$, its order, and the arithmetic that is left undefined
leaves undefined; writing the conclusion as $\lambda_n(T[E]) = 0$ says the same
thing wherever the product is defined and remains a statement where it is not.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to \mathbb C$ belong to
$L^1(\mu \times \nu)$. Then:

1. for $\mu$-almost every $x$, the section $f_x$ belongs to $L^1(\nu)$;
2. for $\nu$-almost every $y$, the section $f^y$ belongs to $L^1(\mu)$;
3. after assigning the value $0$ on the exceptional parameter sets, the
   section-integral functions are integrable; and
4. the three integrals agree:
$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

1. for $\mu$-almost every $x$, the section $f_x$ belongs to $L^1(\nu)$;
2. for $\nu$-almost every $y$, the section $f^y$ belongs to $L^1(\mu)$;
3. after assigning the value $0$ on the exceptional parameter sets, the
   section-integral functions are integrable; and
4. the three integrals agree:
$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

nonnegative simple measurable function

$(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$, so the $E_j\in\mathcal A$ are pairwise disjoint and
$c_j\ge0$. Its
**simple integral** is
$$\int s\,d\mu:=\sum_{j=1}^m c_j\mu(E_j),$$

$0\cdot(+\infty)=0$ is fixed once and for all.

representation.

**nonnegative Lebesgue integral** is

The set of admissible simple minorants is nonempty because it contains the zero
function, which is simple (Nonnegative simple measurable functions).

Let $f:X\to\mathbb R$ be measurable. Its positive and negative parts are
$$f^+:=\max\{f,0\},\qquad f^-:=\max\{-f,0\};$$
they are measurable by
Closure properties of measurable functions used by the integral and
satisfy $f=f^+-f^-$ and $|f|=f^++f^-$.

most one of $\int f^+\,d\mu$ and $\int f^-\,d\mu$ is $+\infty$, in which case
