Let $d,m\in\mathbb N$, let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an open time interval, let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^d$ be open, and let $\mathcal O\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open and convex. Put $Q=I\times\Omega$. A first-order conservation system on $\mathcal O$ consists of fluxes $F_j\in C^1(\mathcal O;\mathbb R^m)$, $1\leq j\leq d$, and the equation
$$\partial_tU+\sum_{j=1}^d\partial_{x_j}F_j(U)=0.$$
A state field $U:Q\to\mathcal O$ is locally bounded if it is measurable and essentially bounded on every compact subset of $Q$. For an open set $Q$, $g\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(Q)$ means $g$ is measurable and $\int_K|g|<\infty$ for every compact $K\subseteq Q$. Require also $U,F_1(U),\ldots,F_d(U)\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(Q;\mathbb R^m)$. These fields then define regular distributions componentwise. The conservation system holds in distributions on $Q$ when, for every real-valued $\varphi\in C_c^\infty(Q;\mathbb R^m)$,
$$\int_Q\left(U\cdot\partial_t\varphi+\sum_{j=1}^dF_j(U)\cdot\partial_{x_j}\varphi\right)\,dx\,dt=0.$$
This is the test-function meaning of the displayed derivative equation, using the distributional derivative convention in the supplied mathematics. The pairing is bilinear, without complex conjugation.

For an initial-value problem on $(0,T)\times\Omega$, $T>0$, let $U_0:\Omega\to\mathcal O$ be measurable and locally integrable. A test function up to the initial boundary is the restriction of a smooth function defined on a neighborhood of $[0,T)\times\Omega$, with compact support in $[0,T)\times\Omega$; its value at $t=0$ need not vanish. The initial-value weak identity is
$$\int_0^T\!\!\int_\Omega\left(U\cdot\partial_t\varphi+\sum_{j=1}^dF_j(U)\cdot\partial_{x_j}\varphi\right)\,dx\,dt+\int_\Omega U_0(x)\cdot\varphi(0,x)\,dx=0$$
for every such real vector test function. The integral identity is required only when the displayed integrands are locally integrable on the test support.

A convex entropy-flux pair for the system is a function $\eta\in C^2(\mathcal O;\mathbb R)$ that is convex on the convex state domain $\mathcal O$ and functions $q_j\in C^1(\mathcal O;\mathbb R)$ satisfying
$$Dq_j(V)=D\eta(V)\,DF_j(V)\qquad(V\in\mathcal O,\ 1\leq j\leq d),$$
where convexity means $\eta((1-\theta)V+\theta W)\leq(1-\theta)\eta(V)+\theta\eta(W)$ for $V,W\in\mathcal O$ and $\theta\in[0,1]$, and $D\eta,Dq_j$ are row derivatives while $DF_j$ is the Jacobian matrix. For a state field $U$, require $\eta(U),q_1(U),\ldots,q_d(U)\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}$ before using their distributions. The entropy inequality on $Q$ means
$$\partial_t\eta(U)+\sum_{j=1}^d\partial_{x_j}q_j(U)\leq0,$$
with the sign convention that this holds exactly when
$$\int_Q\left(\eta(U)\,\partial_t\psi+\sum_{j=1}^dq_j(U)\,\partial_{x_j}\psi\right)\,dx\,dt\geq0$$
for every nonnegative $\psi\in C_c^\infty(Q)$. With initial data, add $\int_\Omega\eta(U_0)\psi(0,x)\,dx$ and require $\eta(U_0)\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}$. A weak solution satisfying this inequality is entropy-admissible relative to that pair.

This is the test-function meaning of the displayed derivative equation, using the distributional derivative convention in the supplied mathematics. The pairing is bilinear, without complex conjugation.

For an initial-value problem on $(0,T)\times\Omega$, $T>0$, let $U_0:\Omega\to\mathcal O$ be measurable and locally integrable. Let $n\in\mathbb R^d$ have $|n|=1$, let $s\in\mathbb R$, and set $\Sigma=\{(t,x)\in I\times\Omega:n\cdot x=st\}$. Suppose $U$ is piecewise $C^1$ across $\Sigma$, satisfies $U_t+\sum_jDF_j(U)\partial_{x_j}U=0$ classically on each open side, and the state, flux, and entropy compositions are locally integrable. Let $\eta\in C^2(\mathcal O;\mathbb R)$ be convex and let $q_j\in C^1(\mathcal O;\mathbb R)$ satisfy $Dq_j(V)=D\eta(V)DF_j(V)$ for every $V\in\mathcal O$. With $[G]=G_R-G_L$, the distributional entropy residual is
$$\partial_t\eta(U)+\sum_{j=1}^d\partial_{x_j}q_j(U)=\left(\sum_{j=1}^dn_j[q_j(U)]-s[\eta(U)]\right)\delta_\Sigma.$$
Here $\delta_\Sigma$ pairs with integration in $t$ and spatial $(d-1)$-dimensional measure on $\{x\in\Omega:n\cdot x=st\}$. The entropy inequality $\partial_t\eta(U)+\sum_j\partial_{x_j}q_j(U)\leq0$ holds near the interface if and only if $\sum_jn_j[q_j(U)]-s[\eta(U)]\leq0$ at every interface point. Entropy admissibility is an additional condition; the conservation jump equality alone does not imply it.

For a one-dimensional system $U_t+\partial_xF(U)=0$ with $F\in C^1(\mathcal O;\mathbb R^m)$ on an open state domain $\mathcal O\subseteq\mathbb R^m$, the system is strictly hyperbolic at $V\in\mathcal O$ if the Jacobian $DF(V)$ has $m$ distinct real eigenvalues. Write them in increasing order as $\lambda_1(V)<\cdots<\lambda_m(V)$. For states $U_L,U_R\in\mathcal O$ and speed $s\in\mathbb R$ satisfying the Rankine–Hugoniot equality
$$F(U_R)-F(U_L)=s(U_R-U_L),$$
assume strict hyperbolicity at both states. The jump is a $k$-Lax shock, $1\leq k\leq m$, if
$$\lambda_k(U_R)<s<\lambda_k(U_L),$$
and also $\lambda_{k-1}(U_L)<s$ when $k>1$, and $s<\lambda_{k+1}(U_R)$ when $k<m$. The outer inequality is omitted at each endpoint $k=1$ or $k=m$.

Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a < b$ and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be
continuous on $[a,b]$ (Continuity of $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ at a point of $A$ and on $A$: the $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ condition, its agreement with $\lim_{x \to c} f(x) = f(c)$ at a limit point, and continuity at an isolated point, Intervals of $\mathbb{R}$: the nine order-convex forms, nondegeneracy, and length) and
differentiable at every point of $(a,b)$ as a function on $[a,b]$
(The derivative $f'(c) = \lim_{x \to c} \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c}$ of $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ at a point $c \in A$ that is a limit point of $A$, and differentiability on a set). Then there is $c \in (a,b)$ with

$$f(b) - f(a) \;=\; f'(c)\,(b - a) .$$

Equivalently, since $b - a \ne 0$, there is $c \in (a,b)$ at which
$f'(c) = \bigl(f(b)-f(a)\bigr)/(b-a)$: the derivative somewhere inside equals
the average rate of change across the whole interval.

**Continuity on the closed interval cannot be dropped.** Differentiability at
every point of $(a,b)$ alone does not suffice: a function on $[0,1]$,
differentiable at every point of $(0,1)$ with derivative constantly $1$, for
which no $c$ works, is exhibited later on this page as a false statement, and
the companion page works the same witness out in full.

Let $a < b$ be reals, let $G : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at every
point of $[a,b]$ as a function on $[a,b]$ (The derivative $f'(c) = \lim_{x \to c} \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c}$ of $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ at a point $c \in A$ that is a limit point of $A$, and differentiability on a set; at $a$ and $b$
this is the one-sided derivative), let $f := G'$, and suppose $f$ is integrable
on $[a,b]$ (The lower and upper Darboux integrals of a bounded $f$ on $[a,b]$ as $\sup_P L(f,P)$ and $\inf_P U(f,P)$, Darboux integrability as their equality, and the notation $\int_a^b f$). Then

$$\int_a^b f \;=\; G(b) - G(a) .$$

**Both hypotheses are needed and neither is removable.** A function may be
differentiable everywhere with $G'$ not integrable — then the left-hand side does
not exist (an everywhere differentiable function with unbounded derivative) — and an
integrable $f$ need not be the derivative of anything
(the sign function); both witnesses are on the
companion page.

**No continuity of $f$ is assumed**, which is what makes this the working form:
the theorem evaluates $\int_a^b f$ for every integrable derivative, not only for
continuous integrands.

Let $f:U\to V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be totally differentiable at $a\in U$ and let $g:V\to\mathbb R^p$ be totally differentiable at $f(a)$. Then $g\circ f$ is totally differentiable at $a$ and

$$D(g\circ f)(a)=Dg(f(a))\circ Df(a).$$

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

before.claim: If $a=b$, the profile and initial data are constant. For every compactly supported test, integration of $\varphi_t$ over $[0,T)$ gives $-\varphi(0,x)$ and integration of $\varphi_x$ over $\mathbb R$ gives zero. The weak identity follows; the same calculation with the constants $\eta(a)$ and $q(a)$ gives equality in every entropy identity.

Suppose $a>b$. Apply [F5] to $F$ on $[b,a]$ to obtain $s=F'(\xi)$ for some $\xi\in(b,a)$. Apply [F5] to $F'$ on any subinterval of $[b,a]$; since its derivative $F''$ is positive, $F'$ is strictly increasing there. Hence $F'(b)<s<F'(a)$, which is the scalar Lax pattern in [F4].

Suppose $a<b$. Applying [F5] to $F'$ on any subinterval of $[a,b]$ shows it is strictly increasing, so it has an inverse $g$ on $[F'(a),F'(b)]$. This inverse is continuous: for each interior $z$, strict inequalities $F'(z-\delta)<F'(z)<F'(z+\delta)$ trap $g(y)$ near $z$ whenever $y$ is sufficiently near $F'(z)$, and the endpoint argument is one-sided. For $y=F'(z)$, the difference quotient $(g(y+h)-z)/h$ equals $(x-z)/(F'(x)-F'(z))$ with $x=g(y+h)$; as $h\to0$, continuity gives $x\to z$, and differentiability of $F'$ gives limit $1/F''(z)$. Thus $g'(y)=1/F''(g(y))$ on the interior. Applying [F7] to $u(t,x)=g(x/t)$ gives $u_t=-x/(t^2F''(u))$ and $u_x=1/(tF''(u))$, whence $u_t+F'(u)u_x=0$. The constant branches solve the equation too, and the profile is continuous at both fan edges.

The shock is constant on each open side, so the classical equation holds there. Its traces are $u_L=a$ and $u_R=b$, and the Rankine–Hugoniot coefficient is $[F]-s[u]=F(b)-F(a)-s(b-a)=0$. By [F2] under [F8], the distributional equation holds on $(0,T)\times\mathbb R$.
The traces at each fan edge agree, so both the state and flux jumps vanish there. By [F2], the distributional conservation residual is zero; hence the weak equation holds on $(0,T)\times\mathbb R$.

On any compact spatial set, $u(t,\cdot)$ differs from $u_0$ only between $0$ and $st$, an interval of length $|s|t$, and $|u-u_0|\leq|a-b|$. Hence $\|u(t,\cdot)-u_0\|_{L^1(K)}\leq |a-b||s|t$. Apply the interior weak identity from step 2.1 to $\chi_\epsilon\varphi$. The term $\int u\chi_\epsilon'\varphi$ tends to $\int u_0\varphi(0,\cdot)$ by the displayed local $L^1$ estimate and uniform continuity of $\varphi$; the terms over $0<t<2\epsilon$ tend to zero because $u,F(u)$ and the test derivatives are bounded on the compact support. Taking the limit gives the initial weak identity.

Let $\eta\in C^2(\mathbb R)$ be convex with compatible flux $q$, and let $C(z)=F(b)+s(z-b)$ be the chord joining $(b,F(b))$ to $(a,F(a))$. Applying [F5] to $F'$ between $\xi_1$ and $\xi_2$ shows $F'(\xi_1)<F'(\xi_2)$; rearranging the secant-slope inequality gives $F(z)<C(z)$. At the endpoints $F=C$. $$[q]-s[\eta]=-\int_b^a\eta'(z)(F'(z)-s)\,dz=\int_b^a\eta''(z)(F(z)-C(z))\,dz\leq0.$$
The integral identity follows by applying [F6] to the $C^1$ function $\eta'(F-C)$; its endpoint values are zero. By [F3] under [F8] the entropy residual is nonpositive. Apply the cutoff argument of step 3.1 to this interior entropy inequality. The entropy density is Lipschitz on $[b,a]$, so the local $L^1$ trace estimate in step 3.1 gives the initial entropy term; boundedness makes the omitted time strip vanish.

For $k\notin[b,a]$, $\eta_k$ is affine on the state interval and $[q_k]-s[\eta_k]=0$ by the Rankine–Hugoniot equality. For $b\leq k\leq a$, direct substitution gives $[q_k]-s[\eta_k]=2(F(k)-C(k))\leq0$, with equality at $k=b,a$. Apply [F3] and the cutoff argument of step 3.1 to the interior Kružkov inequality. Both $\eta_k$ and $q_k$ are Lipschitz on $[b,a]$, so the local trace and bounded-strip limits give the required initial term.

Write $\alpha=F'(a)$ and $\beta=F'(b)$, so $\alpha<\beta$ by [A1]. The fan and the initial step can differ only on $[\min(0,\alpha t),\max(0,\beta t)]$, whose length is $t(\max(0,\beta)-\min(0,\alpha))\leq t(|\alpha|+|\beta|)$. Since $F$ is Lipschitz on $[a,b]$, its composition has the same local strong-trace property. Apply the same cutoff argument as in step 3.1 to the interior weak identity of step 2.2; the local $L^1$ bound makes the cutoff boundary term converge to the prescribed initial value, and boundedness makes the omitted time strip vanish. For each compatible convex $C^2$ pair, [F7] and $q'=\eta'F'$ give $\partial_t\eta(u)+\partial_xq(u)=\eta'(u)(u_t+F'(u)u_x)=0$ in the fan. Outside the fan both compositions are constant. Apply the cutoff argument of step 4.2 to this interior identity; the Lipschitz continuity of $\eta$ and $q$ on $[a,b]$ gives the required initial entropy term.

This proves every stated inequality, with equality for the fan.

before.quote:
Let $n \ge 1$ and **assume the Axiom of Countable Choice**
([[def-countable-choice]]). Then:

1. For every $u \in \mathbb{R}^n$ with $u \ne 0$ and every real $c$, the affine
   hyperplane
   $$H_{u,c} \;:=\; \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : \langle u,x\rangle = c \,\}$$
   ([[def-euclidean-inner-product]]) is Lebesgue measurable with
   $\lambda_n(H_{u,c}) = 0$, and so is every subset of it.
2. Every proper linear subspace $W \subsetneq \mathbb{R}^n$
   ([[def-linear-subspace]]) is Lebesgue measurable with $\lambda_n(W) = 0$.

At $n = 1$ a hyperplane is the singleton $\{c/u_0\}$ and the only proper linear
subspace is $\{0\}$.

Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be open, $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^d$ be open, $\mathcal O\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be the state domain of a conservation system, $n\in\mathbb R^d$ satisfy $|n|=1$, and $s\in\mathbb R$. The planar interface and its two open sides are
$$\Sigma=\{(t,x)\in I\times\Omega:n\cdot x-st=0\},\qquad Q^-=\{n\cdot x-st<0\},\qquad Q^+=\{n\cdot x-st>0\}.$$
A state field is piecewise $C^1$ across $\Sigma$ if on each side it is $C^1$ and, near every point of $\Sigma$, each side field is the restriction of a $C^1$ map from a neighborhood in $I\times\Omega$ into $\mathcal O$. The left and right traces $U_L,U_R:\Sigma\to\mathcal O$ are the restrictions of those extensions to $\Sigma$; they are independent of the chosen extensions because they agree with the same field on their respective open sides. For any state or flux quantity $G$ with these traces, define its jump by $[G]=G_R-G_L$. A planar shock profile is such a piecewise $C^1$ state field with its specified constant interface normal $n$ and speed $s$; the definition does not assert that it solves a conservation system.

Let $d,m\in\mathbb N$, let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an open time interval, let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^d$ be open, and let $\mathcal O\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open and convex. Put $Q=I\times\Omega$. A first-order conservation system on $\mathcal O$ consists of fluxes $F_j\in C^1(\mathcal O;\mathbb R^m)$, $1\leq j\leq d$, and the equation
$$\partial_tU+\sum_{j=1}^d\partial_{x_j}F_j(U)=0.$$
A state field $U:Q\to\mathcal O$ is locally bounded if it is measurable and essentially bounded on every compact subset of $Q$. For an open set $Q$, $g\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(Q)$ means $g$ is measurable and $\int_K|g|<\infty$ for every compact $K\subseteq Q$. Require also $U,F_1(U),\ldots,F_d(U)\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(Q;\mathbb R^m)$. These fields then define regular distributions componentwise. The conservation system holds in distributions on $Q$ when, for every real-valued $\varphi\in C_c^\infty(Q;\mathbb R^m)$,
$$\int_Q\left(U\cdot\partial_t\varphi+\sum_{j=1}^dF_j(U)\cdot\partial_{x_j}\varphi\right)\,dx\,dt=0.$$
This is the test-function meaning of the displayed derivative equation, using the distributional derivative convention in the supplied mathematics. The pairing is bilinear, without complex conjugation.

For an initial-value problem on $(0,T)\times\Omega$, $T>0$, let $U_0:\Omega\to\mathcal O$ be measurable and locally integrable. A test function up to the initial boundary is the restriction of a smooth function defined on a neighborhood of $[0,T)\times\Omega$, with compact support in $[0,T)\times\Omega$; its value at $t=0$ need not vanish. The initial-value weak identity is
$$\int_0^T\!\!\int_\Omega\left(U\cdot\partial_t\varphi+\sum_{j=1}^dF_j(U)\cdot\partial_{x_j}\varphi\right)\,dx\,dt+\int_\Omega U_0(x)\cdot\varphi(0,x)\,dx=0$$
for every such real vector test function. The integral identity is required only when the displayed integrands are locally integrable on the test support.

A convex entropy-flux pair for the system is a function $\eta\in C^2(\mathcal O;\mathbb R)$ that is convex on the convex state domain $\mathcal O$ and functions $q_j\in C^1(\mathcal O;\mathbb R)$ satisfying
$$Dq_j(V)=D\eta(V)\,DF_j(V)\qquad(V\in\mathcal O,\ 1\leq j\leq d),$$

Spatial coordinates in physical volume integrals are measured in metres. Assume Countable Choice for the stated Fourier and Sobolev space conventions. The velocity is a vector field $u:I\times\mathbb T_L^3\to\mathbb R^3$ with SI units $\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$; the mass density is a constant primitive parameter $\rho_0>0$ in $\mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}$; the dynamic viscosity is a constant primitive parameter $\mu>0$ in $\mathrm{Pa\,s}$; and the mechanical pressure $p$ has units $\mathrm{Pa}$. The body-force density is zero (its SI unit is $\mathrm{N\,m^{-3}}$), and there is no temperature variable in this model.

For classical fields take $u\in C^1(I;C^2(\mathbb T_L^3;\mathbb R^3))$ and $p\in C^1(I;C^1(\mathbb T_L^3))$. Adopt incompressibility $\operatorname{div}u=0$ and the local momentum balance
$$\rho_0\bigl(\partial_tu+\operatorname{div}(u\otimes u)\bigr)=\operatorname{div}\sigma,\qquad \sigma=-pI_3+2\mu D(u),\qquad D(u)=\tfrac12\bigl(\nabla u+(\nabla u)^{\mathsf T}\bigr).$$
Here $\sigma$ is the Cauchy stress, so its traction on an oriented surface with unit normal $n$ is $\sigma n$; $D(u)$ is the symmetric rate-of-deformation tensor; and $\nabla$ has units $\mathrm{m^{-1}}$. Every term in the momentum balance has units $\mathrm{N\,m^{-3}}$. Since $\operatorname{div}u=0$, this equation is equivalently
$$\partial_tu+\operatorname{div}(u\otimes u)+\nabla\pi=\nu\Delta u,\qquad \nu=\mu/\rho_0>0,\qquad \pi=p/\rho_0.$$
where kinematic viscosity $\nu$ and kinematic pressure $\pi$ have units $\mathrm{m^2\,s^{-1}}$ and $\mathrm{m^2\,s^{-2}}$, respectively. All fields are periodic in each spatial coordinate; this is an ideal cell, not a wall-bounded vessel.

For the weak regime, use the global unforced periodic Leray–Hopf class. The spaces are $H$, the real $L^2$ vector fields whose divergence vanishes distributionally on $\mathbb T_L^3$, with unrestricted constant Fourier mode, and $V=H\cap H^1$, where $H^1$ consists of fields and first weak derivatives in $L^2$; use normalized spatial norms. Weak time continuity and energy spaces. A **global unforced periodic Leray–Hopf

$$\int_0^\infty\!\big[(u,\partial_t\phi)+(u\otimes u,\nabla\phi)-\nu(\nabla u,\nabla\phi)\big]dt+(u_0,\phi(0))=0.$$

$$\|u(t)\|_2^2+2\nu\int_0^t\|\nabla u(s)\|_2^2ds\le\|u_0\|_2^2,$$

$$\|u(t)\|_2^2+2\nu\int_s^t\|\nabla u(\tau)\|_2^2d\tau\le\|u(s)\|_2^2.$$

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Let $X$ be a set and let $R \subseteq X \times X$ be a binary relation on $X$.
Call $R$ **entire on $X$** when

$$\text{for every } x \in X \text{ there is } y \in X \text{ with } x \mathbin{R} y .$$

The **Axiom of Dependent Choice**, written $\mathrm{DC}$, is the following
statement.

> For every nonempty set $X$, every relation $R$ entire on $X$, and every
> $a \in X$, there is a function $x : \mathbb{N} \to X$ (A function is a relation $f$ with $(a,b) \in f$ and $(a,c) \in f$ implying $b = c$; $f : A \to B$, the value $f(a)$, domain and codomain,

> $$x_0 = a \qquad \text{and} \qquad x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1} \ \text{ for every } n \in \mathbb{N}.$$

Here a sequence in $X$ means a function from $\mathbb{N}$ to $X$, not necessarily
a real-valued sequence. As everywhere in this library $\mathbb{N}$ contains $0$, and the sequence is
indexed from $0$; the term $x_0$ is the prescribed starting point $a$ and every
later term is related to its predecessor.

**What DC adds to what came before.** Choice function and
The Axiom of Choice select one element from each member of a family that is
fixed in advance, and The Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$) does the same for a family indexed
by $\mathbb{N}$. In both, the family is given before any selection is made. DC is
the principle needed when the $n$-th set to select from is not known until the
first $n$ selections have been made: here the admissible values of $x_{n+1}$ are
exactly the $R$-successors of $x_n$, so the family being chosen from is built
along the choosing. Thus the displayed recursion is directly an instance of
DC; it is not itself an application of the fixed-family formulation of
countable choice. This observation concerns the input to the two axioms and
makes no claim about a nonimplication between them.

**The starting point may be dropped.** The formally weaker statement obtained by
deleting the clause $x_0 = a$ — for every nonempty $X$ and every entire $R$ there
is a sequence with $x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1}$ for all $n$ — is an immediate
consequence of the form above, since $X$ is nonempty and any of its elements may
be taken as $a$. Conversely, assume the start-free form, and fix $X$, $R$ and $a$ as above. Let $P$ be the set of all functions $p:k\to X$ with nonzero $k\in\mathbb N$, $p(0)=a$, and $p(i)\mathbin R p(i+1)$ whenever $i+1<k$. It is a set by Separation inside $\mathcal P(\mathbb N\times X)$ (The power set $\mathcal{P}(x) = \{\, z : z \subseteq x \,\}$, The Cartesian product $A \times B := \{\, z \in \mathcal{P}(\mathcal{P}(A \cup B)) : \exists a \in A\ \exists b \in B\ z = (a,b) \,\}$, The Axiom Schema of Separation: for each formula $\varphi$, $\forall \bar p\,\forall x\,\exists y\,\forall z\,(z \in y \leftrightarrow (z \in x \wedge \varphi(z,\bar p)))$); a natural is the set of its predecessors (On $\mathbb{N}$ the order is membership: $m < n \iff m \in n$). The singleton path $\{(0,a)\}$ lies in $P$.

On $P$ let $p\mathbin S q$ mean that $q$ extends $p$ by exactly one new last entry. This relation is entire: for one particular $p:k\to X$, write $k=j+1$ (Every nonzero natural number is a successor); an $R$-successor $y$ of $p(j)$ exists, and $q=p\cup\{(k,y)\}$ is the required extension. This is existential instantiation for that path, not a simultaneous choice of successors. Start-free DC now supplies a sequence $(p_n)$ with $p_n\mathbin S p_{n+1}$; its first path need not be the singleton path, but every path in $P$ already starts at $a$.

Their graphs are nested. By induction (The principle of mathematical induction), $p_n$ has at least $n+1$ entries: the initial path is nonempty, and every step adds one entry. Hence $x=\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb N}p_n$ is a function with domain $\mathbb N$ and values in $X$. Indeed, nestedness makes all common values agree, every natural index eventually lies in a path, and no path has indices outside $\mathbb N$. Each path starts at $a$, so $x(0)=a$; for any $i$, a sufficiently long path contains both $i$ and $i+1$, giving $x(i)\mathbin R x(i+1)$. Replacement and Union form this union of the sequence of graphs. Thus the start-free and prescribed-start forms are equivalent in ZF. Every use below retains the prescribed-start convention.

**$R$ need not be an order and the terms need not be distinct.** What DC delivers
is a sequence, that is a function $\mathbb{N} \to X$, not a chain in the
order-theoretic sense (Chain in a poset). The relation may be symmetric, and the
sequence may repeat a value or be constant; all that is asserted is
$x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1}$ at every index.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Let $X$ be a set and let $R \subseteq X \times X$ be a binary relation on $X$.
Call $R$ **entire on $X$** when

$$\text{for every } x \in X \text{ there is } y \in X \text{ with } x \mathbin{R} y .$$

The **Axiom of Dependent Choice**, written $\mathrm{DC}$, is the following
statement.

> For every nonempty set $X$, every relation $R$ entire on $X$, and every
> $a \in X$, there is a function $x : \mathbb{N} \to X$ (A function is a relation $f$ with $(a,b) \in f$ and $(a,c) \in f$ implying $b = c$; $f : A \to B$, the value $f(a)$, domain and codomain,

> $$x_0 = a \qquad \text{and} \qquad x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1} \ \text{ for every } n \in \mathbb{N}.$$

Here a sequence in $X$ means a function from $\mathbb{N}$ to $X$, not necessarily
a real-valued sequence. As everywhere in this library $\mathbb{N}$ contains $0$, and the sequence is
indexed from $0$; the term $x_0$ is the prescribed starting point $a$ and every
later term is related to its predecessor.

**What DC adds to what came before.** Choice function and
The Axiom of Choice select one element from each member of a family that is
fixed in advance, and The Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$) does the same for a family indexed
by $\mathbb{N}$. In both, the family is given before any selection is made. DC is
the principle needed when the $n$-th set to select from is not known until the
first $n$ selections have been made: here the admissible values of $x_{n+1}$ are
exactly the $R$-successors of $x_n$, so the family being chosen from is built
along the choosing. Thus the displayed recursion is directly an instance of
DC; it is not itself an application of the fixed-family formulation of
countable choice. This observation concerns the input to the two axioms and
makes no claim about a nonimplication between them.

**The starting point may be dropped.** The formally weaker statement obtained by
deleting the clause $x_0 = a$ — for every nonempty $X$ and every entire $R$ there
is a sequence with $x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1}$ for all $n$ — is an immediate
consequence of the form above, since $X$ is nonempty and any of its elements may
be taken as $a$. Conversely, assume the start-free form, and fix $X$, $R$ and $a$ as above. Let $P$ be the set of all functions $p:k\to X$ with nonzero $k\in\mathbb N$, $p(0)=a$, and $p(i)\mathbin R p(i+1)$ whenever $i+1<k$. It is a set by Separation inside $\mathcal P(\mathbb N\times X)$ (The power set $\mathcal{P}(x) = \{\, z : z \subseteq x \,\}$, The Cartesian product $A \times B := \{\, z \in \mathcal{P}(\mathcal{P}(A \cup B)) : \exists a \in A\ \exists b \in B\ z = (a,b) \,\}$, The Axiom Schema of Separation: for each formula $\varphi$, $\forall \bar p\,\forall x\,\exists y\,\forall z\,(z \in y \leftrightarrow (z \in x \wedge \varphi(z,\bar p)))$); a natural is the set of its predecessors (On $\mathbb{N}$ the order is membership: $m < n \iff m \in n$). The singleton path $\{(0,a)\}$ lies in $P$.

On $P$ let $p\mathbin S q$ mean that $q$ extends $p$ by exactly one new last entry. This relation is entire: for one particular $p:k\to X$, write $k=j+1$ (Every nonzero natural number is a successor); an $R$-successor $y$ of $p(j)$ exists, and $q=p\cup\{(k,y)\}$ is the required extension. This is existential instantiation for that path, not a simultaneous choice of successors. Start-free DC now supplies a sequence $(p_n)$ with $p_n\mathbin S p_{n+1}$; its first path need not be the singleton path, but every path in $P$ already starts at $a$.

Their graphs are nested. By induction (The principle of mathematical induction), $p_n$ has at least $n+1$ entries: the initial path is nonempty, and every step adds one entry. Hence $x=\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb N}p_n$ is a function with domain $\mathbb N$ and values in $X$. Indeed, nestedness makes all common values agree, every natural index eventually lies in a path, and no path has indices outside $\mathbb N$. Each path starts at $a$, so $x(0)=a$; for any $i$, a sufficiently long path contains both $i$ and $i+1$, giving $x(i)\mathbin R x(i+1)$. Replacement and Union form this union of the sequence of graphs. Thus the start-free and prescribed-start forms are equivalent in ZF. Every use below retains the prescribed-start convention.

**$R$ need not be an order and the terms need not be distinct.** What DC delivers
is a sequence, that is a function $\mathbb{N} \to X$, not a chain in the
order-theoretic sense (Chain in a poset). The relation may be symmetric, and the
sequence may repeat a value or be constant; all that is asserted is
$x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1}$ at every index.

Define $D_\sigma(\Omega)=\{a\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb R^3):\operatorname{div}a=0\}$, where divergence is the distributional divergence (equal to the classical divergence for these smooth fields), $H$ as its closure in $L^2(\Omega;\mathbb R^3)$, and $V$ as its closure in $H_0^1(\Omega;\mathbb R^3)$; here $H_0^1$ is the closure of compactly supported smooth vector fields in the $H^1$ norm, and $H^1$ uses square-integrable fields and first weak derivatives. The adopted no-slip condition means $u(t)\in V$, not a pointwise boundary value. This closure convention does not identify $V$ with every divergence-free member of $H_0^1$ on an arbitrary open set and does not assert a boundary trace theorem.

Take a constant mass density $ho_0>0$ in $\mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}$, a constant dynamic viscosity $\mu>0$ in $\mathrm{Pa\,s}$, and zero body-force density in $\mathrm{N\,m^{-3}}$. For classical fields $u\in C^1(I;C^2(\Omega;\mathbb R^3))$ and $p\in C^1(I;C^1(\Omega))$, adopt $\operatorname{div}u=0$, the Cauchy stress $\sigma=-pI_3+2\mu D(u)$ with $D(u)=	frac12(
abla u+(
abla u)^{\mathsf T})$, and the local balance $ho_0(\partial_tu+\operatorname{div}(u\otimes u))=\operatorname{div}\sigma$ in the interior. The velocity has units $\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, pressure and stress have units $\mathrm{Pa}$, spatial derivatives have units $\mathrm{m^{-1}}$, and $
u=\mu/ho_0$ has units $\mathrm{m^2\,s^{-1}}$. No temperature field is included.

For the weak regime, take $u\in C_w([0,\infty);H)\cap L^\infty(0,\infty;H)\cap L^2_{m loc}(0,\infty;V)$, with $u(0)=u_0\in H$ and strong $H$ trace at zero; $u_0$ is an initial velocity in $\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$. Here $C_w$ means continuity of every fixed $H$-pairing, and each time-dependent Bochner space uses strongly measurable maps with the indicated norm, locally on every finite interval. Interpret this model through the solenoidal variational identity: for every compactly time-supported $C^1$ curve $\phi:[0,\infty)	o V$,
$$
\int_0^\infty\! igl[(u,\partial_t\phi)_{L^2}+(u\otimes u,
abla\phi)_{L^2}-
u(
abla u,
abla\phi)_{L^2} igr]dt+(u_0,\phi(0))_{L^2}=0.
$$

abla\phi=\sum_{i,j}u_i u_j\partial_j\phi_i$, and $

$$D_\sigma(\Omega)=\{a\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb R^3):\operatorname{div}a=0\}.$$
Let $H$ be the closure of $D_\sigma(\Omega)$ in

Let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^3$ be bounded and open, assume the Axiom of
Choice, let $\nu>0$, and let $u_0\in H$ for the bounded closure spaces
defined above. There exists
$$u\in C_w([0,\infty);H)\cap L^\infty(0,\infty;H)\cap L^2_{\rm loc}(0,\infty;V)$$
with $u(0)=u_0$ and $\|u(t)-u_0\|_H\to0$ as $t\downarrow0$, satisfying for
every compactly time-supported $C^1$ map $\phi:[0,\infty)\to V$,
$$\int_0^\infty\!\big[(u,\partial_t\phi)+(u\otimes u,\nabla\phi)-\nu(\nabla u,\nabla\phi)\big]dt+(u_0,\phi(0))=0.$$
It also satisfies

and there is a full-measure set $S\subset(0,\infty)$ such that for every

The conclusion is a velocity result for the specified unforced closure-space

$(u\otimes u):\nabla\phi=\sum_{i,j}u_i u_j\partial_j\phi_i$ and

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

continuous on $[a,b]$ (Continuity of $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ at a point of $A$ and on $A$: the $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ condition, its agreement with $\lim_{x \to c} f(x) = f(c)$ at a limit point, and continuity at an isolated point, Intervals of $\mathbb{R}$: the nine order-convex forms, nondegeneracy, and length) and
differentiable at every point of $(a,b)$ as a function on $[a,b]$
(The derivative $f'(c) = \lim_{x \to c} \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c}$ of $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ at a point $c \in A$ that is a limit point of $A$, and differentiability on a set). Then there is $c \in (a,b)$ with

$$f(b) - f(a) \;=\; f'(c)\,(b - a) .$$

Equivalently, since $b - a \ne 0$, there is $c \in (a,b)$ at which
$f'(c) = \bigl(f(b)-f(a)\bigr)/(b-a)$: the derivative somewhere inside equals
the average rate of change across the whole interval.

**Continuity on the closed interval cannot be dropped.** Differentiability at
every point of $(a,b)$ alone does not suffice: a function on $[0,1]$,
differentiable at every point of $(0,1)$ with derivative constantly $1$, for
which no $c$ works, is exhibited later on this page as a false statement, and
the companion page works the same witness out in full.

before.claim: By [F2], $D_x\ge0$ for almost every $x$. Since its spatial integral is zero, $D_x=0$ for almost every $x$. Fix any such $x$ and write $g(v)=\log(f(x,v)/f_{\rm ref})$, where $f_{\rm ref}>0$ is a constant with the units of $f$. The integrand defining $D_x$ is continuous and nonnegative in the collision variables. If it were positive at any elastic quadruple, it would be bounded below by a positive constant on a relatively open neighborhood; full support would make that neighborhood have positive measure, contradicting $D_x=0$. Therefore $f(v)f(w)=f(v')f(w')$ for every elastic quadruple, equivalently $g(v)+g(w)=g(v')+g(w')$.

For arbitrary $a,z\in\mathbb R^3$ and any rotation $R\in SO(3)$, the incoming pair $(a+z,a-z)$ and outgoing pair $(a+Rz,a-Rz)$ have equal total momentum $2a$ and equal total squared speed $2|a|^2+2|z|^2$. The collision identity from step 1.1 gives
$$g(a+z)+g(a-z)=g(a+Rz)+g(a-Rz).$$
Thus for fixed $a$ and radius $|z|$, the left side is independent of the direction of $z$.

Fix a unit vector $\xi$ and any other unit vector $\eta$. Choose a rotation taking $\xi$ to $\eta$, put $z=s\xi$ in step 2.1, and expand each side at $s=0$ using [F3]. The constant and linear terms cancel in each symmetric pair. Dividing the resulting equality by $s^2$ and taking $s\to0$ gives $\xi^{\mathsf T}D^2g(a)\xi=\eta^{\mathsf T}D^2g(a)\eta$. Hence the quadratic form of the symmetric Hessian is constant on the unit sphere. Testing $e_i$ gives equal diagonal entries; testing $(e_i+e_j)/\sqrt2$ gives zero off-diagonal entries. Therefore $D^2g(a)=\lambda(a)I$.

Since the mixed second derivatives vanish, $\partial_i g(v)$ is constant along every coordinate segment in a direction $e_j$ with $j\ne i$, by [F4]. Connecting points with the same $i$th coordinate by three coordinate segments shows $\partial_i g(v)=G_i(v_i)$ for a differentiable one-variable function $G_i$. The Hessian identity in step 3.1 yields $G_i'(v_i)=G_j'(v_j)$ for every pair $i\ne j$ and every independent choice of $v_i,v_j$. Fixing $v_j$ while varying $v_i$ shows $G_i'$ is constant; equality then makes the constants the same $\lambda$. Thus $G_i(s)=\lambda s+b_i$, and integrating the gradient along coordinate segments gives
$$g(v)=\alpha+b\cdot v+\frac{\lambda}{2}|v|^2$$
for constants $\alpha\in\mathbb R$, $b\in\mathbb R^3$, and $\lambda\in\mathbb R$.

Because $f$ is integrable and positive on $\mathbb R^3$, $\lambda$ cannot be positive: the quadratic term then makes $e^{g(v)}$ nonintegrable at infinity. If $\lambda=0$, an affine exponential is either constant or grows on a half-space, and is again nonintegrable. Hence $\lambda<0$. Completing the square gives $g(v)=\alpha' - |v-U|^2/(2\theta)$ with $\theta=-1/\lambda>0$ and $U=-b/\lambda$. Exponentiating gives the asserted profile.

Conversely, for $g(v)=\alpha'-|v-U|^2/(2\theta)$, the sum $g(v)+g(w)$ depends only on $v+w$ and $|v|^2+|w|^2$. These are conserved on every elastic quadruple by [F1], so $A=B$ pointwise and the integrand defining $D_x$ vanishes.

For a nonnegative velocity density $f$ with finite absolute third moment, set $n:=\int f\,dv$ and, where $n>0$, set $u:=n^{-1}\int vf\,dv$ and $T:=m(3k_Bn)^{-1}\int|v-u|^2f\,dv$, using the particle mass $m>0$, Boltzmann constant $k_B>0$, and Lebesgue measure fixed in the kinetic-density definition. Where also $T>0$, put $\theta:=k_BT/m$ and define
$$M[f](v):=n(2\pi\theta)^{-3/2}\exp(-|v-u|^2/(2\theta)).$$
For a fixed relaxation time $\tau>0$ measured in seconds, define the single-species Bhatnagar–Gross–Krook (BGK) relaxation operator by
$$Q_{\rm BGK}(f):=\frac{M[f]-f}{\tau}.$$
The corresponding accelerated homogeneous model with dimensionless parameter $\epsilon>0$ is $\partial_t f=Q_{\rm BGK}(f)/\epsilon$. This is a prescribed relaxation model. It is distinct from the binary collision operator and does not by itself assert a derivation from microscopic mechanics or an inhomogeneous hydrodynamic limit.

Let $v_*=1\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, $\omega_3(v):=\sum_{j=0}^3(|v|/v_*)^j$, let $\tau>0$ be a relaxation time in seconds, and let $\epsilon>0$ be dimensionless. Let $f_0:\mathbb R^3\to[0,\infty)$ be a finite-valued measurable velocity density with units fixed by the kinetic-density definition, with $\int\omega_3f_0\,dv<\infty$, number density $n>0$, and strictly positive centered second moment. Let $M=M[f_0]$ be its positive-temperature Gaussian from the single-species BGK definition. Fix a constant reference density $f_{\rm ref}>0$ with the same units as $f_0$ and assume $\int f_0|\log(f_0/f_{\rm ref})|\,dv<\infty$, with $0\log0:=0$ and the integrand $f_0|\log(f_0/f_{\rm ref})|$ assigned value zero where $f_0=0$. Define
$$f^\epsilon(t,v):=M(v)+e^{-t/(\epsilon\tau)}(f_0(v)-M(v)),\qquad t\ge0\text{ in seconds}.$$
Then $f^\epsilon\ge0$, has the same mass, momentum, and kinetic energy as $f_0$ for every $t$, belongs to $C^1([0,\infty);L^1(\omega_3\,dv))$, and solves, as an equality in $L^1(\omega_3\,dv)$,
$$\partial_t f^\epsilon=\frac{M[f^\epsilon]-f^\epsilon}{\epsilon\tau},\qquad f^\epsilon(0)=f_0.$$
A solution means a nonnegative $C^1([0,\infty);L^1(\omega_3\,dv))$ function satisfying this equality at each time. The solution is unique among nonnegative solutions in this function class whose density and temperature remain strictly positive. Moreover,
$$\int_{\mathbb R^3}\omega_3|f^\epsilon(t)-M|\,dv =e^{-t/(\epsilon\tau)}\int_{\mathbb R^3}\omega_3|f_0-M|\,dv,$$
and for every $T_*>0$,
$$\int_0^{T_*}\int_{\mathbb R^3}\omega_3|f^\epsilon-M|\,dv\,dt \le\epsilon\tau\int_{\mathbb R^3}\omega_3|f_0-M|\,dv.$$
Thus the equilibrium limit is exact for each fixed $t>0$ and in spacetime weighted $L^1$, but need not be uniform at $t=0$. This branch has stationary homogeneous Euler moments; it gives no evolving inhomogeneous Euler limit.

Give $\Omega$ the completed, unnormalised pushforward of Lebesgue measure on $C=\prod_{j=1}^3[0,L_j)$ under the quotient map, as in the kinetic-density definition. Let $f:\Omega\times\mathbb R^3\times I\to(0,\infty)$ be $C^1$ in $(x,t)$ and $C^2$ in $v$, with $v$ measured in metres per second and $f$ in the units assigned by the kinetic-density definition. Fix a constant $f_{\rm ref}>0$ with the same units as $f$. Put $\ell=\log(f/f_{\rm ref})$, $A=f(x,v,t)f(x,w,t)$, and $B=f(x,v',t)f(x,w',t)$. Use the elastic collision set $Q_{\rm el}=\{(v,w,v',w')\in\mathbb R^{12}:v+w=v'+w',\ |v|^2+|w|^2=|v'|^2+|w'|^2\}$ with its relative Borel sigma-algebra and the nonnegative countably additive measure $\nu$ invariant under particle exchange in either pair and incoming/outgoing interchange, together with the weak operator $Q_\nu$ from the elastic-collision definition. Assume for each $t$ that $f$, $f|v|^2$, and $f|\ell|$ are integrable over $\Omega\times\mathbb R^3$. On each compact time interval assume a common integrable envelope in $(x,v)$ for $|(1+\ell)\partial_t f|$; at each $t$ assume $(1+|\ell|)|v\cdot\nabla_x f|$ is integrable over $\Omega\times\mathbb R^3$. In addition, assume
$$f(1+|v|)|\ell|,\quad (1+|\ell|)|\partial_t f|,\quad (1+|\ell|)|v|\,|\nabla_x f|\in L^1_{\rm loc}(I\times\Omega\times\mathbb R^3,dt\,dx\,dv),$$
so the entropy density, entropy flux, and local differentiation terms are integrable on compact time-space regions. Define
$$D(x,t):=\frac14\int_{Q_{\rm el}}(A-B)\log(A/B)\,d\nu.$$
Assume that $D$ is measurable and locally integrable on $I\times\Omega$, and that for each $t$ its spatial section belongs to $L^1(\Omega)$. At every $(x,t)$ assume $f(x,\cdot,t)\in\mathcal D_\nu$ and $1,\ell(x,\cdot,t)\in\mathcal S_{f(x,\cdot,t)}$, with the measurability and absolute-convergence conditions of the elastic-collision definition. With $\delta\varphi=\varphi(v)+\varphi(w)-\varphi(v')-\varphi(w')$, assume
$$\int_{\mathbb R^3}\varphi(v)Q_\nu(f)(v)\,dv=\frac14\int_{Q_{\rm el}}(B-A)\delta\varphi\,d\nu$$
for those two tests, and suppose $\partial_t f+v\cdot\nabla_x f=Q_\nu(f)$. Define
$$h(x,t):=\int_{\mathbb R^3}f\log(f/f_{\rm ref})\,dv,\qquad J_H(x,t):=\int_{\mathbb R^3}v f\log(f/f_{\rm ref})\,dv,$$
$$H(t):=\int_\Omega h(x,t)\,dx,\qquad D_{\rm tot}(t):=\int_\Omega D(x,t)\,dx.$$
Then the local entropy balance holds in distributions: for every $\eta\in C_c^\infty(I\times\Omega)$,
$$\int_I\int_\Omega\bigl(h\,\partial_t\eta+J_H\cdot\nabla_x\eta-D\eta\bigr)\,dx\,dt=0.$$
Moreover, $D(x,t)\ge0$ for almost every $(x,t)$. The periodic global entropy $H$ is differentiable and
$$\frac{dH}{dt}=-D_{\rm tot}(t)\le0.$$
The inequality is conditional on the adopted weak collision identity; it is not a derivation from reversible many-particle mechanics or a kinetic-PDE existence theorem.

Let $n>0$, $u\in\mathbb R^3$, $T>0$, particle mass $m>0$, and Boltzmann constant $k_B>0$. Set $\theta=k_BT/m$ and define $M_{n,u,T}(v):=n(2\pi\theta)^{-3/2}\exp(-|v-u|^2/(2\theta))$. Its Lebesgue moments are
$$\int_{\mathbb R^3}M_{n,u,T}\,dv=n,\qquad \int_{\mathbb R^3}vM_{n,u,T}\,dv=nu,$$
$$m\int_{\mathbb R^3}(v-u)\otimes(v-u)M_{n,u,T}\,dv=nk_BT\,I_3,\qquad \frac m2\int_{\mathbb R^3}|v-u|^2(v-u)M_{n,u,T}\,dv=0,$$
and
$$\frac m2\int_{\mathbb R^3}|v|^2M_{n,u,T}\,dv =\frac{mn|u|^2}{2}+\frac{3nk_BT}{2}.$$
Thus its pressure tensor is isotropic and its centered heat flux vanishes; these conclusions concern this Gaussian profile and do not impose isotropy on a general kinetic density.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to \mathbb C$ belong to
$L^1(\mu \times \nu)$. Then:

1. for $\mu$-almost every $x$, the section $f_x$ belongs to $L^1(\nu)$;
2. for $\nu$-almost every $y$, the section $f^y$ belongs to $L^1(\mu)$;
3. after assigning the value $0$ on the exceptional parameter sets, the
   section-integral functions are integrable; and
4. the three integrals agree:
$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

Let $a < b$ be reals and let $u, v : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at
every point of $[a,b]$ as functions on $[a,b]$ (The derivative $f'(c) = \lim_{x \to c} \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c}$ of $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ at a point $c \in A$ that is a limit point of $A$, and differentiability on a set). Suppose
$u'$ and $v'$ are integrable on $[a,b]$ (The lower and upper Darboux integrals of a bounded $f$ on $[a,b]$ as $\sup_P L(f,P)$ and $\inf_P U(f,P)$, Darboux integrability as their equality, and the notation $\int_a^b f$). Then $uv'$
and $u'v$ are integrable and

$$\int_a^b u\,v' \;=\; u(b)v(b) - u(a)v(a) \;-\; \int_a^b u'\,v .$$

**The integrability of $u'$ and $v'$ is a hypothesis, not a formality.** Without
it the two integrals in the display need not exist at all, and the identity is
then not false but ill-formed; that is
the false statement that deletes it on the companion
page. The hypothesis is automatic when $u$ and $v$ are continuously
differentiable, since a continuous function on $[a,b]$ is integrable
(A continuous function on $[a,b]$ is Riemann integrable, by Heine-Cantor and Riemann's criterion).

The initial difference is at most $C_\chi\int_\Omega\int\omega_2|f^\varepsilon(0)-M(0)|$, since $\psi$ has degree at most two. Both tend to zero by the two stated convergence hypotheses. e0$. For each fixed velocity, integrate $\psi f^\varepsilon$ against $\partial_t\chi+v\cdot
abla_x\chi$ and use [F4] in time and in each spatial coordinate. The time boundary is $-\int_\Omega\psi f^\varepsilon(0,x,v)\chi(0,x)\,d^3x$, and opposite periodic spatial boundaries cancel. Integrate this identity in velocity using [F3]. Indeed, $\psi$ has degree at most two, so $|\psi|$ and $|\psi||v|$ are bounded by constants times $\omega_3$; the displayed moment, time-derivative, and summed-transport envelopes make the grouped terms absolutely integrable. The initial term is integrable by the same moment bound at $t=0$. Thus step 1.1 gives the weak moment identity
$$\int_0^{T_*}\int_\Omega\int_{\mathbb R^3}\psi f^\varepsilon(\partial_t\chi+v\cdot
abla_x\chi)\,d^3v\,d^3x\,dt+\int_\Omega\int_{\mathbb R^3}\psi f^\varepsilon(0,x,v)\chi(0,x)\,d^3v\,d^3x=0.$$
The spatial integration by parts was performed at each fixed velocity before applying Fubini to the summed transport and final test-gradient terms, so no separate weighted spatial derivative bound has been assumed.

Apply [F1] to the Gaussian moments in step 3.1. The multiplier $m$ gives density $\rho$ and flux $\rho u$; the three multipliers $mv_i$ give momentum $\rho u$ and flux tensor $\rho u\otimes u+pI_3$; the multiplier $m|v|^2/2$ gives energy $E$ and flux $(E+p)u$. Applying the scalar identity componentwise to a vector test gives the momentum weak identity. Thus all three Euler equations hold in distributions, and their weak identities include exactly the initial values of the displayed Gaussian moments, identified by the $\omega_2$ initial convergence. These are the stated initial traces of the $C^1$ limiting fields.

The residuals of the three displayed Euler equations are continuous because the limiting fields are $C^1$. If a residual component were nonzero at an interior point, it would have one strict sign on a sufficiently small coordinate ball in $(0,T_*)\times\Omega$. Choose concentric balls within that chart and a nonnegative smooth bump from [F5], equal to one on the inner ball and supported in the outer ball; extend it by zero to the periodic cylinder. Its pairing with the residual would have strict sign, contradicting the distributional identity from step 4.1. Every residual therefore vanishes pointwise for $0<t<T_*$.

The observables [F2] identify $\rho=mn$ and the physical kinetic-energy density. The Gaussian moments in [F1] give $E=\rho|u|^2/2+3nk_BT/2$ and $p=nk_BT$, with precisely the stated SI units. The argument has used weighted strong convergence and its initial counterpart as assumptions, not derived them from small $\varepsilon$ or entropy. The full conclusion is conditional on the adopted physical model [A1] and convergence hypotheses [A2], with no empirical validity claim.

Let $I\subset\mathbb R$ be a bounded open time interval measured in seconds and let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^3$ be a fixed bounded open spatial domain measured in metres whose boundary is locally a Lipschitz graph after rigid coordinate changes. Take $\rho_0>0$ kilograms per cubic metre and $\mu_0>0$ pascal seconds as primitive branch-local physical parameters: this forced branch adopts them as constant density and dynamic shear viscosity inputs and derives neither from another framework nor from observations. Let $u:I\times\Omega\to\mathbb R^3$ be a twice continuously differentiable velocity in metres per second, $p:I\times\Omega\to\mathbb R$ a once continuously differentiable pressure multiplier in pascals, and $b:I\times\Omega\to\mathbb R^3$ a continuous body-acceleration field in metres per second squared. Define $D=(\nabla u+\nabla u^{\mathsf T})/2$ and the stress tensor $\sigma=-pI_3+2\mu_0D$ in pascals, where $I_3$ is the $3\times3$ identity and $(\operatorname{div}\sigma)_i=\sum_{j=1}^3\partial_{x_j}\sigma_{ij}$.

The forced incompressible Newtonian branch adopts

$$\operatorname{div}u=0,\qquad \rho_0\bigl(\partial_tu+(u\cdot\nabla)u\bigr)=\rho_0b+\operatorname{div}\sigma.$$

Equivalently, since $\mu_0$ is constant and $\operatorname{div}u=0$, its momentum equation is

$$\rho_0\bigl(\partial_tu+(u\cdot\nabla)u\bigr)+\nabla p=\mu_0\Delta u+\rho_0b.$$

The derived kinematic viscosity is $\nu_{\mathrm{phys}}=\mu_0/\rho_0$ in square metres per second. Pressure is a constraint multiplier, not an equation-of-state pressure. For a stationary solid wall, the separately selected no-slip boundary datum is $u=0$ on the wall; neither this trace nor the body force follows from the interior balance. This is a forced branch of the Newtonian model: it adds the prescribed acceleration field to the unforced branch and makes no claim of solution existence or empirical validity.

Use the Newtonian spacetime and Cartesian inertial-chart convention from the earlier definition titled “Classical frames, primitive quantities and SI units”: time is absolute, $M$ is an oriented Euclidean affine three-space with no distinguished origin, and a Cartesian inertial chart is an orientation-preserving affine isometry $X:M\to\mathbb R^3$ paired with that time coordinate. Choose the positive $X_1$ axis and restrict this branch to fields depending only on absolute time $t$ and the coordinate $x:=X_1$; $u$ is the signed scalar velocity component along that axis. Here a frame means this adapted Cartesian inertial chart, not an observer congruence or a basis field. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an open interval of $x$ measured in metres, let $T_f>0$ be a final time measured in seconds, and take the space-time domain to be $\Omega\times(0,T_f)$. The measurable fields are mass density $\rho:\Omega\times(0,T_f)\to(0,\infty)$ in kilograms per cubic metre, velocity $u:\Omega\times(0,T_f)\to\mathbb R$ in metres per second, and specific entropy $s:\Omega\times(0,T_f)\to\mathbb R$ in joules per kilogram kelvin.

Adopt a local-equilibrium constitutive chart on the open state domain $\mathcal U=(0,\infty)\times\mathbb R$ with coordinates $(v,s)$ and a $C^2$ fundamental relation $e:\mathcal U\to\mathbb R$ for specific internal energy in joules per kilogram. Define the derived specific heat at constant pressure and ratio of specific heats by $c_p:=c_v+R$ and $\gamma:=c_p/c_v=1+R/c_v>1$. Choose $v_*>0$ in cubic metres per kilogram, $T_*>0$ in kelvins, and $s_*\in\mathbb R$ in joules per kilogram kelvin as reference data. Adopt the calorically perfect ideal-gas relation
$$e(v,s)=c_vT_*\left(\frac{v_*}{v}\right)^{\gamma-1}\exp\left(\frac{s-s_*}{c_v}\right),$$
with the conventional additive energy reference for which the specific internal energy is zero at zero temperature. Define the thermodynamic temperature and pressure maps by $T(v,s):=\partial_s e(v,s)$ and $p(v,s):=-\partial_v e(v,s)$, holding the other state coordinate fixed. Direct differentiation gives
$$T(v,s)=\frac{e(v,s)}{c_v}>0,\qquad p(v,s)=(\gamma-1)\frac{e(v,s)}{v}>0.$$
For density and entropy coordinates define the state-pressure map $p_{\mathrm{th}}(\rho,s):=p(1/\rho,s)$ for $\rho>0$ and $s\in\mathbb R$. The spacetime state map is $v(t,x):=1/\rho(t,x)$ and $(t,x)\mapsto(v(t,x),s(t,x))\in\mathcal U$. It assigns the specific internal-energy, temperature, and thermodynamic-pressure fields by
$$e_{\mathrm{int}}(t,x):=e(v(t,x),s(t,x)),\qquad T(t,x):=(\partial_s e)(v(t,x),s(t,x)),\qquad p_{\mathrm{th}}(t,x):=p_{\mathrm{th}}(\rho(t,x),s(t,x))=-(\partial_v e)(v(t,x),s(t,x)).$$
Consequently $T(t,x)=e_{\mathrm{int}}(t,x)/c_v$ and $p_{\mathrm{th}}(t,x)=(\gamma-1)e_{\mathrm{int}}(t,x)/v(t,x)=(\gamma-1)\rho(t,x)e_{\mathrm{int}}(t,x)=R\rho(t,x)T(t,x)$. At fixed specific entropy $s$, the state-pressure map is proportional to $\rho^\gamma$, so $\left.\partial_\rho p_{\mathrm{th}}(\rho,s)\right|_s=\gamma p_{\mathrm{th}}(\rho,s)/\rho$; define the positive isentropic sound-speed map by $c_{\mathrm{th}}(\rho,s):=\sqrt{\left.\partial_\rho p_{\mathrm{th}}(\rho,s)\right|_s}=\sqrt{\gamma p_{\mathrm{th}}(\rho,s)/\rho}$. Thus $\gamma$ is dimensionless, sound speed has units of metres per second, and pressure has units of pascals. This is a constant-specific-heat ideal-gas approximation, restricted to a regime where that closure is adopted.

Define momentum density $m(t,x):=\rho(t,x)u(t,x)$ in kilograms per square metre second and total energy density $E(t,x):=\rho(t,x)(e_{\mathrm{int}}(t,x)+u(t,x)^2/2)$ in joules per cubic metre. details.actual_current_public_excerpt:
Use the Newtonian spacetime and Cartesian inertial-chart convention from the earlier definition titled “Classical frames, primitive quantities and SI units”: time is absolute, $M$ is an oriented Euclidean affine three-space with no distinguished origin, and a Cartesian inertial chart is an orientation-preserving affine isometry $X:M\to\mathbb R^3$ paired with that time coordinate. Choose the positive $X_1$ axis and restrict this branch to fields depending only on absolute time $t$ and the coordinate $x:=X_1$; $u$ is the signed scalar velocity component along that axis. Here a frame means this adapted Cartesian inertial chart, not an observer congruence or a basis field. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an open interval of $x$ measured in metres, let $T_f>0$ be a final time measured in seconds, and take the space-time domain to be $\Omega\times(0,T_f)$. The measurable fields are mass density $\rho:\Omega\times(0,T_f)\to(0,\infty)$ in kilograms per cubic metre, velocity $u:\Omega\times(0,T_f)\to\mathbb R$ in metres per second, and specific entropy $s:\Omega\times(0,T_f)\to\mathbb R$ in joules per kilogram kelvin.

Adopt a local-equilibrium constitutive chart on the open state domain $\mathcal U=(0,\infty)\times\mathbb R$ with coordinates $(v,s)$ and a $C^2$ fundamental relation $e:\mathcal U\to\mathbb R$ for specific internal energy in joules per kilogram. Let $c_v>0$ be the adopted specific-heat-at-constant-volume parameter and $R>0$ the adopted specific gas-constant parameter, each in joules per kilogram kelvin. Define the derived specific heat at constant pressure and ratio of specific heats by $c_p:=c_v+R$ and $\gamma:=c_p/c_v=1+R/c_v>1$. Choose $v_*>0$ in cubic metres per kilogram, $T_*>0$ in kelvins, and $s_*\in\mathbb R$ in joules per kilogram kelvin as reference data. Adopt the calorically perfect ideal-gas relation
$$e(v,s)=c_vT_*\left(\frac{v_*}{v}\right)^{\gamma-1}\exp\left(\frac{s-s_*}{c_v}\right),$$
with the conventional additive energy reference for which the specific internal energy is zero at zero temperature. Define the thermodynamic temperature and pressure maps by $T(v,s):=\partial_s e(v,s)$ and $p(v,s):=-\partial_v e(v,s)$, holding the other state coordinate fixed. Direct differentiation gives
$$T(v,s)=\frac{e(v,s)}{c_v}>0,\qquad p(v,s)=(\gamma-1)\frac{e(v,s)}{v}>0.$$
For density and entropy coordinates define the state-pressure map $p_{\mathrm{th}}(\rho,s):=p(1/\rho,s)$ for $\rho>0$ and $s\in\mathbb R$. The spacetime state map is $v(t,x):=1/\rho(t,x)$ and $(t,x)\mapsto(v(t,x),s(t,x))\in\mathcal U$. It assigns the specific internal-energy, temperature, and thermodynamic-pressure fields by
$$e_{\mathrm{int}}(t,x):=e(v(t,x),s(t,x)),\qquad T(t,x):=(\partial_s e)(v(t,x),s(t,x)),\qquad p_{\mathrm{th}}(t,x):=p_{\mathrm{th}}(\rho(t,x),s(t,x))=-(\partial_v e)(v(t,x),s(t,x)).$$
Consequently $T(t,x)=e_{\mathrm{int}}(t,x)/c_v$ and $p_{\mathrm{th}}(t,x)=(\gamma-1)e_{\mathrm{int}}(t,x)/v(t,x)=(\gamma-1)\rho(t,x)e_{\mathrm{int}}(t,x)=R\rho(t,x)T(t,x)$. At fixed specific entropy $s$, the state-pressure map is proportional to $\rho^\gamma$, so $\left.\partial_\rho p_{\mathrm{th}}(\rho,s)\right|_s=\gamma p_{\mathrm{th}}(\rho,s)/\rho$; define the positive isentropic sound-speed map by $c_{\mathrm{th}}(\rho,s):=\sqrt{\left.\partial_\rho p_{\mathrm{th}}(\rho,s)\right|_s}=\sqrt{\gamma p_{\mathrm{th}}(\rho,s)/\rho}$. Thus $\gamma$ is dimensionless, sound speed has units of metres per second, and pressure has units of pascals. This is a constant-specific-heat ideal-gas approximation, restricted to a regime where that closure is adopted.

Define momentum density $m(t,x):=\rho(t,x)u(t,x)$ in kilograms per square metre second and total energy density $E(t,x):=\rho(t,x)(e_{\mathrm{int}}(t,x)+u(t,x)^2/2)$ in joules per cubic metre. The corresponding numerical state is $U(t,x):=(\rho(t,x),m(t,x),E(t,x))\in\mathbb R^3$. For $\gamma>1$, set
$$\mathcal G_\gamma=\left\{(\rho,m,E):\rho>0,\quad E-\frac{m^2}{2\rho}>0\right\},\qquad p(U)=(\gamma-1)\left(E-\frac{m^2}{2\rho}\right).$$
Since $\rho(t,x)>0$ and $e_{\mathrm{int}}(t,x)>0$, $U(t,x)\in\mathcal G_\gamma$. For this state, $E-m^2/(2\rho)=\rho e_{\mathrm{int}}$ and $p(U(t,x))=p_{\mathrm{th}}(t,x)$, so the numerical and thermodynamic pressure maps agree. With $u=m/\rho$, its one-dimensional Euler flux and isentropic sound speed are
$$F(U)=\left(m,\frac{m^2}{\rho}+p(U),u(E+p(U))\right),\qquad c(U)=\sqrt{\frac{\gamma p(U)}{\rho}}.$$
The components of $F$ are mass flux in kilograms per square metre second, momentum flux in pascals, and energy flux in watts per square metre. The speed $c$ is in metres per second.

Adopt the inviscid one-dimensional branch with zero body acceleration, zero specific heat supply, zero conductive heat flux, and isotropic three-dimensional Cauchy stress $\sigma=-p_{\mathrm{th}}I_3$ in the tension-positive convention in which traction on an outward unit normal $n$ is $\sigma n$; here $I_3$ is the $3\times3$ identity matrix. Its restriction to the selected axis is the scalar normal stress $\sigma_{\mathrm{1D}}:=\sigma_{11}=-p_{\mathrm{th}}$ in pascals, so the one-dimensional momentum flux is $\rho u^2-\sigma_{\mathrm{1D}}=\rho u^2+p_{\mathrm{th}}$. In the following weak identities, write $p:=p_{\mathrm{th}}$. Assume the locally integrable conservative variables, fluxes, entropy density, and entropy flux satisfy the identities in the distributional sense. Let $\rho_0,m_0,E_0,S_0\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega)$ be the initial mass density in kilograms per cubic metre, momentum density in kilograms per square metre second, total energy density in joules per cubic metre, and entropy density in joules per cubic metre kelvin, respectively. Require all displayed densities, fluxes, and products to be locally integrable up to $t=0$: their absolute values have finite integrals on every compact subset of $\Omega\times[0,T_f)$ in the relative topology, using the fields for $t>0$. This requirement assigns no point values at $t=0$ and asserts no strong initial trace. Test functions $\phi,\psi,\eta,\zeta\in C^1(\Omega\times[0,T_f))$ are compactly supported in space-time and vanish near $T_f$; $\zeta$ is nonnegative, and tests may be nonzero at $t=0$. Then adopt
$$\int_0^{T_f}\!\!\int_\Omega\left(\rho\,\partial_t\phi+\rho u\,\partial_x\phi\right)\,dx\,dt+\int_\Omega\rho_0\phi(0,x)\,dx=0,$$
$$\int_0^{T_f}\!\!\int_\Omega\left(\rho u\,\partial_t\psi+(\rho u^2+p)\partial_x\psi\right)\,dx\,dt+\int_\Omega m_0\psi(0,x)\,dx=0,$$
$$\int_0^{T_f}\!\!\int_\Omega\left(E\,\partial_t\eta+u(E+p)\partial_x\eta\right)\,dx\,dt+\int_\Omega E_0\eta(0,x)\,dx=0,$$
and
$$\int_0^{T_f}\!\!\int_\Omega\left(\rho s\,\partial_t\zeta+\rho u s\,\partial_x\zeta\right)\,dx\,dt+\int_\Omega S_0\zeta(0,x)\,dx\le0.$$
The last inequality is a separately adopted physical entropy inequality. It is not deduced from the conservative equations or from smooth-flow identities. This postulate specifies a physical model and its idealized local-equilibrium closure; it does not assert existence or uniqueness of a weak solution, prove that actual matter obeys the model, or identify a computed state with an experimental observation.

1.1 By [A1] and [F4], scalar $L^2(D,\lambda)$ and $L^1(D,\lambda)$ are complete. The $H$ norm is the finite $\ell^2$ product of the component $L^2$ norms. For a matrix field $A$, $\|A\|_K=\int_D|A|_F\,d\lambda$, and
$$\|A\|_K\le\sum_{i,j}\|A_{ij}\|_1\le d\|A\|_K.$$
Thus a Cauchy sequence in either $H$ or $K$ is Cauchy in each scalar component; the component limits exist by [F4], and the displayed norm formulas show convergence to their assembled vector or matrix field. Hence $H$ and $K$ are Banach spaces under [A1]. [A1, F1, F4, construct, algebra]

1.2 For representatives $v,w$, the Frobenius norm satisfies $|v(x)\otimes w(x)|_F=|v(x)|\,|w(x)|$. Holder's inequality [F3] therefore gives $\|v\otimes w\|_K=\int_D|v|\,|w|\,d\lambda\le\|v\|_H\|w\|_H<\infty$. Changing either representative on a null set changes the product only on a null set [F1], so the tensor is well-defined as a $K$-class. The same estimate applied to differences proves continuity of the bilinear tensor map. [F1, F3, given, algebra]

1.3 By [F2], choose simple $H$-valued maps $U_n$ with $U_n(\omega)\to U(\omega)$ in $H$ outside a measurable null set. Each $U_n\otimes U_n$ is a finite-valued measurable $K$-valued simple map. Step 1.2 gives
$$\|U_n\otimes U_n-U\otimes U\|_K\le \|U_n-U\|_H(\|U_n\|_H+\|U\|_H)\longrightarrow0$$
outside that null set, since norm convergence makes $(\|U_n\|_H)$ bounded there. Hence $U\otimes U$ is strongly measurable. [F2, step 1.2, construct, algebra]

2.1 Holder's inequality on the probability space gives $\mathbb E\|U\|_H\le(\mathbb E\|U\|_H^2)^{1/2}<\infty$. Together with the given strong measurability, [F5] makes $U$ Bochner integrable. The identity $|v\otimes v|_F=|v|^2$ gives $\|U(\omega)\otimes U(\omega)\|_K=\|U(\omega)\|_H^2$ for almost every $\omega$, so its norm is integrable as well; [F5] and step 2.1 make $U\otimes U$ Bochner integrable and yield the displayed norm identity. [A1, F3, F5, step 2.1, given, algebra] ∎

before.quote:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Let $(D,\mathcal D,\lambda)$, $H$, and the finite-second-moment probability law $\mu$ be as in the Definition. For every $\psi\in H$, the integral defining $S_\psi(v)$ is finite and independent of the representatives of $v$ and $\psi$. The map $S_\psi:H\to\mathbb R$ is linear and continuous, with
$$|S_\psi(v)|\le \|v\|_H\|\psi\|_H.$$
Its centered observable $f_\psi(v)=S_\psi(v)-\int_H S_\psi\,d\mu$ is Borel measurable and belongs to $L^2(\mu)$.

Assume AC. Let $(\mathsf X,\mathcal X)$ be countably generated, let $P$ be a
$\phi$-irreducible probability kernel ([[def-phi-irreducible-chain]], [[def-measure-kernel-and-probability-kernel]]), aperiodic
([[def-general-state-aperiodic-markov-chain]]), and Harris recurrent relative
to $\phi$ ([[def-harris-recurrent-markov-chain]]) with invariant probability
$\pi$, and let $(X_k)_{k\ge0}$ be a stationary
$P$-chain whose canonical left shift preserves its path law and whose
shift-invariant measurable events have probability zero or one. We take the
initial law to be $\pi$, which implies stationarity by
[[thm-invariant-initial-law-makes-the-chain-stationary]]. Let
$f:\mathsf X\to\mathbb R$
be Borel with $\pi(f)=0$. Define
$\sigma_f^2=\pi(f^2)+2\sum_{k\ge1}\operatorname{Cov}_{\pi}(f(X_0),f(X_k))$
only when the covariance series is absolutely convergent and the CLT is
established, as in
[[def-long-run-variance-for-stationary-markov-chain]].

Each of the following six conditions is sufficient for absolute convergence
of the covariance series and
$$\frac1{\sqrt n}\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}f(X_k)\Rightarrow N(0,\sigma_f^2):$$

1. $P$ has polynomial total-variation rate of order $m>1$ with an integrable
   envelope ([[def-polynomial-ergodicity-with-integrable-rate-envelope]]),
   and $f$ is essentially bounded under $\pi$ (there is $B<\infty$ with
   $|f|\le B$ $\pi$-almost everywhere).
2. $P$ has polynomial total-variation rate of order $m>0$ with an integrable
   envelope ([[def-polynomial-ergodicity-with-integrable-rate-envelope]]),
   $f\in L^{2+\delta}(\pi)$ for some $\delta>0$
   ([[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]]), and
   $m\delta>2+\delta$.
3. $P$ is geometrically ergodic ([[def-geometric-and-uniform-ergodicity-for-mcmc-clt]]) and $f\in L^{2+\delta}(\pi)$ for some
   $\delta>0$ ([[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]]).
4. $P$ is geometrically ergodic ([[def-geometric-and-uniform-ergodicity-for-mcmc-clt]]) and
   $\pi\bigl(f^2\log^+|f|\bigr)<\infty$, with
   $0\log^+0:=0$.
5. $P$ is geometrically ergodic ([[def-geometric-and-uniform-ergodicity-for-mcmc-clt]]), reversible with respect to $\pi$ in the symmetric-flow sense ([[def-general-state-reversibility-by-symmetric-flow-measure]]), and $f\in L^2(\pi)$ ([[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]]).
6. $P$ is uniformly ergodic ([[def-geometric-and-uniform-ergodicity-for-mcmc-clt]]) and $f\in L^2(\pi)$ ([[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]]).

In case 4, the displayed logarithmic moment implies $f\in L^2(\pi)$: on $\{|f|\le e\}$ one has $f^2\le e^2$, and on $\{|f|>e\}$ one has $f^2\le f^2\log|f|$.

When $\sigma_f^2=0$, the zero-variance lemma
[[lem-zero-long-run-variance-gives-degenerate-clt]] gives the degenerate
normal limit from absolute covariance summability. Finite variance of $f$
alone is not one of the sufficient conditions.

Let $(X_k)_{k\ge0}$ be a stationary time-homogeneous Markov chain with invariant probability $\pi$, and let $f$ be real Borel with $\pi(f)=0$ and $\pi(f^2)<\infty$. For $k\ge0$, set $\gamma_k:=\operatorname{Cov}_{\pi}(f(X_0),f(X_k))$. When the Markov-chain CLT $n^{-1/2}\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}f(X_k)\Rightarrow N(0,\sigma_f^2)$ holds with finite variance parameter and $\sum_{k\ge1}|\gamma_k|<\infty$, the **covariance long-run variance** is
$$\sigma^2_{\mathrm{LR}}(f):=\gamma_0+2\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}\gamma_k.$$

This definition does not infer a CLT from covariance summability, or infer that a weak-limit variance equals the covariance sum. Whenever $\sigma^2_{\mathrm{LR}}(f)$ is used as the variance parameter in a CLT or MCSE claim, that equality must be established by the theorem being applied. For example, the local Poisson-equation theorem proves the equality under its square-integrable solution hypotheses.

Assume AC. Let $(Y_k)_{k\ge0}$ be a centered strictly stationary real sequence with $\mathbb E[Y_0^2]<\infty$, and define $S_n=\sum_{k=1}^nY_k$. Each of the following is sufficient:

1. There is $B<\infty$ with $|Y_0|\le B$ almost surely and $\sum_{n\ge1}\alpha_Y(n)<\infty$.
2. For some $\delta>0$, $\mathbb E|Y_0|^{2+\delta}<\infty$ and $\sum_{n\ge1}\alpha_Y(n)^{\delta/(2+\delta)}<\infty$.
3. For some $a\in(0,1)$, $\alpha_Y(n)=O(a^n)$ and $\mathbb E[Y_0^2\log^+|Y_0|]<\infty$, where $\log^+u=\max(0,\log u)$ for $u>0$ and $0\log^+0:=0$.

In each case the covariance series
$$\sigma_Y^2:=\mathbb E[Y_0^2]+2\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}\operatorname{Cov}(Y_0,Y_k)$$
converges absolutely and is nonnegative, and
$$n^{-1/2}S_n\Rightarrow N(0,\sigma_Y^2).$$
This includes the degenerate law $N(0,0)$ when $\sigma_Y^2=0$, as in [[lem-zero-long-run-variance-gives-degenerate-clt]]. The coefficient $\alpha_Y$ and strict stationarity have the meanings in [[def-mixing-coefficients-for-stationary-markov-chain]].

Let $Y=(Y_k)_{k\ge0}$ be a process on a probability space whose finite-dimensional laws are invariant under common nonnegative time shifts; call this strict stationarity. For $j\ge0$, set $\mathcal F_j^-:=\sigma(Y_0,\ldots,Y_j)$ and $\mathcal F_j^+:=\sigma(Y_j,Y_{j+1},\ldots)$. For $n\ge1$, define the **strong-mixing coefficient** by
$$\alpha_Y(n):=\sup_{j\ge0}\ \sup_{\substack{A\in\mathcal F_j^-\\B\in\mathcal F_{j+n}^+}}|\mathbb P(A\cap B)-\mathbb P(A)\mathbb P(B)|.$$

Define the **uniform-mixing coefficient** by
$$\phi_Y(n):=\sup_{j\ge0}\ \sup_{\substack{A\in\mathcal F_j^-\\\mathbb P(A)>0}}\ \sup_{B\in\mathcal F_{j+n}^+}|\mathbb P(B\mid A)-\mathbb P(B)|.$$

For square-integrable real random variables $U,V$ with positive variances, write
$$\operatorname{Corr}(U,V):=\frac{\operatorname{Cov}(U,V)}{\sqrt{\operatorname{Var}(U)\operatorname{Var}(V)}}.$$
For each $n\ge1$, let $\mathcal C_n$ consist of the triples $(j,U,V)$ such that $j\ge0$, $U,V$ are real and square-integrable, $U$ and $V$ are measurable with respect to $\mathcal F_j^-$ and $\mathcal F_{j+n}^+$ respectively, and both have positive variance. Define the **maximal-correlation coefficient** by
$$\rho_Y(n):=\sup\Bigl(\{0\}\cup\{|\operatorname{Corr}(U,V)|:(j,U,V)\in\mathcal C_n\}\Bigr),$$
where square-integrability is in the sense of [[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]]. Thus $\rho_Y(n)=0$ when there is no admissible pair, as for a constant process. The process is called strongly mixing, uniformly mixing, or rho-mixing, respectively, when the corresponding coefficient tends to zero. These coefficients are distinct conditions; no implication between them is included in this definition.

$$\frac1{\sqrt n}\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}f(X_k)\Rightarrow N(0,\sigma_f^2):$$

1. $P$ has polynomial total-variation rate of order $m>1$ with an integrable
   envelope ([[def-polynomial-ergodicity-with-integrable-rate-envelope]]),
   and $f$ is essentially bounded under $\pi$ (there is $B<\infty$ with
   $|f|\le B$ $\pi$-almost everywhere).
2. $P$ has polynomial total-variation rate of order $m>0$ with an integrable
   envelope ([[def-polynomial-ergodicity-with-integrable-rate-envelope]]),
   $f\in L^{2+\delta}(\pi)$ for some $\delta>0$
   ([[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]]), and
   $m\delta>2+\delta$.
3. $P$ is geometrically ergodic ([[def-geometric-and-uniform-ergodicity-for-mcmc-clt]]) and $f\in L^{2+\delta}(\pi)$ for some
   $\delta>0$ ([[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]]).
4. $P$ is geometrically ergodic ([[def-geometric-and-uniform-ergodicity-for-mcmc-clt]]) and
   $\pi\bigl(f^2\log^+|f|\bigr)<\infty$, with
   $0\log^+0:=0$.
5. $P$ is geometrically ergodic ([[def-geometric-and-uniform-ergodicity-for-mcmc-clt]]), reversible with respect to $\pi$ in the symmetric-flow sense ([[def-general-state-reversibility-by-symmetric-flow-measure]]), and $f\in L^2(\pi)$ ([[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]]).
6. $P$ is uniformly ergodic ([[def-geometric-and-uniform-ergodicity-for-mcmc-clt]]) and $f\in L^2(\pi)$ ([[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]]).

In case 4, the displayed logarithmic moment implies $f\in L^2(\pi)$: on $\{|f|\le e\}$ one has $f^2\le e^2$, and on $\{|f|>e\}$ one has $f^2\le f^2\log|f|$.

When $\sigma_f^2=0$, the zero-variance lemma
[[lem-zero-long-run-variance-gives-degenerate-clt]] gives the degenerate
normal limit from absolute covariance summability. Finite variance of $f$
alone is not one of the sufficient conditions.

Let $(X_k)_{k\ge0}$ be a stationary time-homogeneous Markov chain with invariant probability $\pi$, and let $f$ be real Borel with $\pi(f)=0$ and $\pi(f^2)<\infty$. For $k\ge0$, set $\gamma_k:=\operatorname{Cov}_{\pi}(f(X_0),f(X_k))$. When the Markov-chain CLT $n^{-1/2}\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}f(X_k)\Rightarrow N(0,\sigma_f^2)$ holds with finite variance parameter and $\sum_{k\ge1}|\gamma_k|<\infty$, the **covariance long-run variance** is
$$\sigma^2_{\mathrm{LR}}(f):=\gamma_0+2\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}\gamma_k.$$

This definition does not infer a CLT from covariance summability, or infer that a weak-limit variance equals the covariance sum. Whenever $\sigma^2_{\mathrm{LR}}(f)$ is used as the variance parameter in a CLT or MCSE claim, that equality must be established by the theorem being applied. For example, the local Poisson-equation theorem proves the equality under its square-integrable solution hypotheses.

Assume AC. Let $(Y_k)_{k\ge0}$ be a centered strictly stationary real sequence with $\mathbb E[Y_0^2]<\infty$, and define $S_n=\sum_{k=1}^nY_k$. Each of the following is sufficient:

1. There is $B<\infty$ with $|Y_0|\le B$ almost surely and $\sum_{n\ge1}\alpha_Y(n)<\infty$.
2. For some $\delta>0$, $\mathbb E|Y_0|^{2+\delta}<\infty$ and $\sum_{n\ge1}\alpha_Y(n)^{\delta/(2+\delta)}<\infty$.
3. For some $a\in(0,1)$, $\alpha_Y(n)=O(a^n)$ and $\mathbb E[Y_0^2\log^+|Y_0|]<\infty$, where $\log^+u=\max(0,\log u)$ for $u>0$ and $0\log^+0:=0$.

In each case the covariance series
$$\sigma_Y^2:=\mathbb E[Y_0^2]+2\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}\operatorname{Cov}(Y_0,Y_k)$$
converges absolutely and is nonnegative, and
$$n^{-1/2}S_n\Rightarrow N(0,\sigma_Y^2).$$
This includes the degenerate law $N(0,0)$ when $\sigma_Y^2=0$, as in [[lem-zero-long-run-variance-gives-degenerate-clt]]. The coefficient $\alpha_Y$ and strict stationarity have the meanings in [[def-mixing-coefficients-for-stationary-markov-chain]].

Let $Y=(Y_k)_{k\ge0}$ be a process on a probability space whose finite-dimensional laws are invariant under common nonnegative time shifts; call this strict stationarity. For $j\ge0$, set $\mathcal F_j^-:=\sigma(Y_0,\ldots,Y_j)$ and $\mathcal F_j^+:=\sigma(Y_j,Y_{j+1},\ldots)$. For $n\ge1$, define the **strong-mixing coefficient** by
$$\alpha_Y(n):=\sup_{j\ge0}\ \sup_{\substack{A\in\mathcal F_j^-\\B\in\mathcal F_{j+n}^+}}|\mathbb P(A\cap B)-\mathbb P(A)\mathbb P(B)|.$$

Define the **uniform-mixing coefficient** by
$$\phi_Y(n):=\sup_{j\ge0}\ \sup_{\substack{A\in\mathcal F_j^-\\\mathbb P(A)>0}}\ \sup_{B\in\mathcal F_{j+n}^+}|\mathbb P(B\mid A)-\mathbb P(B)|.$$

For square-integrable real random variables $U,V$ with positive variances, write
$$\operatorname{Corr}(U,V):=\frac{\operatorname{Cov}(U,V)}{\sqrt{\operatorname{Var}(U)\operatorname{Var}(V)}}.$$
For each $n\ge1$, let $\mathcal C_n$ consist of the triples $(j,U,V)$ such that $j\ge0$, $U,V$ are real and square-integrable, $U$ and $V$ are measurable with respect to $\mathcal F_j^-$ and $\mathcal F_{j+n}^+$ respectively, and both have positive variance. Define the **maximal-correlation coefficient** by
$$\rho_Y(n):=\sup\Bigl(\{0\}\cup\{|\operatorname{Corr}(U,V)|:(j,U,V)\in\mathcal C_n\}\Bigr),$$
where square-integrability is in the sense of [[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]]. Thus $\rho_Y(n)=0$ when there is no admissible pair, as for a constant process. The process is called strongly mixing, uniformly mixing, or rho-mixing, respectively, when the corresponding coefficient tends to zero. These coefficients are distinct conditions; no implication between them is included in this definition.
