On $\Omega_0\times I$ the adopted equations and boundary conditions are

$$\Delta_h\phi+\partial_z^2\phi=0,\qquad -h<z<0,$$

$$\partial_z\phi(x,-h,t)=0,$$

$$\partial_t\eta(x,t)=\partial_z\phi(x,0,t),\qquad \partial_t\phi(x,0,t)+g\eta(x,t)-\frac{\gamma}{\rho}\Delta_h\eta(x,t)=0.$$

after.quote:
On $\Omega_0\times I$ the adopted equations and boundary conditions are

$$\Delta_h\phi+\partial_z^2\phi=0,\qquad -h<z<0,$$

$$\partial_z\phi(x,-h,t)=0,$$

$$\partial_t\eta(x,t)=\partial_z\phi(x,0,t),\qquad \partial_t\phi(x,0,t)+g\eta(x,t)-\frac{\gamma}{\rho}\Delta_h\eta(x,t)=0.$$

Form the polynomial ring $\mathbb R[x]$
([[def-polynomial-ring-over-a-commutative-ring]]) and define the **complex
numbers** by the quotient ring
$$\mathbb C:=\mathbb R[x]/(x^2+1)$$
([[def-quotient-ring]]). Write $a$ for the constant class $a+(x^2+1)$ and set
$$i:=x+(x^2+1).$$
Thus $i^2=-1$ in the quotient. The constant-class map
$\mathbb R\to\mathbb C$ is the specified real map; its injectivity and the
field structure are proved in [[thm-complex-numbers-form-a-field]], after which
$\mathbb C/\mathbb R$ is a field extension in the sense of
[[def-field-extension-generated-subfields-and-simple-extension]].

$\mathbb C=\mathbb R[x]/(x^2+1)$ is a field containing the embedded copy of
$\mathbb R$. Every complex number has a unique form $a+bi$ with $a,b\in\mathbb R$,
and
$$ (a+bi)+(u+vi)=(a+u)+(b+v)i, $$
$$ (a+bi)(u+vi)=(au-bv)+(av+bu)i. $$
If $a+bi\ne0$, then
$$ (a+bi)^{-1}=\frac{a-bi}{a^2+b^2}. $$

Let $\iota_{\mathbb R}\colon\mathbb N\to\mathbb R$ be the canonical-natural map
of [[def-canonical-natural]], and let $j\colon\mathbb R\to\mathbb C$ be the real
embedding $j(x)=x+i0$ from [[def-complex-numbers-and-arithmetic]]. For every
$n\in\mathbb N$, the factorial $n!$ is nonzero by
[[def-factorial-and-falling-factorial]], so
$\iota_{\mathbb R}(n!)>0$ by [[lem-of-naturals-positive]] and consequently
$j(\iota_{\mathbb R}(n!))\ne0$ in the complex field
[[thm-complex-numbers-form-a-field]].

For $z\in\mathbb C$, define
$$ \exp z:=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{z^n}{j(\iota_{\mathbb R}(n!))}. $$
whenever this complex series converges. Inside a complex expression we
abbreviate the embedded denominator $j(\iota_{\mathbb R}(n!))$ by $n!$, so the
same definition may be written $\exp z=\sum z^n/n!$ without identifying a
natural number with a complex number. Powers and series are those of
[[def-complex-integer-powers]] and
[[def-complex-series-power-series-and-absolute-convergence]]. The convergence
for every $z\in\mathbb C$ is discharged by
[[lem-complex-exponential-series-converges-everywhere]].

The complex exponential is entire, and

$$ \exp'(z)=\exp z $$

for every $z\in\mathbb C$.

For all $z,w\in\mathbb C$, $\exp(z+w)=\exp z\exp w$. For real $x$, the complex value $\exp(x+0i)$ equals the published real exponential $e^x$. The conventions and prerequisite facts used below are recorded in [[def-complex-exponential]], [[lem-complex-exponential-series-converges-everywhere]], [[lem-cauchy-product-of-absolutely-convergent-complex-series]], [[def-real-exponential-function-and-e]], [[lem-binomial-theorem-over-complex-numbers]], [[thm-binomial-closed-formula]].

For real $x,y$, $\exp(x+iy)=e^x(\cos y+i\sin y)$ and $|\exp(x+iy)|=e^x$. In particular $e^{i\pi}+1=0$. The conventions and prerequisite facts used below are recorded in [[thm-complex-exponential-addition-and-real-extension]], [[thm-eulers-formula]], [[lem-complex-conjugation-and-modulus-laws]], [[thm-pythagorean-and-parity-identities-for-all-six-trigonometric-functions]], [[cor-exponential-reciprocal-and-positivity]], [[thm-quarter-turn-values-and-shift-formulas]], [[def-pi-via-first-positive-cosine-zero]].

Let $\gamma$ be the unique smallest positive zero of cosine supplied by [[thm-cosine-has-a-smallest-positive-zero]]. Define
$$\pi:=2\gamma.$$

Thus $\pi>0$ and $\pi/2=\gamma$.

Let $f:U\to V$ and $g:V\to\mathbb C$, where $U,V\subseteq\mathbb C$ are open. If $f$ is complex differentiable at $a\in U$ and $g$ is complex differentiable at $f(a)$, then $g\circ f$ is complex differentiable at $a$ and

$$ (g\circ f)'(a)=g'(f(a))f'(a). $$

For $x\in\mathbb R$, define
$$\sinh x:=\frac{\exp x-\exp(-x)}2,\qquad\cosh x:=\frac{\exp x+\exp(-x)}2,$$
$$\tanh x:=\frac{\sinh x}{\cosh x},\qquad\operatorname{sech}x:=\frac1{\cosh x}.$$
For $x\ne0$, define
$$\coth x:=\frac{\cosh x}{\sinh x},\qquad\operatorname{csch}x:=\frac1{\sinh x}.$$

The positivity of $\exp$ makes $\cosh x>0$ for every $x$. If $x\ne0$, then
$x\ne-x$, so strict increase of $\exp$ makes $\exp x\ne\exp(-x)$; hence
$\sinh x\ne0$. Thus all four quotients above are defined on exactly their
stated domains ([[cor-exponential-reciprocal-and-positivity]],
[[thm-exponential-is-strictly-increasing]]).

For all real $x,y$,
$$\sinh(x+y)=\sinh x\cosh y+\cosh x\sinh y,\qquad\cosh(x+y)=\cosh x\cosh y+\sinh x\sinh y,$$
$$\cosh^2x-\sinh^2x=1,\qquad(\sinh x)'=\cosh x,\qquad(\cosh x)'=\sinh x.$$
Moreover $\sinh:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ is odd, strictly increasing, and onto;
$\cosh:\mathbb R\to[1,\infty)$ is even and positive, and its restriction
to $[0,\infty)$ is strictly increasing and onto $[1,\infty)$; and
$\tanh:\mathbb R\to(-1,1)$ is strictly increasing and onto. On their declared domains,
$$(\tanh x)'=\operatorname{sech}^2x,\quad(\coth x)'=-\operatorname{csch}^2x,\quad(\operatorname{sech}x)'=-\operatorname{sech}x\tanh x,\quad(\operatorname{csch}x)'=-\operatorname{csch}x\coth x.$$

Let $A, B \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ with
$g[A] \subseteq B$ and let $f : B \to \mathbb{R}$, so that the composite
$f \circ g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ is defined. Let $c \in A$ be a limit point of
$A$ (Limit point, isolated point, adherent point, derived set, and dense subset of $\mathbb{R}$) at which $g$ is differentiable
(The derivative $f'(c) = \lim_{x \to c} \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c}$ of $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ at a point $c \in A$ that is a limit point of $A$, and differentiability on a set), put $b := g(c)$, and suppose $b$ is a limit point of $B$
at which $f$ is differentiable. Then $f \circ g$ is differentiable at $c$ and

$$(f \circ g)'(c) \;=\; f'\bigl(g(c)\bigr)\,g'(c) .$$

**Both limit-point hypotheses are needed, and neither is automatic.** That $c$
is a limit point of $A$ is what makes $g'(c)$ and $(f \circ g)'(c)$ defined
symbols; that $b = g(c)$ is a limit point of $B$ is what makes $f'(b)$ one.
Nothing forces the second: $g$ may be differentiable at $c$ and send $c$ to an
isolated point of $B$, and there $f'(b)$ is not defined and the formula asserts
nothing.

**No case analysis appears anywhere.** The naive difference-quotient proof
writes $\frac{f(g(x)) - f(g(c))}{g(x) - g(c)} \cdot \frac{g(x) - g(c)}{x - c}$
and then has to say what happens where $g(x) = g(c)$, which may occur at points
arbitrarily close to $c$. Carathéodory's factorisation never divides by the
inner increment, so the difficulty does not arise.

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $c \in A$ be a limit point of $A$
(Limit point, isolated point, adherent point, derived set, and dense subset of $\mathbb{R}$), let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at $c$
(The derivative $f'(c) = \lim_{x \to c} \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c}$ of $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ at a point $c \in A$ that is a limit point of $A$, and differentiability on a set) and let $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$. Then:

1. $f + g$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c) + g'(c)$;
2. $\alpha f$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(\alpha f)'(c) = \alpha f'(c)$;
3. $fg$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(fg)'(c) = f'(c)g(c) + f(c)g'(c)$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the
   point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and is a limit point of $A_0$, the quotient

after.quote:
Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be a nonempty open interval and let $E$ be an oriented three-dimensional Euclidean affine space, so the adopted Newtonian spacetime is $I\times E$ with absolute time $t\in I$. Define $\mathrm{SO}(3):=\{Q\in\mathbb R^{3\times3}:Q^{\mathsf T}Q=I_3,\ \det Q=1\}$. Use an adapted Cartesian inertial chart $\mathbf r:E\to\mathbb R^3$, an orientation-preserving affine isometry whose linear part lies in $\mathrm{SO}(3)$; inertial charts are related by $t^*=t+t_0$ and $\mathbf r^*=Q\mathbf r+vt+a$, with constant $t_0$ in seconds, constant $Q\in\mathrm{SO}(3)$, $v\in\mathbb R^3$ constant in metres per second, and $a\in\mathbb R^3$ constant in metres. In these coordinates, time is measured in seconds and spatial coordinates $(x_1,x_2,z)$ in metres. Fix $h>0$ metres and horizontal periods $L_1,L_2>0$ metres, and set $\mathbb T^2_L:=\mathbb R^2/(L_1\mathbb Z\times L_2\mathbb Z)$. Use the real constant $\pi$ defined as twice the least positive zero of cosine. A field on $\mathbb T^2_L$ is interpreted by its lift $\widetilde f(\widetilde x)=f([\widetilde x])$ to $\mathbb R^2$, periodic under translations $(L_1n_1,L_2n_2)$ for integers $n_1,n_2$; on products with $I$ and $[-h,0]$, $C^r$ means the lifted field has continuous ordinary coordinate partial derivatives through total order $r$, with continuous one-sided extensions at $z=-h,0$. Define $\nabla_h:=(\partial_{x_1},\partial_{x_2})$ and $\Delta_h:=\partial_{x_1}^2+\partial_{x_2}^2$ on these lifts. The real first-order fields are unrestricted formal perturbation coefficients, rather than finite-displacement interfaces: $\phi:\mathbb T^2_L\times[-h,0]\times I\to\mathbb R$ and $\eta:\mathbb T^2_L\times I\to\mathbb R$ are those of the postulated model; they are at least $C^3$ and $C^2$ respectively, with units metres squared per second and metres. The model parameters are constant density $\rho>0$ in kilograms per cubic metre, downward gravitational acceleration $-g e_z$ with $g>0$ in metres per second squared, and surface tension $\gamma>0$ in newtons per metre. They satisfy

$$\Delta_h\phi+\partial_z^2\phi=0\quad(-h<z<0),\qquad \partial_z\phi(x,-h,t)=0,$$

$$\partial_t\eta(x,t)=\partial_z\phi(x,0,t),\qquad \partial_t\phi(x,0,t)+g\eta(x,t)-\frac{\gamma}{\rho}\Delta_h\eta(x,t)=0.$$

Let $\mathbb C:=\mathbb R[X]/(X^2+1)$ be the complex field and $i:=[X]$, so $i^2=-1$. Let $\exp:\mathbb C\to\mathbb C$ be the series-defined complex exponential, $\exp w:=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}w^n/n!$. For $m=(m_1,m_2)\in\mathbb Z^2\setminus\{(0,0)\}$ define the wavevector $\mathbf k:=2\pi(m_1/L_1,m_2/L_2)\in\mathbb R^2$ in inverse metres and its magnitude $k:=|\mathbf k|>0$. The phase terms $\mathbf k\cdot\widetilde x$ and $\omega t$ are dimensionless. For $\omega\in\mathbb C$ in inverse seconds, define the mode factor on the quotient torus by

$$q_m([x],t):=\exp\bigl(i(\mathbf k\cdot\widetilde x-\omega t)\bigr),$$

where $\widetilde x\in\mathbb R^2$ is any representative of $[x]\in\mathbb T^2_L$. If $\widetilde x$ changes by $(L_1n_1,L_2n_2)$, the phase in parentheses changes by $2\pi N$ for $N=m_1n_1+m_2n_2\in\mathbb Z$; the complex-exponential addition law and $e^{i\pi}=-1$ give $\exp(2\pi iN)=1$ for every integer $N$ (by repeated addition for $N\ge0$ and $\exp(w)\exp(-w)=1$ for $N<0$), so $q_m$ is independent of the representative. Its lift is smooth, and $\Delta_hq_m=-k^2q_m$.

A complex mode of angular frequency $\omega$ is a pair $\eta_c(x,t)=Hq_m(x,t)$ and $\phi_c(x,z,t)=F(z)q_m(x,t)$ satisfying the complex-linear extension of the displayed model equations, with $H\in\mathbb C\setminus\{0\}$ in metres and $F\in C^2([-h,0],\mathbb C)$ in metres squared per second; here $C^2([-h,0],\mathbb C)$ means that the first two ordinary derivatives exist on $(-h,0)$ and extend continuously to both endpoints. The real and imaginary parts of any such mode are real-valued formal coefficient solutions of the real linear model, with no restriction on $|H|$. Optional finite-displacement graphs are $z=\varepsilon\eta$ with sufficiently small dimensionless $\varepsilon$ on compact time windows as in the postulate; they impose no amplitude bound on these coefficients and no nonlinear-solution claim. For real $s$ write $e^s:=\exp(s)$, $\sinh s:=(e^s-e^{-s})/2$, $\cosh s:=(e^s+e^{-s})/2$, and $\tanh s:=\sinh s/\cosh s$. Such a nonzero mode exists exactly when

$$\omega^2=\left(gk+\frac{\gamma}{\rho}k^3\right)\tanh(kh),$$

For these hypotheses the right-hand side is positive because $k,h,g,\gamma,\rho>0$ and $\tanh(kh)>0$. Thus for each $m$ the two frequencies $\omega=\pm\sqrt{(gk+(\gamma/\rho)k^3)\tanh(kh)}$, with the positive real square root, admit a nonzero mode. This is a conditional prediction of the stated first-order model, not a measurement or a claim that any actual fluid realizes every assumption.

Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be a nonempty open interval of time and let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ be a nonempty open set of Cartesian spatial coordinates $x=(x_1,x_2,x_3)$, with the standard right-handed orientation. A vector field $u:I\times\Omega\to\mathbb R^3$ is in the regularity class used here if $u$, its first time partial derivatives, its first spatial partial derivatives, and its second spatial partial derivatives all exist and are continuous. Scalar fields have the corresponding stated continuous derivatives: a pressure field $p$ has continuous first spatial partial derivatives; a density field $\rho$ has continuous first time and first spatial partial derivatives and takes values in $(0,\infty)$. A scalar function of one or several displayed real variables is $C^1$ when its first partial derivatives exist and are continuous; piecewise-$C^1$ paths have the meaning in the line-integral definition below. For a scalar field $f$, set $\nabla f=(\partial_{x_1}f,\partial_{x_2}f,\partial_{x_3}f)$; for a vector field $u=(u_1,u_2,u_3)$, set $\operatorname{div}u=\sum_{j=1}^3\partial_{x_j}u_j$, $\operatorname{curl}u=(\partial_{x_2}u_3-\partial_{x_3}u_2,\partial_{x_3}u_1-\partial_{x_1}u_3,\partial_{x_1}u_2-\partial_{x_2}u_1)$, and $\Delta f=\sum_{j=1}^3\partial_{x_j}^2f$, with $\Delta u$ applied componentwise. Define the row-component Jacobian $D_xu=(\partial_{x_j}u_i)_{i,j}$ and $(u\cdot\nabla)u=\sum_{j=1}^3u_j\partial_{x_j}u$.

For constants $\rho_0>0$ and $\mu>0$, define the kinematic-viscosity parameter $\nu=\mu/\rho_0$. The formal constant-density incompressible Navier--Stokes system is

$$\partial_tu+(u\cdot\nabla)u+\rho_0^{-1}\nabla p-\nu\Delta u=0,\qquad \operatorname{div}u=0.$$

Its associated formal Cauchy stress matrix is $\sigma=-pI_3+\mu(D_xu+(D_xu)^{\mathsf T})$. The corresponding steady Stokes system is $\rho_0^{-1}\nabla p-\nu\Delta u=0$ together with $\operatorname{div}u=0$; it omits both the time derivative and convective term. These are definitions of pointwise mathematical systems and do not assert that a physical fluid has a solution with the stated regularity.

For a barotropic branch, let $P:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ have two continuous derivatives and let $V:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ have continuous spatial partial derivatives through order two. The formal compressible Euler system for $u$ and positive density $\rho$ is

$$\partial_t\rho+\operatorname{div}(\rho u)=0,\qquad \partial_tu+(u\cdot\nabla)u=-\rho^{-1}\nabla(P(\rho))-\nabla V.$$

At a constant background density $\rho_0>0$ with $P'(\rho_0)>0$, the positive parameter $c$ defined by $c^2=P'(\rho_0)$ is the sound-speed parameter of this mathematical branch. A separate rotating linear system, for constant $\Omega\in\mathbb R^3$ and scalar field $q$, is $\partial_tu+2\Omega\times u=-\nabla q$ and $\operatorname{div}u=0$.

The vorticity field is $\operatorname{curl}u$. If $\gamma:[a,b]\to\Omega$ is a closed piecewise-$C^1$ oriented curve, with $\gamma(a)=\gamma(b)$, its circulation is $\oint_\gamma u\cdot d\mathbf r$. If $S$ is a compact oriented regular surface patch in $\Omega$ with unit normal $n_S$, its volume-flux observable is $\int_S u\cdot n_S\,dS$. The traction on $S$ is $\sigma n_S$ and the formal resultant force is the componentwise surface integral $\int_S\sigma n_S\,dS$. For a steady field, a streamline is a $C^1$ curve $x:J\to\Omega$ satisfying $x'(s)=u(x(s))$; the parameter $s$ is a curve parameter, not time. A closed material loop on a time interval $J\subseteq I$ is a $C^1$ map $X:J\times[0,1]\to\Omega$ with $X(t,0)=X(t,1)$ and $\partial_tX(t,\theta)=u(t,X(t,\theta))$; the definition asserts no existence of such a map. On an exterior domain, $f(x)\to f_\infty$ uniformly in direction as $|x|\to\infty$ means $\sup_{|e|=1}\|f(re)-f_\infty\|_2\to0$ as $r\to\infty$, using absolute value when the field is scalar.

$f \circ g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ is defined. Let $c \in A$ be a limit point of
$A$ (Limit point, isolated point, adherent point, derived set, and dense subset of $\mathbb{R}$) at which $g$ is differentiable
(The derivative $f'(c) = \lim_{x \to c} \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c}$ of $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ at a point $c \in A$ that is a limit point of $A$, and differentiability on a set), put $b := g(c)$, and suppose $b$ is a limit point of $B$
at which $f$ is differentiable. Then $f \circ g$ is differentiable at $c$ and

$$(f \circ g)'(c) \;=\; f'\bigl(g(c)\bigr)\,g'(c) .$$

**Both limit-point hypotheses are needed, and neither is automatic.** That $c$
is a limit point of $A$ is what makes $g'(c)$ and $(f \circ g)'(c)$ defined
symbols; that $b = g(c)$ is a limit point of $B$ is what makes $f'(b)$ one.
Nothing forces the second: $g$ may be differentiable at $c$ and send $c$ to an
isolated point of $B$, and there $f'(b)$ is not defined and the formula asserts
nothing.

**No case analysis appears anywhere.** The naive difference-quotient proof
writes $\frac{f(g(x)) - f(g(c))}{g(x) - g(c)} \cdot \frac{g(x) - g(c)}{x - c}$
and then has to say what happens where $g(x) = g(c)$, which may occur at points
arbitrarily close to $c$. Carathéodory's factorisation never divides by the
inner increment, so the difficulty does not arise.

   $p \in \mathbb{N}$, every list $u : p \to F^{X}$ and every $j \in X$,

Let $A, B \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ with
$g[A] \subseteq B$ and let $f : B \to \mathbb{R}$, so that the composite
$f \circ g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ is defined. Let $c \in A$ be a limit point of
$A$ (Limit point, isolated point, adherent point, derived set, and dense subset of $\mathbb{R}$) at which $g$ is differentiable
(The derivative $f'(c) = \lim_{x \to c} \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c}$ of $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ at a point $c \in A$ that is a limit point of $A$, and differentiability on a set), put $b := g(c)$, and suppose $b$ is a limit point of $B$
at which $f$ is differentiable. Then $f \circ g$ is differentiable at $c$ and

$$(f \circ g)'(c) \;=\; f'\bigl(g(c)\bigr)\,g'(c) .$$

**Both limit-point hypotheses are needed, and neither is automatic.** That $c$
is a limit point of $A$ is what makes $g'(c)$ and $(f \circ g)'(c)$ defined
symbols; that $b = g(c)$ is a limit point of $B$ is what makes $f'(b)$ one.
Nothing forces the second: $g$ may be differentiable at $c$ and send $c$ to an
isolated point of $B$, and there $f'(b)$ is not defined and the formula asserts
nothing.

**No case analysis appears anywhere.** The naive difference-quotient proof
writes $\frac{f(g(x)) - f(g(c))}{g(x) - g(c)} \cdot \frac{g(x) - g(c)}{x - c}$
and then has to say what happens where $g(x) = g(c)$, which may occur at points
arbitrarily close to $c$. Carathéodory's factorisation never divides by the
inner increment, so the difficulty does not arise.

$$\langle x, y\rangle \;:=\; \sum_{k<n} x_k\,y_k ,$$

**Euclidean norm** of $x$ is

$$\lVert x\rVert_2 \;:=\; \sqrt{\langle x, x\rangle},$$

Squares of nonzero elements are positive, the case $x_k = 0$ giving $x_k^2 = 0$ by
Integer powers $a^m$) and every nonnegative real has a unique nonnegative square
root (Square roots exist: a unique $\sqrt{a} \ge 0$ with $(\sqrt{a})^2 = a$; the positives are $\{x^2 : x \neq 0\}$).

### Both are defined for every $n$, including $n = 0$

At $n = 0$ the set $\mathbb{R}^{0}$ has exactly one element, the empty function,
and it is the zero vector space (The standard list $e : n \to F^{n}$ with $e_i(i) = 1_F$ and $e_i(j) = 0_F$ for $j \ne i$ is an ordered basis of $F^{n}$; hence $\dim_F F^{n} = n$, and $F^{0}$ is the zero space with basis $\varnothing$ and dimension $0$ clause 5); the sum
above is the empty sum, so $\langle x,y\rangle = 0$ and $\lVert x\rVert_2 = 0$.
**This is the first place on this page where the two index regimes diverge, and
the divergence is deliberate.** The published metrics $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ of

### The algebra of the inner product

For all $x, y, z \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$:

1. **Symmetry.** $\langle x,y\rangle = \langle y,x\rangle$, since $x_ky_k = y_kx_k$
   termwise.
2. **Additivity in the first argument.**
   $\langle x + y, z\rangle = \langle x,z\rangle + \langle y,z\rangle$: the list
   $k \mapsto (x_k+y_k)z_k$ is the termwise sum of $k \mapsto x_kz_k$ and
   $k \mapsto y_kz_k$, so Laws of finite sums and finite products clause 1 applies.
3. **Homogeneity in the first argument.**
   $\langle \lambda x, y\rangle = \lambda\langle x,y\rangle$, by
   Laws of finite sums and finite products clause 2.
4. **Bilinearity.** Clauses 2 and 3 together with symmetry give the same two laws
   in the second argument.
5. **Positive definiteness.** $\langle x,x\rangle \ge 0$, and
   $\langle x,x\rangle = 0$ if and only if $x = 0$. Indeed a vanishing sum of
   nonnegative terms has every term $0$ (Laws of finite sums and finite products clause 4), so
   $x_k^{2} = 0$ for every $k < n$, and a nonzero real has a positive square
   (Squares of nonzero elements are positive), whence $x_k = 0$ for every $k < n$ and $x = 0$.
6. **Agreement with the published Euclidean metric.** For $n \ge 1$ and
   $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$,
   $\lVert x - y\rVert_2 = \sqrt{\sum_{k<n}(x_k-y_k)^{2}} = d_2(x,y)$, the two
   sides being the same expression ($\mathbb{R}^n$ as the set of functions $n \to \mathbb{R}$, and $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ are metrics on it). In particular
   $\lVert x\rVert_2 = d_2(x, 0)$.

inequality is obtained from the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality; it is not assumed

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and let $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$, with the Euclidean
inner product and the Euclidean norm as in The Euclidean inner product $\langle x,y\rangle = \sum_{k<n} x_k y_k$ on $\mathbb{R}^n$. Then:

1. **Cauchy-Schwarz.**
   $$\lvert\langle x,y\rangle\rvert \;\le\; \lVert x\rVert_2\,\lVert y\rVert_2 ,$$
   with equality if and only if there is a pair $(\lambda,\mu) \ne (0,0)$ of
   reals with $\lambda x_k = \mu y_k$ for every $k < n$.
2. **$\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm on $\mathbb{R}^{n}$**
   (A norm on a real vector space, the induced metric, and the dictionary with the metric axioms), for **every** $n \in \mathbb{N}$; the metric
   it induces is $d_2$ of $\mathbb{R}^n$ as the set of functions $n \to \mathbb{R}$, and $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ are metrics on it whenever $n \ge 1$.
3. **Parallelogram law.**
   $$\lVert x+y\rVert_2^{2} + \lVert x-y\rVert_2^{2} \;=\; 2\lVert x\rVert_2^{2} + 2\lVert y\rVert_2^{2} .$$
4. **Polarisation.**
   $$\langle x,y\rangle \;=\; \tfrac14\Bigl(\lVert x+y\rVert_2^{2} - \lVert x-y\rVert_2^{2}\Bigr),$$

**Clause 1 is a citation, not a new proof.** The inequality and its equality case
are the published The Cauchy-Schwarz inequality for finite sums, stated there for two lists of
reals; all that happens below is that it is read in the vector notation of
The Euclidean inner product $\langle x,y\rangle = \sum_{k<n} x_k y_k$ on $\mathbb{R}^n$. Re-proving it here would put two proofs of one
statement in the library.

Let $F$ be a field ([[def-field]]), let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and let $F^{n}$ be the
function space on the von Neumann natural $n = \{0, \dots, n-1\}$, with the
pointwise operations ([[def-function-space]], [[def-natural-numbers]],
[[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]). For $i < n$ define the **standard unit vector**
$e_i \in F^{n}$ by

$$e_i(i) = 1_F, \qquad e_i(j) = 0_F \ \text{ for } j < n \text{ with } j \ne i .$$

Then:

1. **Finite sums in a function space are pointwise.** For every set $X$, every
   $p \in \mathbb{N}$, every list $u : p \to F^{X}$ and every $j \in X$,
   $$\Bigl(\sum_{k<p} u_k\Bigr)(j) \;=\; \sum_{k<p} u_k(j),$$
   the right-hand sum being taken in $(F,+,0_F)$. (Stated here for an arbitrary
   $X$ because the companion page needs it at $X = \mathbb{N}$.)
2. $e : n \to F^{n}$ is an ordered basis of $F^{n}$ ([[def-linear-basis]]); in
   particular $e$ is injective and its image $e[n] = \{\, e_i : i < n \,\}$ is a
   basis of $F^{n}$ with $e[n] \approx n$ ([[def-equinumerous]]);
3. for every $\lambda : n \to F$ and every $j < n$,
   $\bigl(\sum_{i<n}\lambda_i e_i\bigr)(j) = \lambda_j$; equivalently the
   coordinate list of $x \in F^{n}$ with respect to the ordered basis $e$
   ([[thm-unique-coordinates-with-respect-to-an-ordered-basis]]) is
   $i \mapsto x(i)$;
4. $F^{n}$ is finite-dimensional over $F$ with $\dim_F F^{n} = n$
   ([[def-dimension]]);
5. at $n = 0$ this reads: $F^{0}$ has exactly one element, the empty function,
   so $F^{0}$ is the zero space, the empty list is its ordered basis,
   $\varnothing$ is its basis and $\dim_F F^{0} = 0$.

Every index runs from $0$, so the coordinates of an element of $F^{n}$ are
$x_0, \dots, x_{n-1}$ and no statement above is restricted to $n \ge 1$.

For all $a,b,c\in\mathbb R^3$, the Euclidean cross product satisfies

$$a\times(b\times c)=b\langle a,c\rangle-c\langle a,b\rangle.$$

before.quote:
Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be a nonempty open interval of time and let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ be a nonempty open set of Cartesian spatial coordinates $x=(x_1,x_2,x_3)$, with the standard right-handed orientation. A vector field $u:I\times\Omega\to\mathbb R^3$ is in the regularity class used here if $u$, its first time partial derivatives, its first spatial partial derivatives, and its second spatial partial derivatives all exist and are continuous. Scalar fields have the corresponding stated continuous derivatives: a pressure field $p$ has continuous first spatial partial derivatives; a density field $\rho$ has continuous first time and first spatial partial derivatives and takes values in $(0,\infty)$. A scalar function of one or several displayed real variables is $C^1$ when its first partial derivatives exist and are continuous; piecewise-$C^1$ paths have the meaning in the line-integral definition below. For a scalar field $f$, set $\nabla f=(\partial_{x_1}f,\partial_{x_2}f,\partial_{x_3}f)$; for a vector field $u=(u_1,u_2,u_3)$, set $\operatorname{div}u=\sum_{j=1}^3\partial_{x_j}u_j$, $\operatorname{curl}u=(\partial_{x_2}u_3-\partial_{x_3}u_2,\partial_{x_3}u_1-\partial_{x_1}u_3,\partial_{x_1}u_2-\partial_{x_2}u_1)$, and $\Delta f=\sum_{j=1}^3\partial_{x_j}^2f$, with $\Delta u$ applied componentwise. Define the row-component Jacobian $D_xu=(\partial_{x_j}u_i)_{i,j}$ and $(u\cdot\nabla)u=\sum_{j=1}^3u_j\partial_{x_j}u$.

For constants $\rho_0>0$ and $\mu>0$, define the kinematic-viscosity parameter $\nu=\mu/\rho_0$. The formal constant-density incompressible Navier--Stokes system is

$$\partial_tu+(u\cdot\nabla)u+\rho_0^{-1}\nabla p-\nu\Delta u=0,\qquad \operatorname{div}u=0.$$

Its associated formal Cauchy stress matrix is $\sigma=-pI_3+\mu(D_xu+(D_xu)^{\mathsf T})$. The corresponding steady Stokes system is $\rho_0^{-1}\nabla p-\nu\Delta u=0$ together with $\operatorname{div}u=0$; it omits both the time derivative and convective term. These are definitions of pointwise mathematical systems and do not assert that a physical fluid has a solution with the stated regularity.

For a barotropic branch, let $P:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ have two continuous derivatives and let $V:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ have continuous spatial partial derivatives through order two. The formal compressible Euler system for $u$ and positive density $\rho$ is

$$\partial_t\rho+\operatorname{div}(\rho u)=0,\qquad \partial_tu+(u\cdot\nabla)u=-\rho^{-1}\nabla(P(\rho))-\nabla V.$$

At a constant background density $\rho_0>0$ with $P'(\rho_0)>0$, the positive parameter $c$ defined by $c^2=P'(\rho_0)$ is the sound-speed parameter of this mathematical branch. A separate rotating linear system, for constant $\Omega\in\mathbb R^3$ and scalar field $q$, is $\partial_tu+2\Omega\times u=-\nabla q$ and $\operatorname{div}u=0$.

The vorticity field is $\operatorname{curl}u$. If $\gamma:[a,b]\to\Omega$ is a closed piecewise-$C^1$ oriented curve, with $\gamma(a)=\gamma(b)$, its circulation is $\oint_\gamma u\cdot d\mathbf r$. If $S$ is a compact oriented regular surface patch in $\Omega$ with unit normal $n_S$, its volume-flux observable is $\int_S u\cdot n_S\,dS$. The traction on $S$ is $\sigma n_S$ and the formal resultant force is the componentwise surface integral $\int_S\sigma n_S\,dS$. For a steady field, a streamline is a $C^1$ curve $x:J\to\Omega$ satisfying $x'(s)=u(x(s))$; the parameter $s$ is a curve parameter, not time. A closed material loop on a time interval $J\subseteq I$ is a $C^1$ map $X:J\times[0,1]\to\Omega$ with $X(t,0)=X(t,1)$ and $\partial_tX(t,\theta)=u(t,X(t,\theta))$; the definition asserts no existence of such a map. On an exterior domain, $f(x)\to f_\infty$ uniformly in direction as $|x|\to\infty$ means $\sup_{|e|=1}\|f(re)-f_\infty\|_2\to0$ as $r\to\infty$, using absolute value when the field is scalar.

For one optional SI interpretation, the dimensions are $[x]=\mathrm m$, $[t]=\mathrm s$, $[u]=\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, $[\rho]=\mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}$, $[p]=\mathrm{Pa}$, $[\mu]=\mathrm{Pa\,s}$, $[\nu]=\mathrm{m^2\,s^{-1}}$, $[V]=[q]=\mathrm{m^2\,s^{-2}}$, and $[\Omega]=\mathrm{s^{-1}}$. Thus $[\operatorname{curl}u]=\mathrm{s^{-1}}$, circulation has units $\mathrm{m^2\,s^{-1}}$, volume flux has units $\mathrm{m^3\,s^{-1}}$, stress has units Pa, and resultant force has units N. In this interpretation $\rho_0,\mu,P,V,\Omega$ are inputs to the displayed formulas, while $\nu=\mu/\rho_0$ and $c^2=P'(\rho_0)$ are derived quantities relative to those formulas; this classification is not asserted to be universal across physical theories.

Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be a nonempty open time interval, let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ be a nonempty open set of Cartesian coordinates, and fix a constant density $\rho_0>0$. Let $u:I\times\Omega\to\mathbb R^3$ have continuous first time derivatives, first spatial derivatives, and second spatial derivatives, and let $p:I\times\Omega\to\mathbb R$ have continuous first spatial derivatives. The formal constant-density incompressible Euler system is the pointwise system

$$\partial_tu+(u\cdot\nabla)u+\rho_0^{-1}\nabla p=0,\qquad \operatorname{div}u=0.$$

Use the Cartesian derivative conventions $\nabla f=(\partial_i f)_{i=1}^3$, $\operatorname{div}u=\sum_i\partial_i u_i$, and $(u\cdot\nabla)u=\sum_j u_j\partial_j u$. The velocity has continuous first time, first spatial, and second spatial derivatives, and pressure has continuous first spatial derivatives. For this inviscid branch define the formal pressure stress by $\sigma_E=-pI_3$. On a compact oriented regular surface patch $S\subset\Omega$ with unit normal $n_S$, define its formal stress resultant to be $\int_S\sigma_En_S\,dS=-\int_Sp n_S\,dS$. A steady solution has $\partial_tu=0$. These definitions impose no boundary condition, assert no solution existence, and do not claim that the system describes an observed fluid.

Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an open time interval, let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ be open, and let $P:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ be $C^2$. Suppose $u:I\times\Omega\to\mathbb R^3$ has continuous first time, first spatial, and second spatial derivatives; $\rho:I\times\Omega\to(0,\infty)$ has continuous first time and first spatial derivatives; and $V:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ is time-independent and $C^2$. Assume pointwise

$$\partial_t\rho+\operatorname{div}(\rho u)=0,\qquad \partial_tu+(u\cdot\nabla)u=-\rho^{-1}\nabla(P(\rho))-\nabla V.$$

For any reference density $\rho_{\rm ref}>0$, define $h(q)=\int_{\rho_{\rm ref}}^q P'(r)/r\,dr$ for $q>0$. A streamline is a $C^1$ curve $x:J\to\Omega$ with $x'(s)=u(x(s))$. If $u$ and $\rho$ are independent of time, every streamline has $|u|^2/2+h(\rho)+V$ constant along it. If in addition $\operatorname{curl}u=0$ on a connected component of $\Omega$, this quantity is constant throughout that component.

For any closed $C^1$ material loop $X:J\times[0,1]\to\Omega$ satisfying $X(t,0)=X(t,1)$, $X_t(t,s)=u(t,X(t,s))$, with $X_s$ and $X_{ts}$ continuous, the circulation $\Gamma(t)=\int_0^1u(t,X(t,s))\cdot X_s(t,s)\,ds$ is constant on $J$. Independently of the Euler assumptions, every $C^2$ vector field $v$ on an open subset of $\mathbb R^3$ obeys the identity

$$ (v\cdot\nabla)v=\nabla(|v|^2/2)-v\times\operatorname{curl}v. $$

No claim is made for shocks, nonbarotropic pressure, nonconservative body forces, or viscous circulation. Under SI interpretation, $u$ is in metres per second, $\rho$ in kilograms per cubic metre, $P$ in pascals, and $h,V$ in square metres per second squared.

Let $D=\{(x,y,z)\in\mathbb R^3:r=(x^2+y^2)^{1/2}>0\}$, let $\rho_0>0$, $p_0\in\mathbb R$, and let $\kappa\ne0$. On $D$ define

$$u_v(x,y,z)=\left(-\frac{\kappa y}{r^2},\frac{\kappa x}{r^2},0\right),\qquad p_v(x,y,z)=p_0-\frac{\rho_0\kappa^2}{2r^2}.$$

For every $R>0$ and fixed $z_0$, the positively oriented circle $\gamma_R(\theta)=(R\cos\theta,R\sin\theta,z_0)$, $0\le\theta\le2\pi$, has circulation $\oint_{\gamma_R}u_v\cdot d\mathbf r=2\pi\kappa$. Consequently no single-valued $C^1$ function $\phi:D\to\mathbb R$ satisfies $u_v=\nabla\phi$ on all of $D$, even though $\operatorname{curl}u_v=0$ there. Both $\operatorname{div}u_v=0$ and $\Delta u_v=0$ on $D$, and the pointwise identity

$$\partial_tu_v+(u_v\cdot\nabla)u_v+\rho_0^{-1}\nabla p_v-\nu\Delta u_v=0$$

holds for every $\nu>0$, with $\partial_tu_v=0$.

Separately, for $\Omega_0\ne0$ set $u_s=(-\Omega_0y,\Omega_0x,0)$ and $p_s=p_0+\rho_0\Omega_0^2r^2/2$ on $\mathbb R^3$. This smooth steady field is divergence-free and satisfies the same constant-density equation for every $\nu>0$. Its Bernoulli quantity $B=|u_s|^2/2+p_s/\rho_0=p_0/\rho_0+\Omega_0^2r^2$ is constant on each circular streamline but varies with $r$. Thus a common Bernoulli constant is not implied for all steady constant-density flows. This example does not contradict a Bernoulli theorem that assumes an irrotational field or a separate barotropic model. Under SI interpretation, $r$ is in metres, the velocities in metres per second, $\kappa$ in square metres per second, $\Omega_0$ in inverse seconds, $\rho_0$ in kilograms per cubic metre, and $p,p_0$ in pascals.

Suppose $u:I\times\Omega\to\mathbb R^3$ has continuous first time, first spatial, and second spatial derivatives; $\rho:I\times\Omega\to(0,\infty)$ has continuous first time and first spatial derivatives; and $V:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ is time-independent and $C^2$. Assume pointwise

$$\partial_t\rho+\operatorname{div}(\rho u)=0,\qquad \partial_tu+(u\cdot\nabla)u=-\rho^{-1}\nabla(P(\rho))-\nabla V.$$

For any reference density $\rho_{\rm ref}>0$, define $h(q)=\int_{\rho_{\rm ref}}^q P'(r)/r\,dr$ for $q>0$. For a steady velocity field, a streamline is a $C^1$ curve $x:J\to\Omega$, where $J\subseteq\mathbb R$ is an interval, satisfying $x'(s)=u(x(s))$ with $u(x)$ denoting its time-independent spatial value. If $u$ and $\rho$ are independent of time, every streamline has $|u|^2/2+h(\rho)+V$ constant along it. If in addition $\operatorname{curl}u=0$ on a connected component of $\Omega$, this quantity is constant throughout that component.

For any closed $C^1$ material loop $X:J\times[0,1]\to\Omega$ satisfying $X(t,0)=X(t,1)$, $X_t(t,s)=u(t,X(t,s))$, with $X_s$ and $X_{ts}$ continuous, the circulation $\Gamma(t)=\int_0^1u(t,X(t,s))\cdot X_s(t,s)\,ds$ is constant on $J$. Independently of the Euler assumptions, every $C^2$ vector field $v$ on an open subset of $\mathbb R^3$ obeys the identity

$$ (v\cdot\nabla)v=\nabla(|v|^2/2)-v\times\operatorname{curl}v. $$

No claim is made for shocks, nonbarotropic pressure, nonconservative body forces, or viscous circulation. Under SI interpretation, $u$ is in metres per second, $\rho$ in kilograms per cubic metre, $P$ in pascals, and $h,V$ in square metres per second squared.
details.actual_fact_text: [F1] [[thm-fd-x09]]: for classical positive-density barotropic Euler with conservative $V$, $h(q)=\int_{\rho_{\rm ref}}^qP'(r)/r\,dr$; steady Bernoulli is constant on streamlines, and a closed $C^1$ material loop has constant circulation under the stated mixed-derivative condition.

Let $n\ge2$ and let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^n$ be a bounded $C^1$ domain, meaning a bounded connected open set whose boundary is locally a $C^1$ graph and which lies on one side of that graph after a rigid change of coordinates. Write $|a|$ for the Euclidean norm, $|
abla w|^2=\sum_{i,j=1}^n|\partial_jw_i|^2$, and $\|g\|_2=(\int_\Omega|g|^2\,dx)^{1/2}$. Suppose pointwise that $
abla\cdot w=0$, $w|_{\partial\Omega}=0$, and $-\mu\Delta w+
abla q=f$. Also assume that a stated constant $C_\Omega>0$ satisfies the zero-trace Poincare inequality $\|v\|_2\le C_\Omega\|
abla v\|_2$ for every $v\in C^1(\overline\Omega;\mathbb R^n)$ with $v|_{\partial\Omega}=0$. Then

$$\|
abla w\|_2\le  rac{C_\Omega}{\mu}\|f\|_2,\qquad \|w\|_2\le  rac{C_\Omega^2}{\mu}\|f\|_2.$$

For the periodic channel cell $Q=\mathbb T_{L_x}	imes(0,h)	imes\mathbb T_{L_z}$, where $\mathbb T_L=\mathbb R/(L\mathbb Z)$ and $L_x,L_z,h>0$. Integrals on $Q$ use Lebesgue measure on one fundamental cell in each periodic coordinate. Every $v\in C^1(\overline Q;\mathbb R^3)$ periodic in the two torus variables and zero on $y=0,h$ satisfies $\|v\|_{L^2(Q)}\le h\|
abla v\|_{L^2(Q)}$. This channel inequality is a separate direct estimate on the periodic cell; it does not treat that cell as a bounded $C^1$ Euclidean domain.

In dimension three, let $ho_0>0$, $
u=\mu/ho_0$, and suppose already-existing time-independent fields $u_{m NS},u_{m S}\in C^2(\overline\Omega;\mathbb R^3)$ and $p_{m NS},p_{m S}\in C^1(\overline\Omega)$ are divergence-free, have the same boundary velocity, and satisfy the constant-density incompressible Navier-Stokes and Stokes equations $ho_0(u_{m NS}\cdot
abla)u_{m NS}+
abla p_{m NS}-\mu\Delta u_{m NS}=0$ and $
abla p_{m S}-\mu\Delta u_{m S}=0$. If $f=-ho_0(u_{m NS}\cdot
abla)u_{m NS}$, then the preceding estimate applies to $w=u_{m NS}-u_{m S}$ and $q=p_{m NS}-p_{m S}$ whenever the stated Poincare bound holds. This is an a-posteriori residual estimate for already-given fields; it asserts no solution existence, no exterior-domain bound, and no error bound from Reynolds number alone. The constant $C_\Omega=h$ established for the periodic channel is not transferred to an exterior domain.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. For $n\ge2$, a bounded $C^1$ domain Omega and $F\in C^1(\overline\Omega;\mathbb R^n)$, $\int_\Omega\operatorname{div}F\,dx=\int_{\partial\Omega}F\cdot\nu\,dS$. Both integrals are finite, with the continuous interior derivative convention and the outward normal on every boundary component.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

before.quote:
For $t\in\mathbb R$, assume fields are independent of any third spatial coordinate, so the cross-section has coordinates $(x,y)$. Use ordinary pointwise Euclidean partial derivatives and set $\Delta=\partial_{xx}+\partial_{yy}$. Let $U_+,U_-\in\mathbb R$ be constant horizontal base velocities, and let the two half-planes $y>0$ and $y<0$ have the same constant density $\rho_0>0$. The unknown interface displacement $\eta(x,t)$ and scalar potentials $\phi_+(x,y,t)$ for $y>0$ and $\phi_-(x,y,t)$ for $y<0$ are smooth, have one-sided traces at $y=0$, satisfy $\Delta\phi_\pm=0$, and decay together with their first derivatives as $y\to+\infty$ and $y\to-\infty$ respectively. The stipulated linear interface equations at $y=0$ are $(\partial_t+U_\pm\partial_x)\eta=\partial_y\phi_\pm$ and continuity of the defined pressure perturbations $p'_\pm=-\rho_0(\partial_t+U_\pm\partial_x)\phi_\pm$. Gravity and surface tension are absent. Complexify this real linear system for the following normal-mode calculation.

For every $k>0$, every nonzero complex amplitude $H$, and every mode of the form $\eta=H e^{ikx+\lambda t}$, $\phi_+=A_+e^{-ky}e^{ikx+\lambda t}$, $\phi_-=A_-e^{ky}e^{ikx+\lambda t}$, set $\overline U=(U_++U_-)/2$ and $\Delta U=U_+-U_-$. The mode equations require

$$\lambda=-ik\overline U\pm \frac{k|\Delta U|}{2}.$$

If $\Delta U\ne0$, one root has positive real part $k|\Delta U|/2$, and its real or imaginary part gives a real exponentially growing solution of the stated linear system.

For the periodic interface $x\in\mathbb T_{2\pi}$, define $\widehat\eta_j=(2\pi)^{-1}\int_0^{2\pi}\eta(x)e^{-ijx}\,dx$ and, for $m\ge0$, $\|\eta\|_{H^m}^2=\sum_{j\in\mathbb Z}(1+j^2)^m|\widehat\eta_j|^2$. Let $H^m(\mathbb T_{2\pi})$ be the completion of trigonometric polynomials in this norm. If $\Delta U\ne0$, then for every fixed $t>0$ this exact mode family has bounded initial $H^m$ norm but unbounded evolved $H^m$ norm as its integer wavenumber $k\to\infty$. Thus no uniform estimate of the form $\|\eta(t)\|_{H^m}\le C_t\|\eta(0)\|_{H^m}$ holds for this family. This is a linear interface-model conclusion, not a theorem of nonlinear turbulent transition, viscous shear-layer behavior, or physical instability in a particular experiment.

before.quote:
Assume there are no mass sources and no diffusion relative to $u$. Adopt a positive reference mass density $\rho_0$, a positive current density $\rho$, a body-acceleration field $b$, a contact traction $t(t,x,n)=\sigma(t,x)n$ depending only on the local outward unit normal $n$, a $C^1$ Cauchy stress field $\sigma$, specific internal energy $e$, positive temperature $T$, specific entropy $s$, heat-flux vector $q$, and specific heat supply $r$, with the types and SI units fixed in the preceding definition. Contact traction and volume-force densities are continuous and locally bounded on the smooth material regions under consideration. There are no surface couples or intrinsic spin angular momentum; a micropolar or couple-stress model is outside this postulate.

For every such material subregion, adopt conservation of mass,

$$\int_{\chi_t(V)}\rho(t,x)\,dx=\int_V\rho_0(a)\,da.$$

In the same inertial chart, adopt the balances of linear and angular momentum,

$$\frac{d}{dt}\int_{\chi_t(V)}\rho u\,dx=\int_{\chi_t(V)}\rho b\,dx+\int_{\partial\chi_t(V)}t(t,x,n)\,dS,$$

$$\frac{d}{dt}\int_{\chi_t(V)}x\times(\rho u)\,dx=\int_{\chi_t(V)}x\times(\rho b)\,dx+\int_{\partial\chi_t(V)}x\times t(t,x,n)\,dS.$$

Adopt the total-energy balance and entropy inequality

$$\frac{d}{dt}\int_{\chi_t(V)}\rho\left(e+\frac{|u|^2}{2}\right)\,dx=\int_{\chi_t(V)}\rho b\cdot u\,dx+\int_{\partial\chi_t(V)}t(t,x,n)\cdot u\,dS-\int_{\partial\chi_t(V)}q\cdot n\,dS+\int_{\chi_t(V)}\rho r\,dx,$$

$$\frac{d}{dt}\int_{\chi_t(V)}\rho s\,dx\ge-\int_{\partial\chi_t(V)}\frac{q}{T}\cdot n\,dS+\int_{\chi_t(V)}\frac{\rho r}{T}\,dx.$$

Here $F$ and $J$ are dimensionless and $A$ has units metres. The material map $\chi$ describes motion of the medium; it is not a change of observer or frame. The Eulerian velocity is the vector field defined by $u(t,\chi(t,a))=\partial_t\chi(t,a)$, measured in m s$^{-1}$. For a differentiable scalar or component field $f$, its material derivative is $D_tf=\partial_tf+u\cdot\nabla f$. Set $L_{ij}=\partial_j u_i$, $D=(L+L^T)/2$, $W=(L-L^T)/2$, $\theta=\operatorname{tr}D=\operatorname{div}u$, and $D_0=D-(\theta/3)I_3$; $L,D,W,\theta,D_0$ have units s$^{-1}$. Define vorticity by

$$\operatorname{curl}u=(\partial_yu_z-\partial_zu_y,\ \partial_zu_x-\partial_xu_z,\ \partial_xu_y-\partial_yu_x),$$

also in s$^{-1}$. In this library, a motion is **material-incompressible** on a region when $\operatorname{div}u=0$ there; **spatially homogeneous density** means $\nabla\rho=0$ there. These are distinct conditions. A **pathline** is a $C^1$ curve $X$ on an interval where the field is defined and the solution exists, satisfying $dX/dt=u(t,X(t))$. A **streamline at time $t_0$** is a $C^1$ integral curve satisfying $dX/ds=u(t_0,X(s))$ for a frozen $t_0$, with curve parameter $s$ measured in seconds. These are different constructions for an unsteady field.

A spatial vector is an element of the Euclidean translation space; its components rotate by $Q$ under a rigid observer change. A spatial second-order tensor is a linear map from that vector space to itself, represented by a $3\times3$ matrix in a Cartesian orthonormal basis; it transforms as $S^*=QSQ^T$. A tensor-valued constitutive response is **objective** when its values at corresponding events satisfy this transformation rule for every $C^2$ rigid observer change. For a stress tensor $\sigma$, use the tension-positive convention in which the traction (force per unit current area) on a surface with outward unit normal $n$ is $\sigma n$. Set $(\operatorname{div}\sigma)_i=\partial_j\sigma_{ij}$; the tensor contraction is $S:T=\sum_{i,j}S_{ij}T_{ij}$. Stress and traction have units Pa $=\mathrm{N\,m^{-2}}=\mathrm{kg\,m^{-1}\,s^{-2}}$.

Within a specified model, a **primitive quantity** is a quantity adopted as input rather than constructed from the other data of that model; a **derived quantity** is assigned by an explicit construction from stated inputs and results. This status is framework-local and is independent of whether its SI unit is base or derived. In the continuum model used on this page, $\rho_0(a)$ is a reference mass-density field in kg m$^{-3}$, $b(t,x)$ is an adopted body-acceleration field in m s$^{-2}$, $e(t,x)$ is specific internal energy (energy per unit mass) in J kg$^{-1}=\mathrm{m^2\,s^{-2}}$, $T(t,x)>0$ is temperature in K, $s(t,x)$ is specific entropy in J kg$^{-1}$ K$^{-1}$, $q(t,x)$ is heat flux (heat-transfer rate per unit area) in W m$^{-2}$, and $r(t,x)$ is specific heat supply (power per unit mass) in W kg$^{-1}$. Their adoption is a physical-model choice, not a consequence of the SI. The current mass density $\rho(t,x)$ means mass per unit current volume and has units kg m$^{-3}$; for a mass-conserving motion, its construction from $\rho_0$ and $\chi$ is established from the stated balance hypotheses in the theorem on this page. A pressure $p$ is a scalar in Pa whose role depends on the selected constitutive branch. The shear and bulk dynamic-viscosity parameters $\mu,\zeta$, when that branch is adopted, have units Pa s $=\mathrm{kg\,m^{-1}\,s^{-1}}$; thermal conductivity $\kappa_T$ has units W m$^{-1}$ K$^{-1}$. The gradient $\nabla$ has units m$^{-1}$. Thus the metre, kilogram, second, and kelvin are SI base units in this dictionary, while density, velocity, acceleration, pressure, energy, power, viscosity, and heat-flux units are derived according to the BIPM SI conventions.

Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an open interval containing $0$, let $B\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ be a bounded open reference region with $C^1$ boundary (locally a $C^1$ graph with the region on one side), and let $U$ be an open neighborhood of $\overline B$. Let $\chi\in C^2(I\times U;\mathbb R^3)$ have orientation-preserving diffeomorphic time slices (bijections onto open images with $C^2$ inverses and positive Jacobian determinant), and satisfy $\chi(0,a)=a$. Here $C^r$ means all coordinate partial derivatives through order $r$ are continuous; write $\Omega_t=\chi_t(B)$ and $u(t,\chi(t,a))=\partial_t\chi(t,a)$. Let $\rho_0\in C^1(\overline B)$ and $\rho\in C^1(\mathcal O)$ be positive mass densities, where $\mathcal O=\{(t,x):t\in I,\ x\in\chi_t(U)\}$. Suppose that for every nonempty bounded open $V$ with compact closure in $B$ and $C^1$ boundary locally a graph with the region on one side and every $t\in I$,
$$\int_{\chi_t(V)}\rho(t,x)\,dx=\int_V\rho_0(a)\,da.$$
Then the pointwise continuity equation
$$\partial_t\rho+\operatorname{div}_x(\rho u)=0$$
holds throughout the balanced physical region $\mathcal O_B:=\{(t,x):t\in I,\ x\in\chi_t(B)\}$. The larger set $\mathcal O$ is only the ambient regularity domain; no balance outside $\chi_t(B)$ is assumed or concluded. This is a conditional deduction in the smooth material model and asserts no extension to weak fields or vacuum.

For every $t\in I$, change of variables and material transport satisfy

$$\int_{\chi_t(K)}q(t,x)\,dx=\int_Kq(t,\chi(t,a))J(t,a)\,da,$$

$$\frac{d}{dt}\int_{\chi_t(K)}q(t,x)\,dx=\int_{\chi_t(K)}\bigl(D_tq(t,x)+q(t,x)\theta(t,x)\bigr)\,dx=\int_{\chi_t(K)}\bigl(\partial_tq+\nabla_x\!\cdot(qu)\bigr)\,dx,$$

where $D_tq=\partial_tq+u\cdot\nabla_xq$ and $\nabla_x\!\cdot(qu)=\sum_{i=1}^3\partial_{x_i}(qu_i)$. Define $M_K(t):=\int_{\chi_t(K)}\rho(t,x)\,dx$. The pointwise continuity equation $D_t\rho+\rho\theta=0$, equivalently $\partial_t\rho+\nabla_x\!\cdot(\rho u)=0$, holds on $\Omega$ if and only if $M_K$ is constant on $I$ for every compact Jordan $K\subset U$, and if and only if $\rho(t,\chi(t,a))J(t,a)=\rho(0,\chi(0,a))J(0,a)$ for all $a\in U$ and $t\in I$. This is a mathematical equivalence; it adopts no physical mass-conservation postulate and asserts no weak-field or vacuum extension.

Let $V\subset\mathbb R^3$ be a bounded open set whose boundary is locally, after a rigid coordinate change, the graph of a $C^1$ function, with $V$ lying locally on one side of that graph. Let $U\subset\mathbb R^3$ be open with $\overline V\subset U$. Let $\phi:U\to\phi(U)$ be a bijection onto an open image with $\phi$ and $\phi^{-1}$ both $C^1$, and let $f:\phi(U)\to\mathbb R$ be continuous. A bounded set is Jordan measurable when its indicator is Riemann integrable by the zero-extension convention; a set has content zero when it has finite cube covers of arbitrarily small total volume. Then $V$ and $\phi(V)$ are bounded open sets with locally $C^1$ graph boundaries, their compact closures are Jordan measurable, $\partial V$ and $\phi(\partial V)$ have content zero, and

$$\int_{\phi(V)}f(x)\,dx=\int_{\phi(\overline V)}f(x)\,dx.$$

Thus a balance integral over an open $C^1$ material region agrees with the compact-Jordan integral on its closure after a $C^1$ diffeomorphic motion.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. For $n\ge2$, a bounded $C^1$ domain Omega and $F\in C^1(\overline\Omega;\mathbb R^n)$, $\int_\Omega\operatorname{div}F\,dx=\int_{\partial\Omega}F\cdot\nu\,dS$. Both integrals are finite, with the continuous interior derivative convention and the outward normal on every boundary component.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Here $C^r$ means all coordinate partial derivatives through order $r$ are continuous; write $\Omega_t=\chi_t(B)$ and $u(t,\chi(t,a))=\partial_t\chi(t,a)$. Let $\rho_0\in C^1(\overline B)$ and $\rho\in C^1(\mathcal O)$ be positive mass densities, where $\mathcal O=\{(t,x):t\in I,\ x\in\chi_t(U)\}$. Suppose that for every nonempty bounded open $V$ with compact closure in $B$ and $C^1$ boundary locally a graph with the region on one side and every $t\in I$,
$$\int_{\chi_t(V)}\rho(t,x)\,dx=\int_V\rho_0(a)\,da.$$
Then the pointwise continuity equation
$$\partial_t\rho+\operatorname{div}_x(\rho u)=0$$
holds throughout the balanced physical region $\mathcal O_B:=\{(t,x):t\in I,\ x\in\chi_t(B)\}$. The larger set $\mathcal O$ is only the ambient regularity domain; no balance outside $\chi_t(B)$ is assumed or concluded. This is a conditional deduction in the smooth material model and asserts no extension to weak fields or vacuum.

For every $t\in I$, change of variables and material transport satisfy

$$\int_{\chi_t(K)}q(t,x)\,dx=\int_Kq(t,\chi(t,a))J(t,a)\,da,$$

$$\frac{d}{dt}\int_{\chi_t(K)}q(t,x)\,dx=\int_{\chi_t(K)}\bigl(D_tq(t,x)+q(t,x)\theta(t,x)\bigr)\,dx=\int_{\chi_t(K)}\bigl(\partial_tq+\nabla_x\!\cdot(qu)\bigr)\,dx,$$

where $D_tq=\partial_tq+u\cdot\nabla_xq$ and $\nabla_x\!\cdot(qu)=\sum_{i=1}^3\partial_{x_i}(qu_i)$. Define $M_K(t):=\int_{\chi_t(K)}\rho(t,x)\,dx$. The pointwise continuity equation $D_t\rho+\rho\theta=0$, equivalently $\partial_t\rho+\nabla_x\!\cdot(\rho u)=0$, holds on $\Omega$ if and only if $M_K$ is constant on $I$ for every compact Jordan $K\subset U$, and if and only if $\rho(t,\chi(t,a))J(t,a)=\rho(0,\chi(0,a))J(0,a)$ for all $a\in U$ and $t\in I$. This is a mathematical equivalence; it adopts no physical mass-conservation postulate and asserts no weak-field or vacuum extension.

Let $V\subset\mathbb R^3$ be a bounded open set whose boundary is locally, after a rigid coordinate change, the graph of a $C^1$ function, with $V$ lying locally on one side of that graph. Let $U\subset\mathbb R^3$ be open with $\overline V\subset U$. Let $\phi:U\to\phi(U)$ be a bijection onto an open image with $\phi$ and $\phi^{-1}$ both $C^1$, and let $f:\phi(U)\to\mathbb R$ be continuous. A bounded set is Jordan measurable when its indicator is Riemann integrable by the zero-extension convention; a set has content zero when it has finite cube covers of arbitrarily small total volume. Then $V$ and $\phi(V)$ are bounded open sets with locally $C^1$ graph boundaries, their compact closures are Jordan measurable, $\partial V$ and $\phi(\partial V)$ have content zero, and

$$\int_{\phi(V)}f(x)\,dx=\int_{\phi(\overline V)}f(x)\,dx.$$

Thus a balance integral over an open $C^1$ material region agrees with the compact-Jordan integral on its closure after a $C^1$ diffeomorphic motion.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. For $n\ge2$, a bounded $C^1$ domain Omega and $F\in C^1(\overline\Omega;\mathbb R^n)$, $\int_\Omega\operatorname{div}F\,dx=\int_{\partial\Omega}F\cdot\nu\,dS$. Both integrals are finite, with the continuous interior derivative convention and the outward normal on every boundary component.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

before.claim:
Fix an admissible $V$ and let $K=\overline V$. By [F4], $K$ is compact Jordan and its open-region integrals equal the corresponding closure integrals. Apply [F3] componentwise to $f=\rho u$; the derivative of its material integral is
$$\int_{P_t}\bigl(\partial_t(\rho u)+\operatorname{div}_x(\rho u\otimes u)\bigr)\,dx.$$
Pointwise mass continuity and the product rule give
$$\partial_t(\rho u)+\operatorname{div}_x(\rho u\otimes u)=\rho D_tu.$$

Substitute the first balance in [A1] into step 1.1 and apply [F5] to $\sigma$, using countable choice from [F6]. This yields
$$\int_{P_t}\bigl(\rho D_tu-\rho b-\operatorname{div}_x\sigma\bigr)\,dx=0.$$
The integrand is continuous because $b$ is continuous and the other fields are $C^1$. Every sufficiently small open ball $Q\Subset\Omega_t$ is such a material region: its inverse image under $\chi_t$ is a bounded $C^1$ region compactly contained in $B$. If a component of the continuous integrand were nonzero at a point, it would have a strict fixed sign on a smaller ball and its integral there could not vanish. Thus $\rho D_tu=\rho b+\operatorname{div}_x\sigma$ pointwise on $\mathcal O_B$.

For each component $i$,
$$\partial_t(\rho u_i)+\sum_j\partial_{x_j}(\rho u_i u_j)
=\rho(\partial_tu_i+u\cdot\nabla_xu_i)+u_i\bigl(\partial_t\rho+\operatorname{div}_x(\rho u)\bigr).$$
The last term is zero by [F2]. Substituting step 2.1 and moving $\operatorname{div}\sigma$ to the flux gives the conservative momentum equation.

Apply [F3] to $\rho(x\times u)$ and use $D_tx=u$ and $u\times u=0$. The transport derivative is $\int_{P_t}x\times(\rho D_tu)\,dx$. Substitute step 2.1 and compare with the angular balance in [A1]; applying [F5] to the moment-stress flux gives
$$\int_{P_t}\bigl(\operatorname{div}_x(x\times\sigma)-x\times\operatorname{div}_x\sigma\bigr)\,dx=0.$$
This residual is continuous, so the fixed-sign-ball argument of step 2.1 makes it zero pointwise. With $\epsilon_{ikl}$ the alternating symbol and $M_{ij}=\sum_{k,l}\epsilon_{ikl}x_k\sigma_{lj}$, direct differentiation gives
$$\bigl(\operatorname{div}_x(x\times\sigma)-x\times\operatorname{div}_x\sigma\bigr)_i
=\sum_{j,l}\epsilon_{ijl}\sigma_{lj}.$$
For $i=1,2,3$ these equations are respectively $\sigma_{32}=\sigma_{23}$, $\sigma_{13}=\sigma_{31}$, and $\sigma_{21}=\sigma_{12}$, hence $\sigma=\sigma^{\mathsf T}$.

If $\sigma$ is symmetric, the component identity in step 3.2 gives $\operatorname{div}_x(x\times\sigma)=x\times\operatorname{div}_x\sigma$. The product rule and $u\times u=0$ give
$$\partial_t(\rho x\times u)+\operatorname{div}_x\bigl(\rho(x\times u)\otimes u\bigr)
=x\times\bigl(\partial_t(\rho u)+\operatorname{div}_x(\rho u\otimes u)\bigr).$$
Use step 3.1 and the stress-divergence identity, then integrate over $P_t$. The transport formula [F3] and divergence theorem [F5] recover the angular-momentum integral balance in [A1].

Dot $\rho D_tu=\rho b+\operatorname{div}\sigma$ from step 2.1 with $u$. The component product rule gives $u\cdot\operatorname{div}\sigma=\operatorname{div}(\sigma^{\mathsf T}u)-\sigma:D_xu$. Since $\sigma$ is symmetric, its contraction with the skew part of $D_xu$ is zero, so $\sigma:D_xu=\sigma:D$. Also $D_tk=u\cdot D_tu$. Combining these identities with [F2] yields
$$\partial_t(\rho k)+\operatorname{div}_x(\rho ku-\sigma^{\mathsf T}u)=\rho b\cdot u-\sigma:D.$$

Apply [F3] to $\rho E$ in the total-energy balance [A1]. Rewrite $(\sigma n)\cdot u=(\sigma^{\mathsf T}u)\cdot n$ and apply [F5] to $\sigma^{\mathsf T}u$ and $q$. The integral of the continuous residual
$$\partial_t(\rho E)+\operatorname{div}_x(\rho Eu-\sigma^{\mathsf T}u+q)-\rho b\cdot u-\rho r$$
is zero on every $P_t$. The fixed-sign-ball argument from step 2.1 proves that this residual vanishes pointwise. Conversely, integrating this local equation and using [F3] and [F5] recovers the material total-energy balance.

Subtract the kinetic equation in step 4.2 from the total-energy equation in step 3.3 and use $E=e+k$. The body-work terms cancel and leave $\partial_t(\rho e)+\operatorname{div}_x(\rho eu+q)=\sigma:D+\rho r$. Expanding the mass-transport term using [F2] gives $\rho D_te=\sigma:D-\operatorname{div}_xq+\rho r$. Conversely, adding this internal-energy equation to the kinetic equation in step 4.2 recovers the total-energy equation in step 3.3.

before.quote: A periodic cell with side lengths $L_1,L_2,L_3>0$ metres is the quotient torus $\mathbb T^3_L:=\mathbb R^3/(L_1\mathbb Z\times L_2\mathbb Z\times L_3\mathbb Z)$. Periodicity identifies opposite faces by the corresponding translations and requires equality of the fields and of each derivative trace required by the selected evolution problem. Paired fluxes then cancel in cell integrals. These identified faces are not physical walls.

Adopt the total-energy balance and entropy inequality

$$\frac{d}{dt}\int_{\chi_t(V)}\rho\left(e+\frac{|u|^2}{2}\right)\,dx=\int_{\chi_t(V)}\rho b\cdot u\,dx+\int_{\partial\chi_t(V)}t(t,x,n)\cdot u\,dS-\int_{\partial\chi_t(V)}q\cdot n\,dS+\int_{\chi_t(V)}\rho r\,dx,$$

$$\frac{d}{dt}\int_{\chi_t(V)}\rho s\,dx\ge-\int_{\partial\chi_t(V)}\frac{q}{T}\cdot n\,dS+\int_{\chi_t(V)}\frac{\rho r}{T}\,dx.$$

Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an open interval containing $0$, let $B\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ be a nonempty bounded open reference region with $C^1$ boundary (locally a $C^1$ graph with the region on one side), and let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ be an open neighborhood of $\overline B$. Let $\chi\in C^2(I\times U;\mathbb R^3)$ be a motion with orientation-preserving diffeomorphic time slices (bijections onto open images with $C^2$ inverses and positive Jacobian determinant) and $\chi(0,a)=a$. Here $C^r$ means all coordinate partial derivatives through order $r$ are continuous. Set $\Omega_t=\chi_t(B)$ and $\mathcal O=\{(t,x):t\in I,\ x\in\chi_t(U)\}$. Use SI units in a classical Cartesian inertial frame. Let $\rho_0\in C^1(\overline B)$ and $\rho:\mathcal O\to(0,\infty)$ be positive densities, and let $u:\mathcal O\to\mathbb R^3$, $e:\mathcal O\to\mathbb R$, $q:\mathcal O\to\mathbb R^3$, and $\sigma:\mathcal O\to\mathbb R^{3\times3}$ be $C^1$; let $b:\mathcal O\to\mathbb R^3$ and $r:\mathcal O\to\mathbb R$ be continuous. Their units are respectively kilograms per cubic metre, metres per second, joules per kilogram, watts per square metre, pascals, metres per second squared, and watts per kilogram. Define $k:=|u|^2/2$, $E:=e+k$, $D_xu=(\partial_{x_j}u_i)_{ij}$, $D:=(D_xu+(D_xu)^{\mathsf T})/2$, $D_t:=\partial_t+u\cdot\nabla_x$, and $A:B:=\sum_{i,j}A_{ij}B_{ij}$. Use rowwise divergence $(\operatorname{div}\sigma)_i=\sum_j\partial_{x_j}\sigma_{ij}$ and vector divergence $\operatorname{div}q=\sum_j\partial_{x_j}q_j$. For every nonempty bounded open $V$ whose closure is compact in $B$ and whose $C^1$ boundary is locally a graph with the region on one side, put $P_t=\chi_t(V)$ and let $n$ be its outward Euclidean unit normal. Use Euclidean surface measure $dS$ with chart density $\sqrt{\det(DY^{\mathsf T}DY)}$.

Adopt, on each such material region,

$$\int_{P_t}\rho\,dx=\int_V\rho_0\,da,\qquad \frac{d}{dt}\int_{P_t}\rho u\,dx=\int_{P_t}\rho b\,dx+\int_{\partial P_t}\sigma n\,dS,$$

$$\frac{d}{dt}\int_{P_t}x\times\rho u\,dx=\int_{P_t}x\times\rho b\,dx+\int_{\partial P_t}x\times\sigma n\,dS,$$

$$\frac{d}{dt}\int_{P_t}\rho E\,dx=\int_{P_t}(\rho b\cdot u+\rho r)\,dx+\int_{\partial P_t}\bigl(u\cdot\sigma n-q\cdot n\bigr)\,dS.$$

The angular-momentum balance is about a fixed inertial origin; assume no surface couples or intrinsic spin. Assume also the Axiom of Choice. On the balanced physical region $\mathcal O_B:=\{(t,x):t\in I,\ x\in\Omega_t\}$, angular momentum gives $\sigma=\sigma^{\mathsf T}$, and the local total-energy balance is

$$\partial_t(\rho E)+\operatorname{div}(\rho E u-\sigma^{\mathsf T}u+q)=\rho b\cdot u+\rho r.$$

It splits into the kinetic and internal-energy balances

$$\partial_t(\rho k)+\operatorname{div}(\rho k u-\sigma^{\mathsf T}u)=\rho b\cdot u-\sigma:D,$$

$$\rho D_t e=\sigma:D-\operatorname{div}q+\rho r.$$

Thus the boundary power flux is $-\sigma^{\mathsf T}u$ and the outward heat flux is $q$. If additionally $b=-\nabla_x\Phi$ for a time-independent $C^1$ scalar potential $\Phi$ defined on an open spatial set containing every $\Omega_t$, measured in joules per kilogram, and $r=0$, then

$$\partial_t\bigl(\rho(E+\Phi)\bigr)+\operatorname{div}\bigl(\rho(E+\Phi)u-\sigma^{\mathsf T}u+q\bigr)=0.$$

Consequently $\int_C\rho(E+\Phi)\,dx$ is constant on any bounded fixed $C^1$ region $C$ with closure contained in the fluid region throughout $I$, with no-slip $u=0$ and insulation $q\cdot n=0$, or on a periodic cell with side lengths $L_j>0$ metres and opposite faces identified by translations when all fields and $\Phi$ are periodic. All local equations above are asserted on $\mathcal O_B$; the larger $\mathcal O$ supplies ambient regularity only. These are deductions for any solution with the stated regularity; the theorem does not assert that a solution exists.

**Fixed-size callback mode.** Inputs are a finite integer $N\ge2$, the specified input law $\mu$ and exact/numerical observable interface, an IID sampler for $\mu$, and a solver callback with a supplied finite computational budget for each invocation. The callback is total, with a measurable success set and measurable successful outputs: for every input $\theta$ it returns either `solver-failed` or a numerical state $s_h(\theta)$ with finite real observable $q_h(\theta)=J_h(s_h(\theta))$, together with a finite $b(\theta)\ge0$ and its supplied pointwise certificate $|Y(\theta)-q_h(\theta)|\le b(\theta)$. A stated failure result is allowed when the finite budget is exhausted; the procedure asserts no universal numerical solver termination theorem.

Draw $\theta_1,\ldots,\theta_N$ independently with law $\mu$ and call the callback exactly once on each draw, including the draws after any earlier failure. If any call fails, return `incomplete` with the failed indices and the collected outputs, and no IID mean/error certificate for $\mu$. Never delete, replace or resample failed cases. If all calls succeed with finite arithmetic values, set
$$\bar q_h=N^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^Nq_i,\qquad s_N^2=(N-1)^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^N(q_i-\bar q_h)^2,\qquad \widehat{se}_N=s_N/\sqrt N,\qquad \bar b=N^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^Nb_i.$$
Return $N,\bar q_h,s_N^2,\widehat{se}_N,\bar b$ and `complete`; if $s_N^2=0$, also return `zero-sample-variance`. This diagnostic asserts neither a deterministic population nor zero estimation error. The sample mean of certificates $\bar b$ is a diagnostic, not a rigorous upper bound on $\mathbb E b$. The plug-in standard error has only the moment/asymptotic interpretation supplied by the sampling theorem, not an exact confidence guarantee. If callback failure has positive $\mu$-probability, conditioning on `complete` changes the input law and does not certify IID sampling of the original $\mu$.

**Optional certified-budget mode.** This retains a separate finite-sample guarantee when externally proved global bounds are available. Inputs are the numerical output law $Y_h$, a total oracle returning independent finite real samples of that law, finite $\epsilon_b,V_h\ge0$, $\epsilon_s>0$, $\delta\in(0,1)$, and a certificate that $Y\in L^1$, $Y_h\in L^2$, $|\mathbb E Y_h-\mathbb E Y|\le\epsilon_b$, $\operatorname{Var}(Y_h)\le V_h$, and the oracle has that IID law. The algorithm does not validate a supplied mathematical certificate. Without the certificate or oracle, return `not-certified`; for an invalid numeric range or nonfinite input, return `invalid-input`. Otherwise set
$$N:=\max\{1,\lceil V_h/(\delta\epsilon_s^2)\rceil\}.$$
Request exactly $N$ samples and return `conditional-budget`, $N$, their mean $\widehat\theta_{h,N}$, tolerance $\epsilon_b+\epsilon_s$, failure bound $\delta$ and RMS upper bound $\sqrt{V_h/N+\epsilon_b^2}$, conditional on the certificate. If an oracle invocation instead fails its total-return contract, return `incomplete` and no guarantee. This mode permits $N=1$ but then supplies no sample variance or plug-in standard error. When implemented through the callback mode, its certificate additionally requires callback success $\mu$-almost surely; the probability guarantee is not conditional on deleting failed inputs.

Neither mode infers a bias/variance certificate from a sample or mesh trend. Numerical bias, physical model discrepancy and measurement uncertainty are different quantities; the latter two are absent unless separately quantified. Both tolerance allocations use the declared observable unit, variance bounds use its square and $\delta$ is dimensionless. The operation counts concern the specified finite callback/oracle contract, not uncontrolled floating-point error.

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ be a probability space and let $Y=J(S)$ and $Y_h=J_h(S_h)$ be a real random fluid observable and its numerical approximation as defined by the random-fluid-observable definition. Assume $Y\in L^1(\mathbb P)$ and $Y_h\in L^2(\mathbb P)$. Set $\theta:=\mathbb E[Y]$, $\theta_h:=\mathbb E[Y_h]$, $b_h:=\theta_h-\theta$, and $\sigma_h^2:=\operatorname{Var}(Y_h)$. For an integer $n\ge1$, let $Y_{h,1},\ldots,Y_{h,n}$ be independent random variables with the law of $Y_h$, on a sampling probability space $(\Omega_s,\mathcal F_s,\mathbb P_s)$, and define $\bar Y_{h,n}:=n^{-1}\sum_{j=1}^nY_{h,j}$. Then

$$\mathbb E_s[(\bar Y_{h,n}-\theta)^2]=\frac{\sigma_h^2}{n}+b_h^2.$$

If finite nonnegative bounds $B_h,V_h$ satisfy $|b_h|\le B_h$ and $\sigma_h^2\le V_h$, and $\epsilon_b\ge B_h$ and $\epsilon_s>0$, then

$$\mathbb P_s\bigl(|\bar Y_{h,n}-\theta|>\epsilon_b+\epsilon_s\bigr)\le\frac{V_h}{n\epsilon_s^2}.$$

The probability is over IID sampling. The bias bound is an external premise, not an output inferred from the sample; no normal approximation or pointwise error guarantee is asserted. If the observable is dimensional, $B_h,\epsilon_b,\epsilon_s$ have its unit, $V_h$ has the squared unit, and the formulas use one consistent output unit.

**Mean certificates and callback qualification.** If a measurable supplied bound $b\ge0$ satisfies $|Y-Y_h|\le b$ almost surely and $\mathbb E b<\infty$, then $|b_h|\le\mathbb E b$. More generally, for a normed state space and an $L$-Lipschitz scalar observable $J$, supplied measurable states with integrable norm difference satisfy $|\mathbb E J(S_h)-\mathbb E J(S)|\le L\mathbb E\|S_h-S\|$, provided the two scalar means exist. These are bounds on mean bias, not pointwise accuracy guarantees. An empirical average of the $b$ values alone is no deterministic upper bound on $\mathbb E b$; a supplied deterministic envelope $b\le B$ does imply $|b_h|\le B$. For a solver callback, assume its success set and successful output/certificate maps are measurable. The IID formulas apply to complete callback output with the original input law only when the callback succeeds almost surely and the stated moments hold. If failure has positive probability, the formulas do not apply to the original input law merely by retaining or conditioning on successful cases.

**Asymptotic sampling branch.** For an infinite IID output sequence, finite $\mathbb E Y_h^2$ implies $s_n^2\to\sigma_h^2$ almost surely, where $s_n^2=(n-1)^{-1}\sum_{j=1}^n(Y_{h,j}-\bar Y_{h,n})^2$ for $n\ge2$. If additionally AC and $\sigma_h^2>0$ are assumed, then $\sqrt n(\bar Y_{h,n}-\theta_h)\Rightarrow N(0,\sigma_h^2)$ and $\sqrt n(\bar Y_{h,n}-\theta_h)/s_n\Rightarrow N(0,1)$, assigning the last quotient zero where $s_n=0$. Consequently, for a supplied $z>0$ and $\alpha\in(0,1)$ such that a standard normal variable $Z$ satisfies $\mathbb P(|Z|\le z)=1-\alpha$, and any deterministic $B\ge|b_h|$,
$$\liminf_{n\to\infty}\mathbb P_s\bigl(|\bar Y_{h,n}-\theta|\le B+z s_n/\sqrt n\bigr)\ge1-\alpha.$$
This interval assertion is asymptotic, unlike the earlier finite-sample inequality. The sample-based $\bar b$ cannot replace deterministic $B$ without another proved bound. No time-series mixing CLT is substituted for the IID law here; dependent sensors require their actual separate long-run variance and assumptions.

Let $X,Y$ be integrable real or complex random variables on one probability
space.

1. For scalars $a,b$,
   $$\mathbb E[aX+bY]=a\,\mathbb E[X]+b\,\mathbb E[Y].$$
2. If $X$ and $Y$ are real-valued and $X\le Y$ almost surely, then
   $$\mathbb E[X]\le\mathbb E[Y].$$
3. $$|\mathbb E[X]|\le\mathbb E[|X|].$$

Let $X:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S,\Sigma)$ be a random element, let
$\mathbb P_X$ be its law, and let $g:(S,\Sigma)\to\mathbb R$ or
$g:(S,\Sigma)\to\mathbb C$ be measurable.

1. If $g\ge0$, then
   $$\mathbb E[g(X)]=\int_S g\,d\mathbb P_X.$$
2. If $g(X)$ is integrable, then $g$ is integrable with respect to
   $\mathbb P_X$ and the same formula holds:
   $$\mathbb E[g(X)]=\int_S g\,d\mathbb P_X.$$

Let $X_i:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S_i,\Sigma_i)$ be random elements on a
common probability space. For each $i$, write

$$\sigma(X_i):=\{X_i^{-1}(B):B\in\Sigma_i\}\subseteq\mathcal F.$$

The family $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ is **independent** when the sigma-algebras
$(\sigma(X_i))_{i\in I}$ are independent in the sense of
Independent sigma-algebras and independent events.

When $\Sigma_i$ is a Borel sigma-algebra, this agrees with the notation
$\sigma(X_i)$ from The sigma-algebra generated by a function.

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ be a probability space.

A family $(\mathcal F_i)_{i\in I}$ of sub-sigma-algebras of $\mathcal F$ is
**independent** when it is independent as a family of event classes in the
sense of Independent families of event classes.

A family $(A_i)_{i\in I}$ of events is **independent** when the singleton event
classes $\bigl(\{A_i\}\bigr)_{i\in I}$ are independent. Equivalently, for every
finite choice of distinct indices $i_0,\dots,i_{n-1}$,

$$\mathbb P\left(\bigcap_{k<n}A_{i_k}\right)=\prod_{k<n}\mathbb P(A_{i_k}).$$

For two events this reduces to the familiar identity
$\mathbb P(A\cap B)=\mathbb P(A)\mathbb P(B)$.

original_exact_quote_rows.quote:
Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ be a probability space.

A family $(\mathcal F_i)_{i\in I}$ of sub-sigma-algebras of $\mathcal F$ is
**independent** when it is independent as a family of event classes in the
sense of Independent families of event classes.

A family $(A_i)_{i\in I}$ of events is **independent** when the singleton event
classes $\bigl(\{A_i\}\bigr)_{i\in I}$ are independent. Equivalently, for every
finite choice of distinct indices $i_0,\dots,i_{n-1}$,

$$\mathbb P\left(\bigcap_{k<n}A_{i_k}\right)=\prod_{k<n}\mathbb P(A_{i_k}).$$

For two events this reduces to the familiar identity
$\mathbb P(A\cap B)=\mathbb P(A)\mathbb P(B)$.

after.exact_statement:
Let $(\Omega,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space and $X$ a real or complex
Banach space. A function $f:\Omega\to X$ is **strongly measurable** (or
**Bochner measurable**) if there are measurable $X$-valued simple functions
$s_n$ and a measurable null set $N$ such that

$$\lim_{n\to\infty}\|s_n(\omega)-f(\omega)\|=0$$

for every $\omega\in\Omega\setminus N$.

This is a norm-convergence condition. It is not, by definition, merely Borel
measurability of $f$ or measurability of every scalar function $x^*\circ f$.
Changing $f$ on a null set preserves strong measurability: enlarge $N$ by that
null set and retain the same approximants.

before.exact_statement:
Let $d\ge1$ be an integer and let $(D,\mathcal D,\lambda)$ be a finite measure space with $0<\lambda(D)<\infty$, interpreted as a spatial region with volume measure $\lambda$. Let $H:=L^2(D,\lambda;\mathbb R^d)$ consist of almost-everywhere equivalence classes of measurable vector fields $v$ with $\int_D|v(x)|^2\,d\lambda(x)<\infty$, where $|\cdot|$ is the Euclidean norm. Give $H$ the norm $\|v\|_H:=(\int_D|v(x)|^2\,d\lambda(x))^{1/2}$ and its norm topology; this is the finite direct sum of the scalar $L^2$ norms. Write $\mathcal B(H)$ for the sigma-algebra generated by the norm-open subsets of $H$. A finite-second-moment random velocity law is a probability measure $\mu$ on $(H,\mathcal B(H))$ such that
$$\int_H \|v\|_H^2\,d\mu(v)<\infty.$$
For a sensor weight $\psi\in H$, define the ideal linear sensor and its centered observable by
$$S_\psi(v):=\int_D v(x)\cdot\psi(x)\,d\lambda(x),\qquad
f_\psi(v):=S_\psi(v)-\int_H S_\psi(w)\,d\mu(w).$$
The sensor reads a weighted spatial average; it does not represent a point evaluation. When $v$ is assigned SI velocity units of metres per second and $\lambda$ is volume in $\mathrm m^d$, assigning $\psi$ units $\mathrm m^{-d}$ makes $S_\psi(v)$ a velocity. Other weight units multiply the sensor units by the corresponding factor. The centered observable is dimensionally the same as the sensor reading.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space, let $p,q\in[1,\infty]$ be
conjugate exponents, and let $f,g$ be measurable real-valued functions.

1. If $1\le p<\infty$ and $q<\infty$ with $f\in\mathcal L^p(\mu)$ and
   $g\in\mathcal L^q(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_p\|g\|_q.$$
2. If $p=1$ and $q=\infty$ with $f\in\mathcal L^1(\mu)$ and
   $g\in L^\infty(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_1\|g\|_\infty.$$
3. If $p=\infty$ and $q=1$ with $f\in L^\infty(\mu)$ and
   $g\in\mathcal L^1(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_\infty\|g\|_1.$$

In every case the right-hand side is finite, so $fg$ is integrable.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space, let $p,q\in[1,\infty]$ be
conjugate exponents, and let $f,g$ be measurable real-valued functions.

1. If $1\le p<\infty$ and $q<\infty$ with $f\in\mathcal L^p(\mu)$ and
   $g\in\mathcal L^q(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_p\|g\|_q.$$
2. If $p=1$ and $q=\infty$ with $f\in\mathcal L^1(\mu)$ and
   $g\in L^\infty(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_1\|g\|_\infty.$$
3. If $p=\infty$ and $q=1$ with $f\in L^\infty(\mu)$ and
   $g\in\mathcal L^1(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_\infty\|g\|_1.$$

In every case the right-hand side is finite, so $fg$ is integrable.

after.exact_statement:
Let $(\Omega,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space and $X$ a real or complex
Banach space. A function $f:\Omega\to X$ is **strongly measurable** (or
**Bochner measurable**) if there are measurable $X$-valued simple functions
$s_n$ and a measurable null set $N$ such that

$$\lim_{n\to\infty}\|s_n(\omega)-f(\omega)\|=0$$

for every $\omega\in\Omega\setminus N$.

This is a norm-convergence condition. It is not, by definition, merely Borel
measurability of $f$ or measurability of every scalar function $x^*\circ f$.
Changing $f$ on a null set preserves strong measurability: enlarge $N$ by that
null set and retain the same approximants.

before.exact_statement:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.
